Asked about the plan to seize Guan Yu, he said 「得之。」, and of Guan Yu's flight he said 「雖去不免。」, naming the next noon as the time [23]. Sun Quan made him Cavalry Commandant and concurrently Director of the Grand Astrologer (騎都尉，領太史令), but Wu Fan kept the essential part of his art from Sun Quan, 「權由是恨之」; when the enfeoffment as Marquis of the Pavilion was about to be issued, Sun Quan, angry that he begrudged him his art, erased his name [20]. 「黃武五年，範病卒。」[22] Pei Songzhi's commentary quotes the *Wulu*: Wu Fan foreknew the day of his own death and told Sun Quan that on a certain day he would lose his "army mentor," and it happened as he said; Pei Songzhi notes that when Wu Fan died Sun Quan had not yet taken the imperial title, so the address 「陛下」 there is wrong [21].

**3. Yan Xiang 嚴象 — courtesy name Wenze (Pei commentary)**

Pei Songzhi's commentary to the Xun Yu biography quotes the *Sanfu Juelu*: 「象字文則，京兆人。少聦博，有膽智。」[4]
(Yan Xiang, courtesy name Wenze, a man of Jingzhao; as a youth clever and broad in learning, with courage and resourcefulness.)

The same note says he went to Yang province as Army-Supervising Imperial Secretary-Middle Assistant to attack Yuan Shu; when Yuan Shu died of illness he was made Inspector of Yang province, and 「建安五年，爲孫策廬江太守李術所殺，時年三十八。」[4] The main text of the same biography gives the context: Cao Cao considered Xun Yu a judge of men and all his recommendations were fit for office, 「唯嚴象爲楊州，韋康爲涼州，後敗亡。」[42] Liu Fu's biography likewise records: 「後孫策所置廬江太守李述攻殺揚州刺史嚴象」[31] — note that here the killer's name is written Li Shu 李述, whereas the *Sanfu Juelu* quoted by Pei writes Li Shu 李術; I give both as the sources have them.

**4. The unnamed messenger**

Pei Songzhi's commentary on Gongsun Zan quotes the *Dianlue*: 「瓚遣行人文則齎書告子續曰」[8] — Gongsun Zan sent a certain Wenze with a letter to his son Gongsun Xu. No surname is given for him there, and I found no separate record identifying him, so he should not be merged with the three above.

**Summary of the evidence**

Yu Jin [3][11][12][16]; Wu Fan [1][20][21][22][23]; Yan Xiang [4] with the main texts at [31] and [42]; the messenger Wenze [8]. Only these three men are explicitly given the courtesy name 文則 in the material; the fourth "Wenze" is an envoy whose surname is not recorded. (By contrast, Su Ze 蘇則 is recorded with the courtesy name Wenshi 文師 [2].)

q: Who were the 'Eight Masters of Wu', and what was each of them famous for?
reply:
## The "Eight Masters of Wu" (八絕)

The term you're asking about corresponds to what the *Sanguozhi* calls the **八絕** ("the Eight Exquisites"), a list of eight persons of Wu, each famous for one special skill. The list comes from **Pei Songzhi's commentary quoting the *Wulu* (吳錄)**:

> 「皇象字休明，廣陵江都人。幼工書。」[1]「嚴武字子卿，衞尉畯再從子也，圍棊莫與爲輩。」[1]「宋壽占夢，十不失一。」[1]「曹不興善畫」[1]「孤城鄭嫗能相人，及範、惇、達八人，世皆稱妙，謂之八絕云。」[1]

("Huang Xiang, courtesy name Xiuming, of Jiangdu in Guangling, was skilled at calligraphy from youth. Yan Wu, courtesy name Ziqing, a second cousin of the Commandant of the Guards Yan Jun, had no peer at *weiqi*. Song Shou interpreted dreams, and did not miss once in ten. Cao Buxing was good at painting. Zheng Yu of Gucheng could read faces — together with [Wu] Fan, [Liu] Dun, and [Zhao] Da, eight persons in all, whom the world all called marvelous, calling them the Eight Exquisites.")

### The eight and what each was famous for

**1. Wu Fan 吳範 (Z. Wenze 文則), of Shangyu, Kuaiji** — divination through calendrical reckoning and "wind and qi" (風氣), reading weather and omens to foretell events.
- 「吳範字文則，會稽上虞人也。以治曆數知風氣聞於郡中。」[26]
- He served Sun Quan and foretold disasters and auspicious signs: 「每有災祥，輒推數言狀。其術多效，遂以顯名。」[26]
- Example: 「以風氣言之，彼以貌來，其實有謀，宜爲之備。」[28] — and the source adds 「其占驗明審如此。」[28]
- Sun Quan made him Cavalry Commandant (騎都尉) and concurrent Grand Astrologer (太史令): 「權以範爲騎都尉，領太史令」[29]
- 「黃武五年，範病卒。」[27]

**2. Liu Dun 劉惇 (Z. Ziren 子仁), of Pingyuan** — master of astrology and divination, especially the *Taiyi* (太乙) method.
- 「劉惇字子仁，平原人也。」[35] and 「以明天官達占數顯於南土。每有水旱寇賊，皆先時處期，無不中者。」[35] — he foretold floods, droughts and banditry, all with accurate dates.
- 「惇於諸術皆善，尤明太乙，皆能推演其事，窮盡要妙，著書百餘篇。」[14] — good at all the arts, especially Taiyi, and wrote over a hundred *pian* of books.
- 「建安中，孫權在豫章，時有星變」[36] — he said the disaster would be in Danyang, and 「是時邊鴻作亂，卒如惇言。」[36]

**3. Zhao Da 趙達, of Henan** — the "Nine Palaces, One Calculation" (九宮一算) art, a prodigy at instant reckoning and finding hidden things.
- 「趙達，河南人也。少從漢侍中單甫受學，用思精密。」[22]
- 「治九宮一算之術，究其微旨，是以能應機立成。對問若神，至計飛蝗，射隱伏，無不中效。」[22]
- His feats: he told the number of beans scattered on a mat — 「達使其人取小豆數斗，播之席上，立處其數，驗覆果信。」[22] — and located a hidden cask of wine and venison by arranging chopsticks: 「達因取盤中隻箸，再三從橫之，乃言：『卿東壁下有美酒一斛，又有鹿肉三斤，何以辭無？』」[22]
- 「又有書簡上作千萬數，著空倉中封之，令達算之。達處如數。」[22]
- Sun Quan repeatedly had him forecast campaigns, but he never revealed his method: 「初，孫權行師征伐，每令達有所推步，皆如其言。權問其法，達終不語，由此見薄，祿位不至。」[24]

**4. Huang Xiang 皇象 (Z. Xiuming 休明), of Jiangdu, Guangling** — **calligraphy**, the best of his day.
- 「皇象字休明，廣陵江都人。幼工書。」[1]
- 「象斟酌其間，甚得其妙，中國善書者不能及也。」[1] — he took the middle course between the two other noted calligraphers of the time, Zhang Zibing and Chen Liangfu, and even the best calligraphers of the Central Plain could not match him.

**5. Yan Wu 嚴武 (Z. Ziqing 子卿)** — **weiqi (圍棋)**, unmatched at the game.
- 「嚴武字子卿，衞尉畯再從子也，圍棊莫與爲輩。」[1] — he was a second cousin (再從子) of the Commandant of the Guards Yan Jun, and no one was his peer at *weiqi*.

**6. Song Shou 宋壽** — **dream interpretation (占夢)**.
- 「宋壽占夢，十不失一。」[1] — he interpreted dreams and was wrong only once in ten times.

**7. Cao Buxing 曹不興** — **painting**.
- 「曹不興善畫，權使畫屏风，誤落筆點素，因就以作蠅。既進御，權以爲生蠅，舉手彈之。」[1] — Sun Quan had him paint a screen; a stray drop of ink on the white silk became a fly, and when it was presented, Sun Quan took it for a live fly and flicked at it with his hand.

**8. Zheng Yu 鄭嫗 of Gucheng** — **physiognomy (相人)**, reading a person's face and fortune.
- 「孤城鄭嫗能相人。」[1]

### Note on the list

The *Wulu* passage enumerates them as Yan Wu, Song Shou, Cao Buxing, Zheng Yu, together with Wu Fan, Liu Dun and Zhao Da — 「及範、惇、達八人」[1], which matches the eight above. Chen Shou's own closing appraisal praises only the three diviners, not the whole eight:

> 「評曰：三子各於其術精矣，其用思妙矣，然君子等役心神，宜於大者遠者，是以有識之士，舍彼而取此也。」[38]

("The three men each were skilled in their art, and their use of mind was ingenious; but a gentleman, who expends his mind equally, should apply it to great and far-reaching things, and so men of discernment forsake the one and take the other.")

### Inferences

**据此推断 (1):** The evidence is that the list appears in Pei Songzhi's note quoting the *Wulu*, with the words 「世皆稱妙，謂之八絕云」[1], while Chen Shou's own appraisal names only 「三子」 and praises them as diviners [38]. From these two facts we may infer that "八絕" was a current popular label of the time recorded by the *Wulu* and preserved by Pei Songzhi, and that in the material retrieved here the term appears only in that note, not in Chen Shou's own text.

**据此推断 (2):** After the *Wulu* list, Pei Songzhi also quotes the *Jinyangqiu*: 「吳有葛衡字思真，明達天官，能爲機巧，作渾天，使地居于中，以機動之，天轉而地止，以上應晷度。」[1] Since the *Wulu* names eight persons individually and Ge Heng is not among them, we may infer that Ge Heng, though another Wu technical marvel, is not counted among the eight.

- 「象斟酌其間，甚得其妙，中國善書者不能及也。」[1] — he took the middle course between the two other noted calligraphers of the time, Zhang Zibing and Chen Liangfu, and even the best calligraphers of the Central Plain could not match him.

**5. Yan Wu 嚴武 (Z. Ziqing 子卿)** — **weiqi (圍棋)**, unmatched at the game.
- 「嚴武字子卿，衞尉畯再從子也，圍棊莫與爲輩。」[1] — he was a second cousin (再從子) of the Commandant of the Guards Yan Jun, and no one was his peer at *weiqi*.

**6. Song Shou 宋壽** — **dream interpretation (占夢)**.
- 「宋壽占夢，十不失一。」[1] — he interpreted dreams and was wrong only once in ten times.

**7. Cao Buxing 曹不興** — **painting**.
- 「曹不興善畫，權使畫屏风，誤落筆點素，因就以作蠅。既進御，權以爲生蠅，舉手彈之。」[1] — Sun Quan had him paint a screen; a stray drop of ink on the white silk became a fly, and when it was presented, Sun Quan took it for a live fly and flicked at it with his hand.

**8. Zheng Yu 鄭嫗 of Gucheng** — **physiognomy (相人)**, reading a person's face and fortune.
- 「孤城鄭嫗能相人。」[1]

### Note on the list

The *Wulu* passage enumerates them as Yan Wu, Song Shou, Cao Buxing, Zheng Yu, together with Wu Fan, Liu Dun and Zhao Da — 「及範、惇、達八人」[1], which matches the eight above. Chen Shou's own closing appraisal praises only the three diviners, not the whole eight:

> 「評曰：三子各於其術精矣，其用思妙矣，然君子等役心神，宜於大者遠者，是以有識之士，舍彼而取此也。」[38]

("The three men each were skilled in their art, and their use of mind was ingenious; but a gentleman, who expends his mind equally, should apply it to great and far-reaching things, and so men of discernment forsake the one and take the other.")

### Inferences

**据此推断 (1):** The evidence is that the list appears in Pei Songzhi's note quoting the *Wulu*, with the words 「世皆稱妙，謂之八絕云」[1], while Chen Shou's own appraisal names only 「三子」 and praises them as diviners [38]. From these two facts we may infer that "八絕" was a current popular label of the time recorded by the *Wulu* and preserved by Pei Songzhi, and that in the material retrieved here the term appears only in that note, not in Chen Shou's own text.

**据此推断 (2):** After the *Wulu* list, Pei Songzhi also quotes the *Jinyangqiu*: 「吳有葛衡字思真，明達天官，能爲機巧，作渾天，使地居于中，以機動之，天轉而地止，以上應晷度。」[1] Since the *Wulu* names eight persons individually and Ge Heng is not among them, we may infer that Ge Heng, though another Wu technical marvel, is not counted among the eight.

q: The Weilüe mentions a man called 'Nukou' ('Slave Bandit'). Who was he, and which other generals' alternative names are given in the same passage?
reply:
**Answer**

"Nukou" (奴寇) is an alternative name of **Zang Ba (臧霸)**, the general whose biography this passage annotates. The information comes from Pei Songzhi's annotation to Zang Ba's biography in the *Sanguozhi*, where he quotes the *Weilüe* (《魏略》):

> 「《魏略》曰：霸一名奴寇。孫觀名嬰子。吳敦名黯奴。尹禮名盧兒。」[1]

("The *Weilüe* says: Ba had the other name Nukou. Sun Guan's name was Yingzi. Wu Dun's name was Anu. Yin Li's name was Lu'er.")

So in the same passage, besides Zang Ba (奴寇), three other men are given alternative names:

| Person | Alternative name given |
|---|---|
| **Zang Ba** 臧霸 | 奴寇 (Nukou) |
| **Sun Guan** 孫觀 | 嬰子 (Yingzi) |
| **Wu Dun** 吳敦 | 黯奴 (Anu) |
| **Yin Li** 尹禮 | 盧兒 (Lu'er) |

**Notes on the sources**

- This block is Pei Songzhi's annotation, and the material is explicitly credited to the *Weilüe*: 「《魏略》曰」[1] — so it should be cited as Pei's annotation quoting the *Weilüe*, not as Chen Shou's own text.
- The passage gives these four only as names/alternative names; it does not state their offices or ranks there. Of the four, the *Sanguozhi* index shows that Zang Ba and Sun Guan each have their own biography (the one this annotation belongs to, and the next), whereas Wu Dun and Yin Li have no separate biography, appearing only within other passages.

**Context of the passage**

The same *Weilüe* quotation continues past the names into events, so it is worth noting what it actually says. It records that in the twenty-fourth year of Jian'an (建安二十四年), Zang Ba sent a detached force to station at Luo (洛); that on the occasion of the death of 太祖, Zang Ba's troops and the Qingzhou soldiers drummed and left on their own initiative:

> 「建安二十四年，霸遣別軍在洛。會太祖崩，霸所部及青州兵，以為天下將亂，皆鳴鼓擅去。」[1]

It then records that after Emperor Wen (文帝) took the throne, he made Cao Xiu commander of Qing and Xu:

> 「文帝即位，以曹休都督青、徐」[1]

and that Zang Ba told Cao Xiu that if given ten thousand foot and horse he could sweep across the Jiangbiao:

> 「若假霸步騎萬人，必能橫行江表。」[1]

Cao Xiu reported this to the emperor: 「休言之於帝」[1], and the emperor, suspicious, took away Zang Ba's troops during an eastern tour:

> 「遂東巡，因霸來朝而奪其兵。」[1]

The naming sentence and this narrative are part of one continuous *Weilüe* quotation, which is why the four alternative names are given together.

q: Who was the Marquis of Panyu, and for what achievement was he given that title?
reply:
## Conclusion

The Marquis of Panyu (番禺侯) was **Lü Dai (吕岱)**, style **Dinggong (定公)**, a general of Wu. The title was granted to him in connection with his campaign in Jiao Province against **Shi Hui (士徽)** and Shi Hui's generals.

## Evidence

Lü Dai's style and the title are confirmed by his biography: 「呂岱字定公，廣陵海陵人也」[4], and the index of names in the text lists him with the appellation 番禺侯.

After the Administrator of Jiaozhi, **Shi Xie (士燮)**, died, Sun Quan acted as follows: 「權以燮子徽為安遠將軍，領九真太守，以校尉陳時代燮。」[1] — Sun Quan appointed Shi Xie's son Shi Hui as General Who Brings Peace to Distant Lands, to oversee Jiuzhen as Administrator, and sent Colonel Chen Shi to replace Shi Xie. Shi Hui refused the order and raised troops at the seaport to resist. Lü Dai memorialized for permission to punish him and crossed the sea: 「岱於是上疏請討徽罪，督兵三千人晨夜浮海。」[1]

Shi Hui, caught off guard, came out to meet him: 「即率兄弟六人肉袒迎岱。岱皆斬送其首」[1] — Shi Hui led his six brothers, baring their shoulders, to welcome Lü Dai; Lü Dai had them all beheaded and sent the heads away. Shi Hui's senior generals then attacked Lü Dai, and it is at this point that the enfeoffment is recorded:

「徽大將甘醴，桓治等率吏民攻岱，岱奮擊大破之，進封番禺侯。」[1]

*"Shi Hui's senior generals Gan Li and Huan Zhi and others led officials and commoners to attack Lü Dai; Lü Dai fought back fiercely and routed them, and was advanced in enfeoffment as Marquis of Panyu."*

The same episode appears in Shi Xie's biography [3], which records that Lü Dai had received the edict to execute Shi Hui: 「而呂岱被詔誅徽」[3]. There, Shi Yi's son Kuang, a General of the Household who had old ties with Lü Dai, was first sent to persuade Shi Hui to submit and confess his guilt; after the brothers came out baring their shoulders, Lü Dai read the edict aloud, and 「即皆伏誅，傳首詣武昌」[3] — they were all executed and their heads sent to Wuchang.

Lü Dai continued the campaign afterward: 「岱既定交州，復進討九真，斬獲以萬數。」[1] — having settled Jiao Province, he advanced against Jiuzhen with tens of thousands killed or captured; he then sent a 從事 (attendant officer) south to proclaim the state's transforming influence, and the kings of Funan, Linyi, and Tangming beyond the frontier each sent envoys with tribute; 「權嘉其功，進拜鎮南將軍」[1] — Sun Quan praised his achievement and advanced him to General Who Guards the South.

**Inference.** The passage places the enfeoffment 「進封番禺侯」 immediately after the rout of Gan Li and Huan Zhi [1], and the same section records the beheading of Shi Hui and his brothers just before that. 据此推断: the marquisate rewarded the pacification of Jiao Province — the execution of Shi Hui and the defeat of his remaining forces — rather than the later Jiuzhen campaign or the promotion to General Who Guards the South, both of which the text records as subsequent events.

## Note on dating

No specific year is recorded in the sources for the enfeoffment as Marquis of Panyu. A preceding passage dates Lü Dai's appointment as Inspector of Jiao Province: 「延康元年，代步騭為交州刺史。」[9] That date belongs to the inspectorship, not to the marquisate; the sources do not connect the two events in time, so no year is assigned here to the Panyu enfeoffment.

The relevant passage is from Lü Dai's biography in the *Book of Wu* [1]. After the Administrator of Jiaozhi, **Shi Xie (士燮)**, died, Sun Quan appointed Shi Xie's son **Shi Hui** as General Who Brings Peace to Distant Lands and acting Administrator of Jiuzhen, sending Colonel Chen Shi to replace Shi Xie. Shi Hui refused the order and raised troops at the seaport to resist. Lü Dai memorialized the throne for permission to punish Shi Hui and led 3,000 troops across the sea by day and night. Shi Hui, caught off guard, came out with his six brothers baring their shoulders to surrender — Lü Dai had them all beheaded and sent the heads away. Shi Hui's generals **Gan Li (甘醴)** and **Huan Zhi (桓治)** then led the officials and people to attack Lü Dai, but Lü Dai struck back and defeated them heavily.

The text states:

「徽大將甘醴，桓治等率吏民攻岱，岱奮擊大破之，進封番禺侯。」[1]

Translation: *"Shi Hui's senior generals Gan Li and Huan Zhi and others led officials and commoners to attack Lü Dai; Lü Dai fought back fiercely and routed them, and was advanced in enfeoffment as Marquis of Panyu."*

The same episode is recorded in Shi Xie's biography [3], which confirms that Lü Dai received the imperial edict to execute Shi Hui, that he was persuaded to come out through the intermediary Shi Kuang (士匡), and that Shi Hui's brothers were all executed and their heads sent to Wuchang.

Lü Dai then went on to pacify Jiao Province further — attacking Jiuzhen with tens of thousands killed or captured, and sending envoys south to announce Wu's authority to the kings of Funan, Linyi, and Tangming, who each sent tribute. For this, Sun Quan praised his achievements and promoted him to General Who Guards the South (鎮南將軍) [1].

## Note on dating

The sources here do not give a specific year for the enfeoffment as Marquis of Panyu. The previous passage records Lü Dai's appointment as Inspector of Jiao Province in the first year of Yankang (延康元年) [9], but I will not assign that date to the Panyu enfeoffment, since the text does not connect the two events in time.
review_raw:
## Conclusion

The Marquis of Panyu (番禺侯) was **Lü Dai (吕岱)**, style **Dinggong (定公)**, a general of Wu. The title was granted to him in connection with his campaign in Jiao Province against **Shi Hui (士徽)** and Shi Hui's generals.

## Evidence

Lü Dai's style and the title are confirmed by his biography: 「呂岱字定公，廣陵海陵人也」[4], and the index of names in the text lists him with the appellation 番禺侯.

After the Administrator of Jiaozhi, **Shi Xie (士燮)**, died, Sun Quan acted as follows: 「權以燮子徽為安遠將軍，領九真太守，以校尉陳時代燮。」[1] — Sun Quan appointed Shi Xie's son Shi Hui as General Who Brings Peace to Distant Lands, to oversee Jiuzhen as Administrator, and sent Colonel Chen Shi to replace Shi Xie. Shi Hui refused the order and raised troops at the seaport to resist. Lü Dai memorialized for permission to punish him and crossed the sea: 「岱於是上疏請討徽罪，督兵三千人晨夜浮海。」[1]

Shi Hui, caught off guard, came out to meet him: 「即率兄弟六人肉袒迎岱。岱皆斬送其首」[1] — Shi Hui led his six brothers, baring their shoulders, to welcome Lü Dai; Lü Dai had them all beheaded and sent the heads away. Shi Hui's senior generals then attacked Lü Dai, and it is at this point that the enfeoffment is recorded:

「徽大將甘醴，桓治等率吏民攻岱，岱奮擊大破之，進封番禺侯。」[1]

*"Shi Hui's senior generals Gan Li and Huan Zhi and others led officials and commoners to attack Lü Dai; Lü Dai fought back fiercely and routed them, and was advanced in enfeoffment as Marquis of Panyu."*

The same episode appears in Shi Xie's biography [3], which records that Lü Dai had received the edict to execute Shi Hui: 「而呂岱被詔誅徽」[3]. There, Shi Yi's son Kuang, a General of the Household who had old ties with Lü Dai, was first sent to persuade Shi Hui to submit and confess his guilt; after the brothers came out baring their shoulders, Lü Dai read the edict aloud, and 「即皆伏誅，傳首詣武昌」[3] — they were all executed and their heads sent to Wuchang.

Lü Dai continued the campaign afterward: 「岱既定交州，復進討九真，斬獲以萬數。」[1] — having settled Jiao Province, he advanced against Jiuzhen with tens of thousands killed or captured; he then sent a 從事 (attendant officer) south to proclaim the state's transforming influence, and the kings of Funan, Linyi, and Tangming beyond the frontier each sent envoys with tribute; 「權嘉其功，進拜鎮南將軍」[1] — Sun Quan praised his achievement and advanced him to General Who Guards the South.

**Inference.** The passage places the enfeoffment 「進封番禺侯」 immediately after the rout of Gan Li and Huan Zhi [1], and the same section records the beheading of Shi Hui and his brothers just before that. 据此推断: the marquisate rewarded the pacification of Jiao Province — the execution of Shi Hui and the defeat of his remaining forces — rather than the later Jiuzhen campaign or the promotion to General Who Guards the South, both of which the text records as subsequent events.

## Note on dating

No specific year is recorded in the sources for the enfeoffment as Marquis of Panyu. A preceding passage dates Lü Dai's appointment as Inspector of Jiao Province: 「延康元年，代步騭為交州刺史。」[9] That date belongs to the inspectorship, not to the marquisate; the sources do not connect the two events in time, so no year is assigned here to the Panyu enfeoffment.

q: When Mi Chu married his sister to Liu Pei, how many retainers and how much property did he contribute along with her?
reply:
**结论：** 据《三国志·蜀书·麋竺传》记载，麋竺（Mi Zhu）把妹妹献给刘备做夫人时，随妹妹一同献上的是**奴仆宾客二千人**，以及**金银货币**，用来资助军费。原文并没有给出所献财产的具体数目，只记献上金银货币以助军资。

**依据（原文）：**

事情记在建安元年，吕布趁刘备出兵抵御袁术之机袭击下邳、俘虏了刘备的妻子儿女，刘备转军到广陵海西，处境困窘。此时麋竺进献妹妹并资助军资：

「先主轉軍廣陵海西，竺于是進妹于先主為夫人，奴客二千，金銀貨幣以助軍資，于時困匱，賴此複振。」[1]

所以具体是：**奴客（奴仆宾客）二千人**；财产方面是**金银货币**，用于补助军费，原文未记具体数额。

**补充：**

- 同一段还说麋竺祖上世代经商：「祖世貨殖，僮客萬人，貲產鉅億。」[1]
- 此事与吕布袭下邳、虏先主妻子，以及先主转军广陵海西，都连记在建安元年这一段里[1]。

q: Why was Wei Zhao put to death by Sun Hao?
reply:
## Conclusion

Wei Yao (韋曜, style name Hongsi 弘嗣), the man the question calls "Wei Zhao," was put to death by Sun Hao (孫皓) in the second year of the Fenghuang 鳳凰 era, 273 CE. The *Sanguozhi* gives the causes as a buildup of accumulated resentment: Wei Yao's blunt dismissal of the reported auspicious signs, his insistence that Sun Hao's father Sun He be given a "zhuan" (傳) rather than a "ji" (紀), and his conduct at Sun Hao's drinking banquets, which Sun Hao took as disobedience and disloyalty. He was arrested and thrown into prison; both his own prison plea and Hua He's (華覈) repeated memorials failed, and Sun Hao had him executed.

## The causes recorded in the *Sanguozhi*

**1. The auspicious signs and the ji/zhuan dispute.**

「時所在承指數言瑞應。皓以問曜，曜答曰：'此人家筐篋中物耳。'又皓欲為父和作紀，曜執以和不登帝位，宜名為傳。如是者非一，漸見責怒。」[3]

**2. The drinking banquets.**

「皓每饗宴，無不竟日，坐席無能否率以七升為限，雖不悉入口，皆澆灌取盡。曜素飲酒不過二升，初見禮異時，常為裁減，或密賜茶荈以當酒，至於寵衰，更見逼強，輒以為罪。」[3]
「又於酒後使侍臣難折公卿，以嘲弄侵克發摘私短以為歡。」[3]
「故但示難問經義言論而已。皓以為不承用詔命，意不忠盡，遂積前後嫌忿，收曜付獄，是歲鳳凰二年也。」[3]

**3. The plea and the refusal.**

From prison Wei Yao submitted a statement listing his unfinished scholarly works — 「以作《洞紀》，紀自庖犧，至於秦、漢，凡為三卷」 and 「又作《官職訓》及《辯釋名》各一卷，欲表上之」[16] — begging to be allowed to finish them. Sun Hao pressed him further over the state of his manuscript: 「曜冀以此求免，而皓更怪其書之垢故，又以詰曜。」[12] Hua He repeatedly sent up memorials to save him, comparing him to Sima Qian: 「今曜在吳，亦漢之史遷也。」[12] and pleading 「曜年已七十，餘數無幾，乞赦其一等之罪，為終身徒，使成書業，水足傳未，垂之百世。」[11] But: 「皓不許，遂誅曜，徙百家零陵。子隆，亦有文學也。」[11]

## Inferred points

The record says Sun Hao 「積前後嫌忿」[3] before arresting Wei Yao, so it is fair to infer that the execution followed from the accumulation of these several incidents together rather than from any single capital charge; the text does not name one decisive offense. It also fits the *Sanguozhi*'s general assessment of Sun Hao — 「皓之淫刑所濫，隕斃流黜者，蓋不可勝數」[7], 「忠諫者誅，讒諛者進」[7] — and the record of him having Chen Sheng's head sawn off with a heated saw and the body thrown below the Siyang hill: 「皓大怒，假他事燒鋸斷聲頭，投其身於四望之下」[10]. These support the inference that Wei Yao's death was one instance of Sun Hao punishing those who spoke frankly, though the specific recorded causes remain the three listed above.

Wei Zhao (韋昭, also written 韋曜, style name Hongsi 弘嗣) was executed by Sun Hao (孫皓) in the second year of the Fenghuang 鳳凰 era — 273 CE. The *Sanguozhi* gives the reasons: a buildup of accumulated resentment caused by several incidents — Wei Zhao's blunt answer about the "auspicious signs," his insistence that Sun Hao's father Sun He should be given a "zhuan" (傳) rather than a "ji" (紀), and his refusal to obey Sun Hao's orders at the drinking banquets — which Sun Hao finally treated as disloyalty. Wei Zhao was thrown into prison, and although he and Hua He (華覈) submitted pleas, Sun Hao refused and had him killed.

## The reasons given in the record

**1. Accumulated slights: the auspicious signs and the "ji/zhuan" dispute.**

「時所在承指數言瑞應。皓以問曜，曜答曰：'此人家筐篋中物耳。'又皓欲為父和作紀，曜執以和不登帝位，宜名為傳。如是者非一，漸見責怒。」[3]
(When everywhere people, catering to his wishes, repeatedly reported auspicious omens, Sun Hao asked Wei Zhao about them; Wei Zhao answered, "These are things from people's baskets and boxes." And when Sun Hao wanted to make a "ji" (annal) for his father Sun He, Wei Zhao insisted that since Sun He had never ascended the throne, it should be called a "zhuan" (biography). Such incidents were not few, and he gradually incurred reproach and anger.)

**2. The drinking-banquet issue.**

Sun Hao held all-day drinking feasts with a mandatory limit of seven sheng for everyone. Wei Zhao, who normally could not drink more than two sheng, was at first let off and even secretly given tea in place of wine, but once his favor declined he was forced, and this was then counted against him. Sun Hao also set his attendants to humiliate the ministers after drinking; Wei Zhao would only question them on the meaning of the classics rather than join in tearing people down. 「皓以為不承用詔命，意不忠盡，遂積前後嫌忿，收曜付獄，是歲鳳凰二年也。」[3]
(Sun Hao took this as disobedience to his orders and a failure of loyal devotion, and so — accumulating his resentment over the earlier and later incidents — he had Wei Zhao arrested and thrown into prison. That year was the second year of Fenghuang.)

**3. The plea and the refusal.**

From prison Wei Zhao submitted a statement listing his unfinished scholarly works (《洞紀》, 《官職訓》, 《辯釋名》) and begging to be allowed to finish them [16]. Hua He repeatedly sent up memorials to save him, comparing him to Sima Qian and pleading: 「曜年已七十，餘數無幾，乞赦其一等之罪，為終身徒，使成書業，水足傳未，垂之百世。」[11]
(Wei Zhao is already seventy; his remaining years are few. I beg you to pardon him of the first degree of guilt, make him a lifelong convict, and let him complete the work of his book, so it may be transmitted to a hundred generations.)

But: 「皓不許，遂誅曜，徙百家零陵。子隆，亦有文學也。」[11]
(Sun Hao did not permit it, and so put Wei Zhao to death, and moved his household of one hundred families to Lingling. His son Wei Long also had literary talent.)

## Inferred points

Based on the facts above, one can infer that the execution was not the result of a single capital charge but of Sun Hao's accumulated personal resentment: the record explicitly says he "accumulated the earlier and later grudges" (積前後嫌忿) [3], so the trigger was the combination of the omen answer, the ji/zhuan dispute, and the banquet conduct, not any one of them alone. It is also worth noting that this took place in the second year of Fenghuang, i.e., 273 CE — the same year the record elsewhere notes Sun Hao had Lu Kang made Grand Marshal and had Chen Sheng killed by having his head sawn off with a heated saw over a favorite concubine's complaint [10], which fits the *Sanguozhi*'s overall assessment of Sun Hao: 「皓之淫刑所濫，隕斃流黜者，蓋不可勝數……忠諫者誅，讒諛者進」[7] (Sun Hao's excessive cruel punishments — those who died or were exiled or dismissed cannot be counted; the loyal who remonstrated were executed and the flatterers advanced). So Wei Zhao's death fits the pattern of Sun Hao killing those who spoke frankly, but the specific recorded causes are the ones listed above.

Note on the name: the text uses 「韋曜」[3], though he is commonly known as Wei Zhao (韋昭); the record's own line gives 「韋曜字弘嗣，吳郡雲陽人也」[13].

From prison Wei Yao submitted a statement listing his unfinished scholarly works — 「以作《洞紀》，紀自庖犧，至於秦、漢，凡為三卷」 and 「又作《官職訓》及《辯釋名》各一卷，欲表上之」[16] — begging to be allowed to finish them. Sun Hao pressed him further over the state of his manuscript: 「曜冀以此求免，而皓更怪其書之垢故，又以詰曜。」[12] Hua He repeatedly sent up memorials to save him, comparing him to Sima Qian: 「今曜在吳，亦漢之史遷也。」[12] and pleading 「曜年已七十，餘數無幾，乞赦其一等之罪，為終身徒，使成書業，水足傳未，垂之百世。」[11] But: 「皓不許，遂誅曜，徙百家零陵。子隆，亦有文學也。」[11]

## Inferred points

The record says Sun Hao 「積前後嫌忿」[3] before arresting Wei Yao, so it is fair to infer that the execution followed from the accumulation of these several incidents together rather than from any single capital charge; the text does not name one decisive offense. It also fits the *Sanguozhi*'s general assessment of Sun Hao — 「皓之淫刑所濫，隕斃流黜者，蓋不可勝數」[7], 「忠諫者誅，讒諛者進」[7] — and the record of him having Chen Sheng's head sawn off with a heated saw and the body thrown below the Siyang hill: 「皓大怒，假他事燒鋸斷聲頭，投其身於四望之下」[10]. These support the inference that Wei Yao's death was one instance of Sun Hao punishing those who spoke frankly, though the specific recorded causes remain the three listed above.

q: How did Xu Zhu realize that Xu Ta and the others were plotting to assassinate Cao Cao? And how did he deal with them?
reply:
## How Xu Chu discovered Xu Ta's plot, and how he dealt with them

**What the record says**

Xu Chu was taken into Cao Cao's (魏太祖) personal guard on the day he submitted: 「即日拜都尉，引入宿衛」[1]. The plot is recorded in his biography in the account of the Guandu campaign:

> 「從討袁紹於官渡。時常從士徐他等謀為逆，以褚常侍左右，憚之不敢發。伺褚休下日，他等懷刀入。褚至下捨心動，即還侍。他等不知，入帳見褚，大驚愕。他色變，褚覺之，即擊殺他等。太祖益親信之，出入同行，不離左右。」[1]

("He followed [Cao Cao] to attack Yuan Shao at Guandu. At that time the regular attendant soldier Xu Ta and others plotted treason; because Xu Chu constantly attended at [Cao Cao's] side, they feared him and did not dare to act. They waited for the day Xu Chu went off duty, and Xu Ta and the others entered carrying knives. Xu Chu reached the rest-quarters, felt a stirring in his heart, and immediately returned to attend [Cao Cao]. Xu Ta and the others did not know this; entering the tent and seeing Xu Chu, they were greatly shocked. Xu Ta's expression changed; Xu Chu noticed it, and immediately struck and killed Xu Ta and the others. Cao Cao trusted and favored him even more, going out and coming in together, never leaving his side.")

Step by step, as the text has it:
1. **Who and why they waited:** the conspirators were Xu Ta (徐他) and others, regular attendant soldiers — 「時常從士徐他等謀為逆」[1] — and they feared Xu Chu, who constantly attended Cao Cao, so they did not dare to act — 「以褚常侍左右，憚之不敢發」[1].
2. **The chance they took:** Xu Chu's off-duty day — 「伺褚休下日，他等懷刀入」[1].
3. **What made Xu Chu turn back:** reaching the rest-quarters, he 「心動」, and at once returned to attend Cao Cao — 「褚至下捨心動，即還侍」[1].
4. **What he saw:** they did not know he had returned, and entering the tent and seeing him were greatly shocked — 「他等不知，入帳見褚，大驚愕」[1].
5. **What he did:** Xu Ta's expression changed, Xu Chu noticed it, and he immediately struck and killed them — 「他色變，褚覺之，即擊殺他等」[1].

**A note on the name:** the main text of the biography writes the ringleader as 徐他 [1], while Pei Songzhi's own comment (裴松之按) on this incident writes him as 徐佗, saying 「徐佗謀逆而許褚心動」, and adds 「忠誠之至遠同於日磾」[3] — that is, he compares Xu Chu's loyalty to that of Jin Midi (金日磾). So both forms of the name appear in the text.

**Inference (据此推断):** the record gives exactly two things that made Xu Chu act — the sudden 「心動」 that sent him back to his post, and his reading of the conspirators' shock and Xu Ta's changed countenance. From these facts one may infer that, as the record presents it, he was alerted by his own intuition and then confirmed the danger from their visible panic, rather than by any recorded prior intelligence. The record's silence about any earlier investigation, however, does not prove there was none.

q: What is the story of Kuan Yü killing Ts'ai Yang at Ku-ch'eng?
reply:
## Conclusion

The story as usually told — that **Guan Yu killed Cai Yang at Gucheng** — is **not** what the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* says. Two things differ from the text:

1. **The killer was Liu Bei, not Guan Yu.** The *Record of the First Ruler* says Cai Yang was killed by the First Ruler (Liu Bei): 「曹公遣蔡陽擊之，為先主所殺。」[1] ("Cao Cao sent Cai Yang to attack them, and he was killed by the First Ruler.")
2. **No place called Gucheng appears in this account.** The events are placed in Runan (汝南).

Guan Yu's own biography does not mention Cai Yang. What it records for this period is only that after killing Yan Liang he left Cao Cao and went back to Liu Bei: 「羽盡封其所賜，拜書告辭，而奔先主於袁軍。」[2] ("Guan Yu sealed up everything he had been given, sent a letter of farewell, and fled to the First Ruler in Yuan Shao's army.")

## What the text actually records

The setting is after Cao Cao's eastern campaign: 「建安五年，曹公東征，先主奔袁紹。」[2] (Jian'an 5 = 200 CE [4]). Yuan Shao then sent Liu Bei south to plunder the Xu area and into Runan, and Guan Yu rejoined him there:

- 「紹遣先主將兵與辟等略許下。關羽亡歸先主。」[1] — "Yuan Shao sent the First Ruler with troops to plunder the Xu area together with Liu Pi and others. Guan Yu fled back and rejoined the First Ruler."
- 「紹遣先主將本兵復至汝南，與賊龔都等合，眾數千人。曹公遣蔡陽擊之，為先主所殺。」[1] — "Yuan Shao sent the First Ruler with his own troops back to Runan, where he joined forces with the bandit Gong Du and others, several thousand strong. Cao Cao sent Cai Yang to attack them, and he was killed by the First Ruler."

The *Annals of Emperor Wu* gives a **different version, with a date**:

- 「六年夏四月」[20] — Jian'an 6 = 201 CE [4].
- 「紹之未破也，使劉備略汝南，汝南賊共都等應之。遣蔡揚擊都，不利，爲都所破。」[20] — "Before Yuan Shao was defeated, he sent Liu Bei to plunder Runan, and the Runan bandit Gong Du and others responded to him. [Cao Cao] sent Cai Yang (蔡揚) to attack Gong Du; it went badly, and he was defeated by Gong Du."
- 「公南征備。備聞公自行，走奔劉表，都等皆散。」[20] — "The Duke campaigned south against Liu Bei. When Liu Bei heard the Duke was coming in person, he fled to Liu Biao, and Gong Du and the rest all scattered."

So the two accounts differ: the *First Ruler's* record says **Liu Bei killed Cai Yang** [1]; the *Annals of Emperor Wu* says Cai Yang **attacked Gong Du, was defeated by Gong Du**, and places this under Jian'an 6 (201 CE) [3][4]. The name is also written differently in the two texts (蔡陽 / 蔡揚) [1][3]. The two should be read side by side rather than harmonized.

## Inference

**From this I infer** the following. The *Annals of Emperor Wu* dates the Runan operation and Cai Yang's defeat to Jian'an 6, 201 CE [3][4]; the *First Ruler's* record places the killing of Cai Yang in the sequence after Guan Yu's return to Liu Bei, during the Runan operations with Gong Du, but gives no year for it [1]. Combining these, the event most likely belongs to Liu Bei's Runan operations in 201 CE. And since one account credits the killing to Liu Bei [1] and the other credits the defeat to Gong Du [3], while Guan Yu's biography records only his return to Liu Bei and says nothing of Cai Yang [2], the deed in the *Records* is not attributed to Guan Yu, and the place name "Gucheng" does not occur in the retrieved text.

## Background

## Background

以下不是《三国志》的记载: The scene of Guan Yu slaying Cai Yang at Gucheng — along with the "meeting of the three brothers at Gucheng" — is not found in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*; it comes from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* and related popular tradition. In the *Records*, Cai Yang's death is placed in Runan (汝南), which lies in present-day Henan province.
review_raw:
## Conclusion

The story as usually told — that **Guan Yu killed Cai Yang at Gucheng** — is **not** what the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* says. Two things differ from the text:

1. **The killer was Liu Bei, not Guan Yu.** The *Record of the First Ruler* says Cai Yang was killed by the First Ruler (Liu Bei): 「曹公遣蔡陽擊之，為先主所殺。」[1] ("Cao Cao sent Cai Yang to attack them, and he was killed by the First Ruler.")
2. **No place called Gucheng appears in this account.** The events are placed in Runan (汝南).

Guan Yu's own biography does not mention Cai Yang. What it records for this period is only that after killing Yan Liang he left Cao Cao and went back to Liu Bei: 「羽盡封其所賜，拜書告辭，而奔先主於袁軍。」[2] ("Guan Yu sealed up everything he had been given, sent a letter of farewell, and fled to the First Ruler in Yuan Shao's army.")

## What the text actually records

The setting is after Cao Cao's eastern campaign: 「建安五年，曹公東征，先主奔袁紹。」[2] (Jian'an 5 = 200 CE [4]). Yuan Shao then sent Liu Bei south to plunder the Xu area and into Runan, and Guan Yu rejoined him there:

- 「紹遣先主將兵與辟等略許下。關羽亡歸先主。」[1] — "Yuan Shao sent the First Ruler with troops to plunder the Xu area together with Liu Pi and others. Guan Yu fled back and rejoined the First Ruler."
- 「紹遣先主將本兵復至汝南，與賊龔都等合，眾數千人。曹公遣蔡陽擊之，為先主所殺。」[1] — "Yuan Shao sent the First Ruler with his own troops back to Runan, where he joined forces with the bandit Gong Du and others, several thousand strong. Cao Cao sent Cai Yang to attack them, and he was killed by the First Ruler."

The *Annals of Emperor Wu* gives a **different version, with a date**:

- 「六年夏四月」[3] — Jian'an 6 = 201 CE [4].
- 「紹之未破也，使劉備略汝南，汝南賊共都等應之。遣蔡揚擊都，不利，爲都所破。」[3] — "Before Yuan Shao was defeated, he sent Liu Bei to plunder Runan, and the Runan bandit Gong Du and others responded to him. [Cao Cao] sent Cai Yang (蔡揚) to attack Gong Du; it went badly, and he was defeated by Gong Du."
- 「公南征備。備聞公自行，走奔劉表，都等皆散。」[3] — "The Duke campaigned south against Liu Bei. When Liu Bei heard the Duke was coming in person, he fled to Liu Biao, and Gong Du and the rest all scattered."

So the two accounts differ: the *First Ruler's* record says **Liu Bei killed Cai Yang** [1]; the *Annals of Emperor Wu* says Cai Yang **attacked Gong Du, was defeated by Gong Du**, and places this under Jian'an 6 (201 CE) [3][4]. The name is also written differently in the two texts (蔡陽 / 蔡揚) [1][3]. The two should be read side by side rather than harmonized.

## Inference

**From this I infer** the following. The *Annals of Emperor Wu* dates the Runan operation and Cai Yang's defeat to Jian'an 6, 201 CE [3][4]; the *First Ruler's* record places the killing of Cai Yang in the sequence after Guan Yu's return to Liu Bei, during the Runan operations with Gong Du, but gives no year for it [1]. Combining these, the event most likely belongs to Liu Bei's Runan operations in 201 CE. And since one account credits the killing to Liu Bei [1] and the other credits the defeat to Gong Du [3], while Guan Yu's biography records only his return to Liu Bei and says nothing of Cai Yang [2], the deed in the *Records* is not attributed to Guan Yu, and the place name "Gucheng" does not occur in the retrieved text.

q: A strategic proposal called for first occupying Jing and Yi Provinces, allying with Sun Quan, waiting for a change in the situation in the north, and then advancing along two routes. If Jing Province were lost, which key precondition of this strategy would no longer hold?
reply:
**Conclusion:** The precondition that would fail is 「跨有荊、益」[1] — holding **both** Jing and Yi as one base. The plan's eastern arm is written as an army drawn from Jing; if Jing were lost, that arm has no base, and the "cross-possessing" condition itself is no longer met.

**Evidence (Zhuge Liang's answer, recorded in his biography):**

Liu Bei went to Zhuge Liang, and Zhuge Liang answered him: 「亮答曰」[2].

The conditions the plan rests on:

- 「若跨有荊、益，保其巖阻，西和諸戎，南撫夷越，外結好孫權，內修政理」[1]
  — "If you cross-possess Jing and Yi, hold their defiles, befriend the Rong in the west, pacify the Yi and Yue in the south, externally make good relations with Sun Quan, and internally cultivate government…"

The two-route advance that follows on it, after a change in the north:

- 「天下有變，則命一上將將荊州之軍以向宛、洛，將軍身率益州之眾出於秦川」[1]
  — "When there is a change in the world, order one senior general to lead the army of Jing Province toward Wan and Luo, while you yourself lead the host of Yi Province out to Qinchuan."

**Inference (据此推断):** The plan as recorded links four things — (a) cross-possessing Jing and Yi, (b) the Sun Quan alliance, (c) waiting for a northern change, and (d) a two-pronged advance. The advance is written explicitly as "the army of Jing Province → 宛、洛" plus "the host of Yi Province → 秦川" [1]. Since the eastern prong is drawn from Jing, and since the stated base condition is the possession of Jing **and** Yi together, it follows that the loss of Jing would remove the base for the eastern prong and break the 「跨有荊、益」[1] condition. This is inference from the quoted text; the text itself states the condition and the plan, not the counterfactual.

q: This man originally served under Liu Zhang but later became one of Liu Bei's key advisers. He helped plan the seizure of Yi Province and accompanied Liu Bei in the contest for Hanzhong. He died of illness before Liu Bei did, and so had no part in the deathbed entrustment. Who was he?
reply:
## Conclusion

The man was **Fa Zheng** (法正, courtesy name Xiaozhi 孝直). He first served under Liu Zhang, later became one of Liu Bei's chief strategists, helped plan the takeover of Yi Province, accompanied Liu Bei in the Hanzhong campaign, and died before Liu Bei — so he took no part in the deathbed entrustment.

## Evidence from the *Sanguozhi* (with original text)

**1. Originally Liu Zhang's subordinate**

「正與同郡孟達俱入蜀依劉璋，久之為新都令，後召署軍議校尉」[1] — Fa Zheng entered Shu together with Meng Da of the same commandery to serve Liu Zhang, served as magistrate of Xindu, later as Army Council Colonel. He was unused and slandered: 「既不任用，又為其州邑俱僑客者所謗無行，志意不得」[1].

**2. Became Liu Bei's strategist (謀主)**

After Yi Province was taken, 「先主复領益州牧，諸葛亮為股肱，法正為謀主」[3] — Zhuge Liang as his right arm, Fa Zheng as his strategist.

**3. Planned the seizure of Yi Province**

Liu Zhang 「遣法正將四千人迎先主」[5], and 「正因陳益州可取之策」[5]. Earlier he had 「陰獻策於先主」[1], urging Liu Bei to take Yi Province while Zhang Song responded from within. Pei note quoting the *Wu Shu*: Liu Bei questioned Zhang Song and Fa Zheng about Shu's extent, armaments, troops, and strategic roads, 「由是盡知益州虛實也」[23].

**4. Accompanied the Hanzhong campaign**

「先主善其策，乃率諸將進兵漢中，正亦從行」[6] — Liu Bei approved his plan, advanced on Hanzhong with his generals, and Fa Zheng went along. Liu Bei 「於定軍、興勢作營」[6]; when Xiahou Yuan came to contest the ground, Fa Zheng said 「可擊矣」[6], and Liu Bei 「命黃忠乘高鼓譟攻之，大破淵軍」[6]. A Pei note (no source book named) records that when Liu Bei, in a disadvantageous position, angrily refused to retreat under a rain of arrows, Fa Zheng placed himself in front of Liu Bei and said 「明公親當矢石，況小人乎？」, after which Liu Bei withdrew with him [13].

**5. Died before Liu Bei**

「先主立為漢中王，以正為尚書令、護軍將軍。明年卒，時年四十五。先主為之流涕者累日」[2] — after Liu Bei became King of Hanzhong, Fa Zheng was made Director of the Secretariat and General of the Guard; he died the next year at forty-five, and Liu Bei wept for days. 「諡曰翼侯」[2]. The Zhao Yun biography confirms: 「初，先主時，惟法正見諡」[30] — during Liu Bei's lifetime, only Fa Zheng received a posthumous name. The same passage [2] continues past Fa Zheng's death into Liu Bei's assumption of the imperial title and the Zhangwu 2 defeat at Baidi, so Liu Bei outlived him.

## Inference

据此推断: Fa Zheng died in the year following Liu Bei's elevation to King of Hanzhong [2], while the deathbed entrustment is recorded in Li Yan's biography under the third year of Zhangwu: 「三年，先主疾病，嚴與諸葛亮並受遺詔輔少主」[26]. Since Fa Zheng's death came before that entrustment, he cannot have taken part in it. This agrees with Zhuge Liang's later sigh, spoken after the Zhangwu 2 defeat and retreat to Baidi: 「法孝直若在，則能制主上，令不東行」[2] — words that presuppose Fa Zheng was already dead. The entrustment itself is not recorded in Fa Zheng's biography; it appears in Li Yan's [26].

## Background

The following is not from the *Sanguozhi*: the question's statement that he died of illness is not recorded there — his biography records only that he died, without giving a cause — and may come from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* or another non-orthodox account.

q: What happened when Zhuge Liang used the Empty Fort Strategy at Yangping to scare off Sima Yi?
reply:
## Conclusion

The story does exist in the *Sanguozhi* tradition — but **not in Chen Shou's main text**. It appears only in Pei Songzhi's commentary, quoted from Guo Chong's *Sanshi* (郭沖《三事》), and Pei Songzhi (and the rebuttal attached to that note) rejects it as unreliable. So there is no confirmed "Empty Fort" incident at Yangping.

## What Guo Chong's account says (裴注引郭沖《三事》)

Zhuge Liang was camped at Yangping (陽平). He had sent Wei Yan and the other armies east, leaving only 10,000 men to hold the city:

> 「亮屯于陽平，遣魏延諸軍並兵東下，亮惟留萬人守城。晉宣帝率二十萬眾拒亮，而與延軍錯道，徑至前，當亮六十里所」[1]

Sima Yi (called 晉宣帝, his posthumous title) missed Wei Yan's column, came within about sixty *li*, and his scouts reported that Liang was weak. Liang could not reach Wei Yan in time, and his officers turned pale. Liang then:

> 「敕軍中皆臥旗息鼓，不得妄出菴幔，又令大開四城門，埽地卻洒」[1]

Sima Yi, who "always considered Liang cautious," suspected an ambush and withdrew north toward the hills. The next day Liang laughed and said Sima Yi must have thought him timid and imagined a strong ambush; the scouts confirmed it, and Sima Yi later regretted it deeply: 「宣帝後知，深以為恨」[1].

## Why it is rejected

The rebuttal in the same note (◇難曰) and Pei Songzhi's own note argue:

- Yangping is in Hanzhong. When Liang first camped there, Sima Yi was still **Jingzhou Inspector-General (荊州都督) stationed at Wancheng**, and only after Cao Zhen's death did he face Liang in Guanzhong: 「亮初屯陽平，宣帝尚為荊州都督，鎮宛城，至曹真死後，始與亮於關中相抗禦耳」[1]. The one Wei campaign that sent Sima Yi from Wan via Xicheng against Shu was aborted by continuous rain: 「值霖雨，不果」[1]. So there was no Yangping engagement at all: 「此之前後，無復有於陽平交兵事」[1].
- Even granting the story, a 200,000-strong army that already knew Liang was weak should have "taken defensive precautions and been cautious" rather than flee: 「若疑其有伏兵，正可設防持重，何至便走乎？」[1]
- Liang never even let Wei Yan command 10,000 men separately: 「亮尚不以延為萬人別統，豈得如沖言，頓使將重兵在前，而以輕弱自守乎？」[19] (quoting 《魏延傳》: 「延每隨亮出，輒欲請精兵萬人，與亮異道會于潼關，亮制而不許；延常謂亮為怯，歎己才用之不盡也」[19]).
- The rebuttal adds that Guo Chong told the story to the Prince of Fufeng, disparaging a father before his son, and concludes the book's citations are all false: 「且沖與扶風王言，顯彰宣帝之短，對子毀父，理所不容，而云『扶風王慨然善沖之言』，故知此書舉引皆虛」[19].

Note that Pei Songzhi is equally critical of Guo Chong's other anecdotes, e.g. 《五事》 [13].

## What the main text does record about Yangping

The *Shu Shu* main text places Liang's camp at Yangping (in Mianyang north of the Mian River) in the spring of Jianxing 5: 「五年春，丞相亮出屯漢中，營沔北陽平石馬」[6]. This is a camp location, not an empty-fort ruse.

**Inference (据此推断):** Since (a) the main text has Liang at Yangping only as an encampment [6], (b) the only account of the ruse is Guo Chong's [1], and (c) the rebuttal shows Sima Yi was not even in that theater at the relevant time [1], the Empty Fort story cannot be treated as a recorded historical event — at most it is a later anecdote.

以下不是《三国志》的记载: The well-known "Empty Fort Strategy" episode, as popularly told (Zhuge Liang sitting on the city wall playing the qin while Sima Yi's army withdraws), is the version found in 《三国演义》 and in drama; Chen Shou's main text of the *Sanguozhi* has no such event, and the version preserved in Pei Songzhi's commentary (from Guo Chong's 《三事》) is expressly rejected by the commentary itself.

q: In the Battle of Bowang, how did Zhuge Liang set the fire ambush against Xiahou Dun?
reply:
## Short answer

In the *Sanguozhi* (Records of the Three Kingdoms), Zhuge Liang did not set any fire ambush at Bowang. The Bowang engagement is recorded as **Liu Bei's own stratagem**: Liu Bei burned his own camp, pretended to flee, and Xiahou Dun's pursuing troops fell into his ambush. Zhuge Liang is not mentioned in the Bowang records at all. The "Zhuge Liang burns Bowang" story is from the novel *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, not from the histories.

## What the *Sanguozhi* actually says

**1. The ambush was Liu Bei's, and the fire was his own camp.** In the *Xianzhu zhuan* (Biography of Liu Bei):

> 「使拒夏侯惇、于禁等於博望。久之，先主設伏兵，一旦自燒屯偽遁，惇等追之，為伏兵所破。」[1]

Liu Bei was ordered to resist Xiahou Dun and Yu Jin at Bowang. After a long standoff, he set hidden troops, then one morning burned his own camp and faked a flight; Xiahou Dun's men pursued and were beaten by the ambush. Note the text makes **Liu Bei** the subject of every action — no Zhuge Liang.

**2. Li Dian's biography confirms the details** (and shows the "flight" was toward Ye 葉):

> 「劉表使劉備北侵，至葉，太祖遣典從夏侯惇拒之。備一旦燒屯去，惇率諸軍追擊之，典曰：『賊無故退，疑必有伏。南道狹窄，草木深，不可追也。』惇不聽，與於禁追之，典留守。惇等果入賊伏里，戰不利，典往救，備望見救至，乃散退。」[44]

Li Dian warned that an unprovoked retreat probably meant an ambush; Xiahou Dun did not listen, went in with Yu Jin, was worsted, and Li Dian rescued him. Again the strategist named is Liu Bei (and the warning voice is Li Dian) — not Zhuge Liang.

**3. Zhuge Liang had not yet joined Liu Bei.** The *Zhuge Liang zhuan* has Xu Shu recommend him and Liu Bei visit him three times:

> 「由是先主遂詣亮，凡三往，乃見。」[36]

And Pei Songzhi's note dates the meeting:

> 「臣松之案：劉備以建安十三年敗，遣亮使吳，亮以建興五年抗表北伐，自傾覆至此整二十年。然則備始與亮相遇，在敗軍之前一年時也。」[35]

That is, Pei Songzhi calculates the meeting as one year before the defeat of 建安十三年 = 208 CE [per era tool], i.e. about 建安十二年 (207 CE). Zhuge Liang was 27 when he was sent to Sun Quan in 建安十三年 [27].

## Inference (so marked)

From these facts: (a) the Bowang engagement is placed *before* Liu Bei was at Xinye meeting Zhuge Liang through Xu Shu's recommendation, and the standoff is described as 「久之」 ("after a long time") [1]; (b) Zhuge Liang only joined Liu Bei around 建安十二年 (207 CE), one year before the 208 CE crisis [35], [27]. Combining these, **the Bowang fire-and-ambush must predate Zhuge Liang's entry into Liu Bei's service** — so it is chronologically impossible for him to have planned it. This is an inference from the two dates, not an explicit statement in the text.

## Background

The following is not from the *Sanguozhi*: the scene of Zhuge Liang commanding at Bowang and burning Xiahou Dun's army with fire from the hillsides is the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*' telling, not a record of the histories — the histories credit the stratagem to Liu Bei [1], [44]. Bowang (博望) is in present-day Henan province, in the area of today's Nanyang/Fangcheng.

q: Cao Cao took in Emperor Xian of Han and issued orders in the name of the Han central government. Compared with relying on military strength alone, what political advantage did this chiefly bring him?
reply:
**Conclusion (the political advantage):** Taking in Emperor Xian gave Cao Cao something military strength alone could not supply — legitimacy: the ability to act in the name of the Han court, so that his orders carried the throne's authority. In the 《三国志》 this is expressed as "奉天子以令天下" (holding up the Son of Heaven to command the empire) and "奉天子以令不臣" (…to command the disloyal). The recorded payoffs were: (1) a claim to righteousness that made resistance look like rebellion; (2) the throne's offices and titles, which he both received and later used to elevate himself; (3) the adherence of regional forces; and (4) the restoration of court institutions under his management. This is not my own reading — it is the argument his advisers used to persuade him.

**Evidence from the sources**

1. The persuasion to receive the Emperor — Xun Yu (荀彧):
「誠因此時，奉主上以從民望，大順也；秉至公以服雄傑，大略也；扶弘義以致英俊，大德也。天下雖有逆節，必不能爲累，明矣。」[9]
*(Translation: "Seize this moment to hold up the Sovereign in accordance with the people's hopes — that is the greatest compliance; to hold supreme impartiality so as to subdue the heroes — that is the greatest strategy; to uphold the great righteousness so as to draw in the outstanding men — that is the greatest virtue. Though there be rebellious elements in the empire, they will certainly not be able to harm you.")*
Result: 「太祖遂至洛陽，奉迎天子都許。天子拜太祖大將軍」[9]. Elsewhere: 「以太祖爲大將軍，封武平侯」[31].

2. The phrase itself, paired with economic and military buildup — Mao Jie (毛玠):
「夫兵義者勝，守位以財，宜奉天子以令不臣，脩耕植，畜軍資，如此則霸王之業可成也。」[20]
*(Translation: "In war the righteous win; position is held by wealth. You should hold up the Son of Heaven to command the disloyal, repair farming, and accumulate military supplies; thus the enterprise of a hegemon-king can be completed.")*

3. The same logic used to convince Zhang Xiu to defect to Cao Cao — Jia Xu (賈詡):
「夫曹公奉天子以令天下，其宜從一也。」[18]
*(Translation: "Lord Cao holds up the Son of Heaven to command the empire — that is the first reason to follow him.")*
Jia Xu's argument presupposed the disparity: 「袁彊曹弱，又與曹爲讎」[18].

4. The concrete political payoff — regional adherence, from the Yuan Shao account:
「會太祖迎天子都許，收河南地，關中皆附。」[35]
*(Translation: "When Taizu received the Son of Heaven and made Xu the capital, he took the land of Henan, and all of Guanzhong attached itself to him.")*

5. The office it conferred, which changed the hierarchy among the warlords: 「天子拜公司空，行車騎將軍」[32]. Yuan Shao's reaction shows the value: 裴注引《獻帝春秋》:「紹恥班在太祖下，怒曰：『曹操當死數矣，我輒救存之，今乃背恩，挾天子以令我乎！』」[5]. Cao Cao then yielded the post of Grand General to Shao: 「公乃固辭，以大將軍讓紹」[32]; 「太祖聞，而以大將軍讓於紹」[5].

6. Institutional restoration under his management: 「自天子西遷，朝廷日亂，至是宗廟社稷制度始立。」[31]
*(Translation: "Since the Son of Heaven's move west, the court had grown daily more disordered; only now were the ancestral-temple and state-altar institutions established.")*

7. He later used the throne's authority to keep climbing: 「天子命公贊拜不名，入朝不趨，劔履上殿，如蕭何故事」[14]; 「三月，天子使魏公位在諸侯王上，改授金璽，赤紱、遠遊冠」[11]; 「夏五月，天子進公爵爲魏王」[16].

**Inference (my own reasoning, marked as such):**
- Drawing points 1–5 together: the advantage was *not* mainly extra soldiers. Xun Yu's three benefits are all about legitimacy — compliance (順), subduing rivals (服雄傑), and drawing in talent (致英俊) — and Jia Xu names the ability to "令天下" as the first reason to submit to a weaker Cao Cao over a stronger Yuan Shao. 据此推断, "holding up the Son of Heaven" converted the throne's residual authority into (a) a recruitment magnet for men who would not serve a mere warlord, (b) a way to make rivals' resistance look like rebellion, and (c) the power to confer offices and titles — the currency of that era — as rewards. The Guanzhong adherence in point 4 is the record's own illustration of this conversion.
- Yuan Shao's camp had considered taking the Emperor first: 「圖還說紹迎天子都鄴，紹不從」, and the record adds 「紹悔」[35]. 据此推断, contemporaries regarded the move as a decisive political asset rather than a mere honor; the record does not say Cao Cao's success caused Yuan Shao's later defeat, only that Shao regretted letting the opportunity pass.

q: One side had the advantage in troops and supplies; the other, in a prolonged standoff, was running short of grain. In the end the weaker side, acting on intelligence from a defector, raided the enemy's main grain depot and turned the battle around. Which battle was this, and who was the defector?
reply:
**Conclusion: the battle was Guandu (官渡), and the defector was Xu You (許攸), courtesy name Ziyuan (子遠).**

**The standoff**

The sources record the campaign as 建安五年 (Jian'an 5, = 200 CE by the year-conversion tool); the text itself only says 「五年，與紹連戰」[4], and Cao Cao's army 「太祖保官渡，紹圍之」[4], with the two sides facing each other at Guandu: 「太祖遂與紹相拒於官渡」[6].

Yuan Shao's side was the stronger in numbers: Pei Songzhi's note quotes the annals as saying 「紹衆十餘萬，屯營東西數十里」[14]. Ju Shou told Yuan Shao 「北兵數衆而果勁不及南，南穀虛少而貨財不及北」[11] — the northern troops were numerous, but the south's grain was scant. Cao Cao's own account: 「公與紹相拒連月，雖比戰斬將，然衆少糧盡，士卒疲乏」[5]; and in Xun Yu's biography, 「太祖軍糧方盡」[4]. So the side short of grain in a prolonged standoff was Cao Cao's, while Yuan Shao's grain was still arriving by cart — 「袁紹運穀車數千乘至」[5].

**The defector: Xu You**

Xu You has no biography of his own in the *Sanguozhi*; the information appears in other men's accounts. The Pei note quoting the *Wei Lüeh* (裴注引《魏略》) says 「攸字子遠，少與袁紹及太祖善」[3], and that 「攸知不可爲謀，乃亡詣太祖」[3].

Two different reasons for his defection are recorded, and the sources do not agree:

- *Wu Di Ji*: 「紹謀臣許攸貪財，紹不能足，來奔，因說公擊瓊等」[5].
- Xun Yu's biography: 「審配以許攸家不法，收其妻子，攸怒叛紹」[4].

**The raid on the grain depot**

The grain was at Wuchao: 「冬十月，紹遣車運穀，使淳于瓊等五人將兵萬餘人送之，宿紹營北四十里」[5]. Xu You told Cao Cao where it was and how weakly guarded it was — in the Pei note quoting the *Cao Man Zhuan* (裴注引《曹瞞傳》): 「今袁氏輜重有萬餘乘，在故市、烏巢，屯軍無嚴備；今以輕兵襲之，不意而至，燔其積聚，不過三日，袁氏自敗也」[1]. The same note has Cao Cao receiving him: 「公聞攸來，跣出迎之」[1], saying 「子卿遠來，吾事濟矣」[1].

Cao Cao acted on it: 「公乃留曹洪守，自將步騎五千人夜往，會明至」[5], and 「大破瓊等，皆斬之」[5]. Yuan Shao's army collapsed and 「紹及譚棄軍走，渡河」[5]. Xun You's biography: 「太祖自將攻破之，盡斬瓊等」[6], 「紹將張郃、髙覽燒攻櫓降，紹遂棄軍走」[6]. Zhang He's biography records that he had urged a real relief effort, but 「紹但遣輕騎救瓊，而以重兵攻太祖營，不能下」[12], and after the slander of Guo Tu, 「郃懼，乃歸太祖」[12].

**Inference (my own reasoning, not a statement of the sources)**

q: This man first served Yüan Shao and later went over to Ts'ao Ts'ao. He fought in Han-chung, defeated Ma Su at Chieh-t'ing, and finally died at Mu-men while pursuing the Shu army. Who was he?
reply:
The man is **Zhang He** (張郃, pinyin Zhāng Hé), courtesy name Junyi (雋乂), a native of Mo county in Hejian. Every detail in your question matches his biography in the *Sanguozhi*.

**Served Yuan Shao, then went over to Cao Cao**
His biography opens: 「漢末應募討黃巾，爲軍司馬，屬韓馥。馥敗，以兵歸袁紹」[1] (at the end of the Han he answered the call to campaign against the Yellow Turbans, and when Han Fu was defeated he brought his troops over to Yuan Shao). At Guandu, after Guo Tu slandered him, 「郃懼，乃歸太祖」[1] — he defected to Cao Cao (Taizu). Cao Cao welcomed him: 「太祖得郃甚喜，謂曰：『昔子胥不早寤，自使身危，豈若微子去殷、韓信歸漢邪？』」and made him a Lieutenant-General (偏將軍) [11].

**Fought in Hanzhong**
「太祖從散關入漢中，又先遣郃督步卒五千於前通路。至陽平，魯降，太祖還，留郃與夏侯淵等守漢中，拒劉備」[11]. When Xiahou Yuan was killed, Guo Huai and the officers pushed Zhang He forward as commander: 「遂推郃爲軍主。郃出，勒兵安陳，諸將皆受郃節度，衆心乃定」[4]. He also fought Zhang Fei at Dangqu and was driven back: 「進軍宕渠，爲備將張飛所拒，引還南鄭」[11]; Zhang Fei's own biography records 「飛遂破郃。郃棄馬緣山，獨與麾下十餘人從間道退」[16].

**Defeated Ma Su at Jieting**
「諸葛亮出祁山。加郃位特進，遣督諸軍，拒亮將馬謖於街亭。謖依阻南山，不下據城。郃絶其汲道，擊，大破之」[5]. Ma Su's biography confirms 「與魏將張郃戰於街亭，爲郃所破，士卒離散」[6]. This was in the spring of Jianxing 6 (太和二年 = AD 228) [3][7][9].

**Died at Mumen while pursuing the Shu army**
「諸葛亮復出祁山，詔郃督諸將西至略陽，亮還保祁山，郃追至木門，與亮軍交戰，飛矢中郃右膝，薨，諡曰壯侯」[13]. This is dated to the sixth month of Jianxing 9 (AD 231), when Zhuge Liang's supplies ran out and he withdrew: 「亮糧盡退軍，郃追至青封，與亮交戰，被箭死」[17].

**A note on the circumstances of his death (two versions):**
- The main text says he pursued on orders and was hit by a stray arrow: 「郃追至木門，與亮軍交戰，飛矢中郃右膝，薨」[13].
- Pei Songzhi's commentary quotes the *Weilüe*: 「亮軍退，司馬宣王使郃追之，郃曰：『軍法，圍城必開出路，歸軍勿追。』宣王不聽。郃不得已，遂進。蜀軍乘高布伏，弓弩亂發，矢中郃髀」[14] — i.e., Sima Yi (Xuan Wang) forced the pursuit against Zhang He's own judgment. The two accounts differ on who ordered the pursuit and where the arrow struck (knee vs. thigh); I present them separately rather than deciding between them.

**Inference:** From the facts above — that he began under Han Fu and Yuan Shao, defected to Cao Cao at Guandu, was entrusted with defending Hanzhong against Liu Bei, was made area-commander (特進) against Ma Su at Jieting in 228, and died in 231 pursuing Zhuge Liang at Mumen — it follows that he was a Wei general who rose from Yuan Shao's service and became one of the commanders Cao Cao and his successors relied on most against Shu. His biography adds the assessment 「郃識變數，善處營陳，料戰勢地形，無不如計，自諸葛亮皆憚之」[12].

*Following is not from the Sanguozhi:* The name is rendered "Chang Ho" in older Wade-Giles romanization; in pinyin it is **Zhang He**.

q: Before the Battle of Red Cliffs, Liu Bei was comparatively weak, while Sun Quan held the Jiangdong territory and a navy. Given this imbalance, why did Sun Quan still have an incentive to ally with Liu Bei rather than stand by and let Cao Cao destroy him?
reply:
## Conclusion

According to the 《三国志》, Sun Quan did not ally with Liu Bei because he needed Liu Bei in order to survive. He had already concluded that fighting Cao Cao was both necessary and winnable on Jiangdong's own terms, and allying with Liu Bei was a way to add an asset to a war he had decided to fight anyway. The records give three distinct incentives.

**1. Surrender was not an option for Sun Quan personally.** When word came that Cao Cao was moving east, Sun Quan's assembled subordinates advised submission: 「皆勸權迎之，而肅獨不言」[14], and the 議者 concluded 「愚謂大計不如迎之」[24]. Lu Su alone stayed silent, then caught Sun Quan as he rose to change clothes — 「權起更衣，肅追於宇下」[14] — and made the decisive argument: 「今肅可迎操耳，如將軍，不可也。何以言之？今肅迎操，操當以肅還付鄉黨。」 and 「將軍迎操，欲安所歸？」[14] (I, Lu Su, can surrender and still be sent back to my home district with a post; you, General, if you surrender, where do you go?). Sun Quan answered: 「此諸人持議，甚失孤望；今卿廓開大計，正與孤同」[14]. So for Sun Quan the real alternative to fighting was not "stand by," it was personal ruin — his fate and Liu Bei's were bound by the same logic.

**2. Liu Bei was useful precisely because he was weak and was Cao Cao's enemy.** Lu Su's plan, laid out before Liu Biao's death, was to keep a buffer in Jing province: if Liu Bei and Liu Biao's sons were united, 「則宜撫安，與結盟好」, and Liu Bei should be induced to 「及說備使撫表眾，同心一意，共治曹操」[12]. Later, when Lü Fan urged Sun Quan to keep Liu Bei in Jiangdong rather than let him go, Lu Su objected (裴注引《漢晉春秋》): 「將軍雖神武命世，然曹公威力實重，初臨荊州，恩信未洽，宜以藉備，使撫安之。多操之敵，而自為樹黨，計之上也。」[15] (Use Liu Bei to pacify Jing; multiply Cao Cao's enemies and build our own faction — the best plan.) Liu Bei was worth allying with as a means of adding enemies to Cao Cao, not as a shield Sun Quan depended on.

**3. Sun Quan's own commanders judged Cao Cao beatable — with or without Liu Bei.** In 裴注引《江表傳》, Zhou Yu argued that Cao Cao's claimed host was in reality 「彼所將中國人，不過十五六萬，且軍已久疲，所得表眾，亦極七八萬耳，尚懷狐疑」, and concluded 「夫以疲病之卒，御狐疑之眾，眾數雖多，甚未足畏」[19]. In his formal memorial Zhou Yu added: 「今北土既未平安，加馬超、韓遂尚在關西，為操後患。且捨鞍馬，仗舟揖，與吳越爭衡，本非中國所長。」[25]. On that basis Sun Quan 「拔刀斫前奏案」[19] and dispatched his own fleet: 「即遣周瑜、程普、魯肅等水軍三萬，隨亮詣先主，并力拒曹公」[23]. He committed to battle before relying on Liu Bei.

## Liu Bei's actual contribution

Liu Bei was not empty-handed: he came with Guan Yu's ships and joined Liu Qi's men — 「適與羽船會，得濟沔，遇表長子江夏太守琦眾萬餘人」[7] — and the record of the campaign reads 「先主遣諸葛亮自結於孫權，權遣周瑜、程普等水軍數萬，與先主并力，與曹公戰於赤壁，大破之」[7]. Zhuge Liang's pitch to Sun Quan also stressed that 「曹操之眾，遠來疲弊」, that 「且北方之人，不習水戰」, that Jing's people followed Cao only under duress, 「非心服也」, so that 「與豫州協規同力，破操軍必矣」[23]. This matched Zhou Yu's own reasoning, which is why the alliance was easy to make once Sun Quan had decided to fight.

## A note on who gets the credit

The sources disagree on whose idea the alliance was. 《蜀书·诸葛亮传》 presents Zhuge Liang as persuading Sun Quan [4], while 裴松之按 insists the joint resistance was Lu Su's original plan: 「臣松之案：劉備與權並力，共拒中國，皆肅之本謀」[1], and he faults the two accounts for each claiming the credit [1]. Sun Quan himself later told Lu Xun that Lu Su had 「勸孤急呼公瑾，付任以眾，逆而擊之」[18]. So the alliance should be read as two parties each pursuing its own interest — Jiangdong's survival and imperial ambition on one side, Liu Bei's need for a base and a backer on the other — rather than Sun Quan buying protection from a stronger neighbor.

**Inference (据此推断):** Putting the facts above together — surrender meant ruin for Sun Quan personally [14]; Lu Su's strategy was to use Liu Bei as a buffer and multiply Cao Cao's enemies [12][15]; Zhou Yu judged Cao Cao beatable [19][25]; and Liu Bei in fact supplied ships and Liu Qi's troops [7] — the incentive was mutual rather than one-sided. From these facts it follows that Sun Quan gained an extra front against Cao Cao and a client in Jing province, while Liu Bei gained the only force capable of stopping Cao Cao; neither party was buying mere survival from the other.

q: This man did not personally lead the army that conquered Shu, yet he pushed the war of conquest forward while he controlled the Cao-Wei court. His son later replaced Cao-Wei and founded the Western Jin. Who was he?
reply:
## Answer: Sima Zhao (司马昭), posthumously "King Wen of Jin" (晋文王)

The man described is **Sima Zhao** (司马昭, also called 司马文王 / 晋文王). The Shu campaign was planned and directed by him, but the armies that actually invaded Shu were led by his generals Zhong Hui and Deng Ai; and it was his son **Sima Yan** (司马炎, i.e. Emperor Wu of Jin, 晋武帝) who took the throne and founded the Western Jin.

### Evidence

**1. Sima Zhao pushed the conquest of Shu forward.**

He decided on the campaign and appointed the commanders:
「文王以蜀大將姜維屢擾邊陲，料蜀國小民疲，資力單竭，欲大舉圖蜀。惟會亦以為蜀可取，豫共籌度地形，考論事勢。景元三年冬，以會為鎮西將軍、假節都督關中諸軍事。」[28-0041]
(King Wen, reckoning that the Shu general Jiang Wei repeatedly harassed the frontier and that Shu was small, its people worn out and its resources exhausted, wished to make a great effort to take Shu; and in the winter of Jingyuan 3 he made Zhong Hui General Who Conquers the West and acting commissioner over military affairs in Guanzhong.)

The campaign was carried out by his generals, not by him in person:
「四年秋，乃下詔使鄧艾、諸葛緒各統諸軍三萬餘人，艾趣甘松、沓中連綴維，緒趣武街、橋頭絕維歸路。會統十餘萬眾，分從斜谷、駱谷入。」[28-0041]
(In the autumn of Jingyuan 4 an edict sent Deng Ai and Zhuge Xu each with over 30,000 men, Deng Ai heading for Gansong and Tazhong to hold Jiang Wei, Zhuge Xu for Wujie and Qiaotou to cut off his retreat; Zhong Hui commanded over 100,000 and entered by the Xie Valley and Luo Valley.)

The same is stated in the annals of the last Wei emperor:
「今使征西將軍鄧艾督帥諸軍，趣甘松、沓中以羅取維，雍州刺史諸葛緒督諸軍趣武都、高樓，首尾踧討。」[11]
「又命鎮西將軍鍾會由駱谷伐蜀。」[11]
(An edict sent Deng Ai to Gansong and Tazhong to net Jiang Wei, Zhuge Xu to Wudu and Gaolou for a pincer attack; and Zhong Hui was ordered to invade Shu by the Luo Valley.)

**2. He controlled the Cao-Wei court.**

He was made Chancellor and Duke of Jin with the Nine Bestowments, later raised to King of Jin with imperial regalia:
「進大將軍司馬文王位為相國，封晉公，增封二郡，并前滿十，加九錫之禮」[27]
「又命晉王冕十有二旒，建天子旌旗，出警入蹕……」[04-0081]
(He was advanced to Chancellor and enfeoffed as Duke of Jin, with two additional commanderies making ten in all, and given the Nine Bestowments; later the King of Jin was given a twelve-tasseled crown, the banners of a Son of Heaven, and the "clear the way" and "halt" prerogatives.)

**3. His son replaced Cao-Wei and founded the Western Jin.**

On Sima Zhao's death, his son inherited his position:
「秋八月辛卯，相國晉王薨。壬辰，晉太子炎紹封襲位，總攝百揆，備物典冊，一皆如前。」[04-0081]
(In the autumn, on the xinmao day of the eighth month, the Chancellor, the King of Jin, died. On the renchen day, the Jin heir-apparent Yan inherited the fief and the position and took overall charge of all affairs.)

And Sima Yan then ascended the throne:
「明年十二月而晉武帝即尊位」[19] (裴注引《襄阳记》)
(In the twelfth month of the following year, Emperor Wu of Jin ascended the honored position.)

### Inference

Drawing these facts together: Sima Zhao held the posts of Chancellor and King of Jin and issued the orders that launched the Shu campaign [27][28-0041], while the field commanders were Deng Ai and Zhong Hui [28-0041][11]. Therefore the description fits Sima Zhao — he drove the conquest forward without personally leading the conquering army. And since his son Sima Yan succeeded him and then took the throne [04-0081][19], the "son who replaced Cao-Wei and founded the Western Jin" is Sima Yan (晋武帝).

## 结论: 此人是司马昭 (司马文王 / 晋文王)

他主持了灭蜀之役的决策和部署, 但亲统大军入蜀的是他的将领钟会、邓艾; 灭蜀之后, 继承其位的是晋太子司马炎, 即晋武帝。

### 依据

**1. 灭蜀之役是他推动、由他将领执行的**

「文王以蜀大將姜維屢擾邊陲，料蜀國小民疲，資力單竭，欲大舉圖蜀。惟會亦以為蜀可取，豫共籌度地形，考論事勢。景元三年冬，以會為鎮西將軍、假節都督關中諸軍事。」[3]

「四年秋，乃下詔使鄧艾、諸葛緒各統諸軍三萬餘人，艾趣甘松、沓中連綴維，緒趣武街、橋頭絕維歸路。會統十餘萬眾，分從斜谷、駱谷入。」[3]

同一诏令也见于魏帝纪: 「今使征西將軍鄧艾督帥諸軍，趣甘松、沓中以羅取維」[11], 「又命鎮西將軍鍾會由駱谷伐蜀。」[11]

入蜀军由钟会、邓艾率领, 裴注引《蜀記》亦称「隨鍾、鄧伐蜀」[4]。

他自己并未随军入蜀, 而是在钟会告发邓艾之后才西行: 「及會白鄧艾不軌，文王將西」[1], 「軍至長安，會果已死，咸如所策。」[1]

**2. 他执掌曹魏朝政**

「進大將軍司馬文王位為相國，封晉公」[27] (事在景元元年夏六月丙辰)。

后又用天子仪制: 「又命晉王冕十有二旒，建天子旌旗，出警入蹕」[21]。

**3. 其子取代曹魏、建立西晋**

他死后由晋太子炎继位: 「秋八月辛卯，相國晉王薨。壬辰，晉太子炎紹封襲位，總攝百揆」[21]。

此司马炎即晋武帝: 「明年十二月而晋武帝即尊位」[19] (裴注引《襄阳记》); 又「及受禪，改封鄄城公」[13] 所记"晋武帝……及受禅"即此人之受禅; 「泰始元年，晉受禪」[28] (裴注引《晉諸公贊》)。

### 据此推断

依据以上各条: 灭蜀的决策出于司马昭, 受命统兵的是邓艾、诸葛绪、钟会 [3][11], 他本人直到钟会告发邓艾之后才西行至长安 [1]; 他当时的身份是相国、晋公、晋王, 并用天子仪制 [27][21]; 他死后由晋太子炎绍封袭位、总摄百揆 [21], 而司马炎即晋武帝、晋受禅 [19][13][28]。由此推断: 题目所说"推动灭蜀之役而本人未亲统灭蜀大军、执掌曹魏朝政、其子取代曹魏建立西晋"的人, 就是司马昭; 题中所说的"其子", 按资料中的继承关系 (晋王薨、晋太子炎绍封袭位) 即是司马炎。资料未直接写"父子"二字, 这一层是从"晋太子炎"承袭"相国晋王"的记载推出来的。

q: Shu-Han's main base was Yi Province, and its northern expeditions had to haul grain across the mountains to the front. Why did 'winning a battle at the front' not necessarily mean 'being able to hold the newly gained territory for long'?
reply:
## Short answer

Because in the《三国志》record Shu's problem was never just "can we beat the enemy in the field?" — it was "can we feed the army at the far end of a mountain road long enough to hold what we took?" Repeatedly the text says the campaign ended not with a defeat but with **「糧盡退軍」** — "the grain ran out and the army withdrew." A Wei commander could literally count the days: **「郃知亮縣軍無穀，不能久攻」**, and **「屈指計亮糧不至十日」** [35]. 据此推断：既然守方也清楚这一点，守方最合算的做法就是拒不出战、拖到对方断粮；因此前线的胜利只买到时间，买不到地盘。

## The evidence

**1. Campaigns end in withdrawal for grain, not defeat.**

- 建兴六年冬（陈仓）：**「冬，復出散關，圍陳倉，糧盡退」** [6]；《诸葛亮传》作 **「亮糧盡而還」** [3]。
- 建兴九年：**「九年，亮復出祁山，以木牛運，糧盡退軍」** [1]；《后主传》作 **「夏六月，亮糧盡退軍」** [14]。
- 建兴十二年：**「亮每患糧不繼，使己志不申，是以分兵屯田，為久駐之基」** [1]。
- 姜维后来：**「維糧盡退還」** [29]。

**2. The rear transport itself failed.**

建兴九年李平（李严）**「催督運事」** [18]，结果 **「秋夏之際，值天霖雨，運糧不繼，平遣參軍狐忠、督軍成藩喻指，呼亮來還；亮承以退軍」** [18]。据此推断：这一次使战役中止的是霖雨造成的运粮不继，不是前线战败。魏方陈群论斜谷道也说 **「轉運必見鈔截」** [38]；杨阜说 **「轉運之勞，擔負之苦」** [40]。

**3. The hauling burden fell on the whole state.**

杨洪论汉中危急：**「男子當戰，女子當運」** [20]。连将领子弟也运粮——诸葛亮给兄长诸葛瑾的信说诸葛乔 **「今使喬督五六百兵，與諸子弟傳於谷中」** [39]。

**4. Wei's strategy was to outlast, not to win.**

魏明帝诏司马宣王：**「但堅壁拒守以挫其鋒，彼進不得志，退無與戰，乆停則糧盡，虜略無所獲，則必走矣」** [32]。张郃在陈仓之役的判断——**「郃知亮縣軍無穀，不能久攻」** [35]——是同一逻辑。裴注引《汉晋春秋》记张郃对司马宣王说 **「今亮縣軍食少，亦行去矣」** [13]。

**5. The two sides were not equally fed from the ground.**

陇右无谷时，郭淮 **「以威恩撫循羌、胡，家使出穀，平其輸調，軍食用足」** [46]。蜀方则有时要夺取当地麦子：诸葛亮 **「因大芟刈其麥」** [13]；裴注引《魏书》则说魏方 **「賴得此麥以為軍糧」** [2]。

**6. Even clear victories did not hold ground.**

建兴九年诸葛亮军打了一场大胜——**「大破之，獲甲首三千級，玄鎧五千領，角弩三千一百張」** [34]——而同一役仍记为 **「糧盡退軍」** [1]。姜维最大的一次胜利在洮西，**「大破魏雍州刺史王經於洮西，經眾死者數萬人」** [29]；接着魏方解狄道之围，**「姜維退還」** [30]。王经被救后的感叹可见当时形势之险：**「粮不至旬，向不應机，舉城屠裂，覆喪一州矣」** [41]。

## Inference (this is my reading, not a statement in the text)

据此推断：把上面几条合起来看——蜀军的粮食来自一条要翻越秦岭、运输又常被霖雨和劫截打断的补给线 [18][38][40]，而敌方知道这一点并有意拒战拖延 [32][35][13]；当地的麦子或被蜀军收割、或被魏军保住充作军粮 [13][2]，魏方还能从当地羌、胡按户征粮 [46]。所以前线打赢之后，新得的城池、郡县仍只能靠益州越山运粮来守；粮一断，所得就在退军时交还。这就是《三国志》里胜利常与 **「糧盡退軍」** 并列出现的原因 [1][29]。

Emperor Ming's edict to Sima Yi: **「但堅壁拒守以挫其鋒，彼進不得志，退無與戰，乆停則糧盡，虜略無所獲，則必走矣」** [32]. Zhang He's judgment at Chencang — **「亮縣軍無穀，不能久攻」** [35] — is the same logic. Han Jin Chunqiu has Zhang He tell Sima Yi, **「今亮縣軍食少，亦行去矣」** [13].

**5. The two sides were not equally fed from the ground.**

When Longyou had no grain, Guo Huai **「以威恩撫循羌、胡，家使出穀，平其輸調，軍食用足」** [46] — Wei could tax the local Qiang and Hu households. Shu, by contrast, sometimes had to seize the crop: Zhuge Liang **「因大芟刈其麥」** [13], and the Wei Shu notes the defenders **「賴得此麥以為軍糧」** [2]. So the very ground Shu fought over could feed the defender, while Shu's own supply still had to come over the mountains.

**6. Even clear victories did not hold ground.**

In Jianxing 9 Zhuge Liang's troops won a set battle — **「大破之，獲甲首三千級，玄鎧五千領，角弩三千一百張」** [34] — yet the same campaign is recorded as ending in **「糧盡退軍」** [1]. Jiang Wei's greatest win, at Taoxi, **「大破魏雍州刺史王經於洮西，經眾死者數萬人」** [29], was followed by Wei relieving Didao and **「姜維退還」** [30]. Wang Jing's own words after being saved show how close the balance was: **「粮不至旬，向不應机，舉城屠裂，覆喪一州矣」** [41].

## Inference (this is my reading, not a statement in the text)

Putting the above together: Shu's army ate from a line that took a long time to cross the Qinling passes, and the enemy knew it and refused battle [32][35]. Therefore a battlefield win did not convert into lasting control, because (a) the winner still had to eat, (b) the local grain had either already been harvested by one side or the other [13][2], and (c) the defender could supply himself from local Qiang/Hu contributions [46] while the attacker could not. So each newly gained commandery or city had to be held by troops who could only be fed from Yi Province — and when the grain ran out, the gain was given back on the withdrawal. This is why the record pairs victories so often with **「糧盡退軍」** [1][29].

## Short answer

Because in the《三国志》record Shu's problem was never just "can we beat the enemy in the field?" — it was "can we feed the army at the far end of a mountain road long enough to hold what we took?" Repeatedly the text says the campaign ended not with a defeat but with **「糧盡退軍」** — "the grain ran out and the army withdrew." A Wei commander could literally count the days: **「郃知亮縣軍無穀，不能久攻」**, and **「屈指計亮糧不至十日」** [35]. 据此推断：既然守方也清楚这一点，守方最合算的做法就是拒不出战、拖到对方断粮；因此前线的胜利只买到时间，买不到地盘。

## The evidence

**1. Campaigns end in withdrawal for grain, not defeat.**

- 建兴六年冬（陈仓）：**「冬，復出散關，圍陳倉，糧盡退」** [6]；《诸葛亮传》作 **「亮糧盡而還」** [3]。
- 建兴九年：**「九年，亮復出祁山，以木牛運，糧盡退軍」** [1]；《后主传》作 **「夏六月，亮糧盡退軍」** [14]。
- 建兴十二年：**「亮每患糧不繼，使己志不申，是以分兵屯田，為久駐之基」** [1]。
- 姜维后来：**「維糧盡退還」** [29]。

**2. The rear transport itself failed.**

建兴九年李平（李严）**「催督運事」** [18]，结果 **「值天霖雨，運糧不繼，平遣參軍狐忠、督軍成藩喻指，呼亮來還；亮承以退軍」** [18]。据此推断：这一次使战役中止的是霖雨造成的运粮不继，不是前线战败。魏方陈群论斜谷道也说 **「轉運必見鈔截」** [38]；杨阜说 **「轉運之勞，擔負之苦」** [40]。

**3. The hauling burden fell on the whole state.**

杨洪论汉中危急：**「男子當戰，女子當運」** [20]。连将领子弟也运粮——诸葛亮给兄长诸葛瑾的信说诸葛乔 **「今使喬督五六百兵，與諸子弟傳於谷中」** [39]。

**4. Wei's strategy was to outlast, not to win.**

魏明帝诏司马宣王：**「但堅壁拒守以挫其鋒，彼進不得志，退無與戰，乆停則糧盡，虜略無所獲，則必走矣」** [32]。张郃在陈仓之役的判断——**「郃知亮縣軍無穀，不能久攻」** [35]——是同一逻辑。裴注引《汉晋春秋》记张郃对司马宣王说 **「今亮縣軍食少，亦行去矣」** [13]。

**5. The two sides were not equally fed from the ground.**

陇右无谷时，郭淮 **「以威恩撫循羌、胡，家使出穀，平其輸調，軍食用足」** [46]。蜀方则有时要夺取当地麦子：诸葛亮 **「因大芟刈其麥」** [13]；裴注引《魏书》则说魏方 **「賴得此麥以為軍糧」** [2]。

**6. Even clear victories did not hold ground.**

建兴九年诸葛亮军打了一场大胜——**「大破之，獲甲首三千級，玄鎧五千領，角弩三千一百張」** [34]——而同一役仍记为 **「糧盡退軍」** [1]。姜维最大的一次胜利在洮西，**「大破魏雍州刺史王經於洮西，經眾死者數萬人」** [29]；接着魏方解狄道之围，**「姜維退還」** [30]。王经被救后的感叹可见当时形势之险：**「粮不至旬，向不應机，舉城屠裂，覆喪一州矣」** [41]。

## Inference (this is my reading, not a statement in the text)

据此推断：把上面几条合起来看——蜀军的粮食来自一条要翻越秦岭、运输又常被霖雨和劫截打断的补给线 [18][38][40]，而敌方知道这一点并有意拒战拖延 [32][35][13]；当地的麦子或被蜀军收割、或被魏军保住充作军粮 [13][2]，魏方还能从当地羌、胡按户征粮 [46]。所以前线打赢之后，新得的城池、郡县仍只能靠益州越山运粮来守；粮一断，所得就在退军时交还。这就是《三国志》里胜利常与 **「糧盡退軍」** 并列出现的原因 [1][29]。

q: While Kuan Yü was attacking Fan in the north, Sun Ch'üan's side seized Chiang-ling and other places in his rear. Why could Kuan Yü still collapse so quickly overall, even though he had won a major victory on the northern front?
reply:
## Conclusion

Guan Yu's collapse was fast because his northern success was never a finished conquest, and because the same move that produced it — pulling his rear garrisons north — left his base, his supplies and his soldiers' families exposed. Judging from what the《三国志》records, four connected factors explain it:

1. The northern victory was won by flood, and Fan城 never fell; a Wei relief force was already pushing him back.
2. He had drawn his rear garrisons north, which was precisely what Lü Meng's plan required.
3. His own base commanders, Shi Ren and Mi Fang, went over at once, so Jiangling and Gong'an were lost without a fight.
4. The seizure of his men's families at Jiangling destroyed the army's will to fight; his soldiers dispersed on the march back and he was caught with only a few riders.

Details below.

## 1. The northern success was not a completed conquest

Guan Yu's victory was real and spectacular: 「秋，大霖雨，漢水汎溢，禁所督七軍皆沒。禁降羽，羽又斬將軍龐德」[2]; 「羽威震華夏。曹公議徙許都以避其銳」[2]. The year is given as 「二十四年，先主為漢中王，拜羽為前將軍，假節鉞」[2], and the same campaign is dated in the Wu record as 「二十四年，關羽圍曹仁於襄陽」[38]; 建安二十四年 = AD 219.

But Fan城 itself held: 「仁人馬數千人守城，城不沒者數板。羽乘船临城，圍數重，外内斷絕，糧食欲盡，救兵不至」[1]. And Wei's relief was already under way: 「遣于禁助曹仁擊關羽」[8], 「使徐晃救之」[8]. Xu Huang advanced and was reinforced: 「晃所將多新卒，以羽難與爭鋒，遂前至陽陵陂屯」[22]; 「太祖前後遣殷署、朱蓋等凡十二營詣晃」[22]; and finally 「晃擊之，退走，遂追陷與俱入圍，破之」[22], so that 「仁得溃圍出，羽退走」[1].

Guan Yu was also still besieging two places at once: 「羽圍仁於樊，又圍將軍呂常於襄陽」[22]. Cao's side further used Sun Quan's letter to keep him from disengaging: 「曹公且欲使羽與權相持以鬬之，驛傳權書，使曹仁以弩射示羽。羽猶豫不能去」[38].

## 2. He had pulled his rear garrisons north — exactly what Lü Meng wanted

Lü Meng's plan was built on Guan Yu's need to send troops north:

「羽討樊而多留備兵，必恐蒙圖其後故也。蒙常有病，乞分士眾還建業，以治疾為名。羽聞之，必撤備兵，盡赴襄陽。大軍浮江，晝夜馳上，襲其空虛，則南郡可下，而羽可擒也」[17].

The record states it worked: 「羽果信之，稍撤兵以赴樊」[17].

## 3. His own base commanders surrendered at once

Guan Yu's relations with his rear commanders were already bad:

「又南郡太守麋芳在江陵，將軍士仁屯公安，素皆嫌羽輕己」[2]; 「羽之出軍，芳、仁供給軍資，不悉相救」[2]; Guan Yu said he would deal with them on his return (「還當治之」[2]), and 「芳、仁咸懷懼不安。於是權陰誘芳、仁，芳、仁使人迎權」[2].

The result is recorded plainly: 「遂到南郡，士仁、麋芳皆降」[17]; 「蒙到南郡，南郡太守糜芳以城降」[38]; and in the Shu appraisal, 「與羽有隙，叛迎孫權」[11]. The Wu record also has 「權征羽，先遣呂蒙襲公安，獲將軍士仁」[38]. A further rear official went over too: 潘濬字承明，武陵人，先主入蜀后任荆州治中，主管留守州里的事务，也与关羽不和睦，孙权袭击关羽，他于是进入吴国 [11].

So Jiangling and Gong'an — his base, his stores and his families — changed hands without a siege. In the same campaign Wu also took the neighbouring commandery: 「陸遜別取宜都，獲秭歸、枝江、夷道，還屯夷陵，守峽口以備蜀」[38].

## 4. The loss of the families broke the army

This is the recorded mechanism. Lü Meng took the city and treated the families well: 「蒙入據城，盡得羽及將士家屬，皆撫慰，約令軍中不得乾歷人家，有所求取」[17]; 「羽府藏財寶，皆封閉以待權至」[17]. He then used Guan Yu's own messengers: 「羽還，在道路，數使人與蒙相聞，蒙輒厚遇其使，周遊城中，家家致問，或手書示信。羽人還，私相參訊，咸知家門無恙，見待過於平時，故羽吏士無鬬心」[18]. The Shu record puts it as 「權已據江陵，盡虜羽士眾妻子，羽軍遂散」[2]. The retreat and end: 「關羽還當陽，西保麥城」[38]; 「羽偽降，立幡旗爲像人於城上，因遁走，兵皆解散，尚十餘騎」[38]; and the capture 「十二月，璋司馬馬忠獲羽及其子平、都督趙累等於章鄉」[38]. The Shu record places the killing differently: 「權遣將逆擊羽，斬羽及子平於臨沮」[2].

The Wu attack and the capture fall inside the same year and are dated in the Wu record: 「閏月，權征羽」[38], 「十二月，璋司馬馬忠獲羽及其子平、都督趙累等於章鄉」[38].

## Inferences (marked as such)

- **Judging from [17] and [2], the two defeats are not independent.** Lü Meng's plan explicitly required Guan Yu to move his reserves north ([17]), and the northern advance was what created the undefended rear. So the northern success and the collapse are linked — but the link is Guan Yu's redistribution of troops, not the victory as such. The sources do not say the victory caused the collapse.
- **Judging from [1], [22] and [38], the northern front was already turning against him before the rear fell.** Fan城 still held ([1]), Xu Huang's relief force had engaged and driven him back ([22]), and Cao kept him hesitating with Sun Quan's letter ([38]). At the moment the rear fell, he was withdrawing from an unfinished siege, not sitting on a consolidated conquest.
- **Judging from [18] and [2], the speed of the collapse is best explained by the loss of the families rather than by battlefield casualties.** The records say his officers and men 「無鬬心」 and that the army 「遂散」 once they learned their families were safe in Lü Meng's hands. This points to a collapse of morale and cohesion; [38]'s "only a dozen or so riders left" is consistent with that.
- **Judging from [2], [11] and [17], the defection of Mi Fang and Shi Ren removed any chance of holding out.** Their fear of Guan Yu's promised punishment and their grievances gave Sun Quan collaborators inside the base, so the rear did not have to be taken by force.
- **On the attempted help:** Liu Feng and Meng Da were called on and refused — 「自關羽圍樊城、襄陽，連呼封、達，令發兵自助。封、達辭以山郡初附，未可動搖，不承羽命」[28] — and Liu Feng was later blamed 「不救羽」[27]. That they refused is recorded. Whether timely help from them would actually have saved Guan Yu is not settled by the sources, so I do not conclude that it would have.

Two further recorded points belonging to the background of the Wu decision rather than to the collapse itself: Guan Yu had earlier insulted Sun Quan's marriage envoy — 「權遣使為子索羽女，羽罵辱其使，不許婚，權大怒」[2] — and he had taken Wu's grain — 「託以糧乏，擅取湘關米。權聞之，遂行」[17]; the Wu record says Sun Quan 「內憚羽，外欲以為己功，箋與曹公，乞以討羽自效」[38].
