## Conclusion

The northern victory at Fan was real, but it was never a decisive conquest, and it left Guan Yu's army in a position that a sudden blow to his rear could destroy. Judging from what the《三国志》records, Guan Yu collapsed quickly for four connected reasons:

1. **The northern victory was won by flood, not by breaking Cao's main force** — the enemy armies were drowned, not destroyed, and Fan城 itself never fell; the Wei relief force under Xu Huang was still coming.
2. **He had drawn his rear garrisons north** — Lü Meng's whole plan was to make him do exactly that.
3. **His own base commanders (Shi Ren, Mi Fang) defected at once**, so Jiangling and Gong'an fell without a fight.
4. **The seizure of his men's families at Jiangling destroyed the army's will to fight** — his soldiers dispersed on the march back, and he was caught at Linju/Zhangxiang with only a few riders.

(Guan Yu left many troops to guard against me; I will pretend to be ill and be recalled to Jianye; he will then withdraw the garrison troops and send them all to Xiangyang; our army will then race up the river by night and day and strike the undefended rear.) This is the decisive mechanism. Lü Meng took the whole city and treated the families well:

「蒙入據城，盡得羽及將士家屬，皆撫慰，約令軍中不得乾歷人家，有所求取」[17]; 「羽府藏財寶，皆封閉以待權至」[17].

Then he used Guan Yu's own messengers to spread the news: 「羽還，在道路，數使人與蒙相聞，蒙輒厚遇其使，周遊城中，家家致問，或手書示信。羽人還，私相參訊，咸知家門無恙，見待過於平時，故羽吏士無鬬心」[18]. And in the Shu record: 「權已據江陵，盡虜羽士眾妻子，羽軍遂散」[2]. The《Wu Zhu Zhuan》gives the sequence: 「關羽還當陽，西保麥城……羽偽降，立幡旗爲像人於城上，因遁走，兵皆解散，尚十餘騎」[38]; 「十二月，璋司馬馬忠獲羽及其子平、都督趙累等於章鄉」[38].

## Inferences (marked as such)

- **Judging from [17] and [2], the two defeats were not independent.** Lü Meng's plan explicitly required Guan Yu to move his reserves north ([17]), and the northern advance was exactly what created the undefended rear. So the northern success and the collapse are causally linked — but the link is Guan Yu's redistribution of troops, not "the victory itself."
- **Judging from [1], [22] and [8], the northern front was turning against him even before Lü Meng struck.** Cao Ren still held Fan, Xu Huang's relief force was already engaged and had pushed Guan Yu back ([22], [1]). Therefore, at the moment the rear fell, Guan Yu was not sitting on a consolidated conquest but was withdrawing from an unfinished siege.
- **Judging from [18] and [2], the speed of the collapse is best explained by the loss of the families, not by casualties.** The records say his officers and men 「無鬬心」 and that the army 「遂散」 when they learned their families were safe in Lü Meng's hands. This is a discipline/morale collapse rather than a battlefield annihilation — consistent with [38]'s "only a dozen or so riders left."
- **Judging from [11], [2] and [17], the defection of Mi Fang and Shi Ren removed any chance of holding out.** Their fear of Guan Yu's promised punishment and their personal grievances gave Sun Quan ready-made collaborators, so the rear did not have to be taken by force.
- **On the attempted help:** Liu Feng and Meng Da were called on and refused: 「自關羽圍樊城、襄陽，連呼封、達，令發兵自助。封、達辭以山郡初附，未可動搖，不承羽命」[28], and Liu Feng was later blamed for 「不救羽」[27]. This is recorded as a fact; whether timely help from them could actually have saved Guan Yu is not something the sources settle — I would not conclude that it would have.

Two side points from the records worth noting: Guan Yu had earlier insulted Sun Quan's marriage envoy — 「權遣使為子索羽女，羽罵辱其使，不許婚，權大怒」[2] — and he had seized Wu's grain — 「託以糧乏，擅取湘關米。權聞之，遂行」[17]; the Wu record says Sun Quan 「內憚羽，外欲以為己功，箋與曹公，乞以討羽自效」[38]. These belong to the background of the Wu decision, not to the collapse itself.

## Conclusion

Guan Yu's collapse was fast because his northern success was never a finished conquest, and because the same move that produced it — pulling his rear garrisons north — left his base, his supplies and his soldiers' families exposed. Judging from what the《三国志》records, four connected factors explain it:

1. The northern victory was won by flood, and Fan城 never fell; a Wei relief force was already pushing him back.
2. He had drawn his rear garrisons north, which was precisely what Lü Meng's plan required.
3. His own base commanders, Shi Ren and Mi Fang, went over at once, so Jiangling and Gong'an were lost without a fight.
4. The seizure of his men's families at Jiangling destroyed the army's will to fight; his soldiers dispersed on the march back and he was caught with only a few riders.

Details below.

## 1. The northern success was not a completed conquest

Guan Yu's victory was real and spectacular: 「秋，大霖雨，漢水汎溢，禁所督七軍皆沒。禁降羽，羽又斬將軍龐德」[2]; 「羽威震華夏。曹公議徙許都以避其銳」[2]. The year is given as 「二十四年，先主為漢中王，拜羽為前將軍，假節鉞」[2], and the same campaign is dated in the Wu record as 「二十四年，關羽圍曹仁於襄陽」[38]; 建安二十四年 = AD 219.

But Fan城 itself held: 「仁人馬數千人守城，城不沒者數板。羽乘船临城，圍數重，外内斷絕，糧食欲盡，救兵不至」[1]. And Wei's relief was already under way: 「遣于禁助曹仁擊關羽」[8], 「使徐晃救之」[8]. Xu Huang advanced and was reinforced: 「晃所將多新卒，以羽難與爭鋒，遂前至陽陵陂屯」[22]; 「太祖前後遣殷署、朱蓋等凡十二營詣晃」[22]; and finally 「晃擊之，退走，遂追陷與俱入圍，破之」[22], so that 「仁得溃圍出，羽退走」[1].

Guan Yu was also still besieging two places at once: 「羽圍仁於樊，又圍將軍呂常於襄陽」[22]. Cao's side further used Sun Quan's letter to keep him from disengaging: 「曹公且欲使羽與權相持以鬬之，驛傳權書，使曹仁以弩射示羽。羽猶豫不能去」[38].

## 2. He had pulled his rear garrisons north — exactly what Lü Meng wanted

Lü Meng's plan was built on Guan Yu's need to send troops north:

「羽討樊而多留備兵，必恐蒙圖其後故也。蒙常有病，乞分士眾還建業，以治疾為名。羽聞之，必撤備兵，盡赴襄陽。大軍浮江，晝夜馳上，襲其空虛，則南郡可下，而羽可擒也」[17].

The record states it worked: 「羽果信之，稍撤兵以赴樊」[17].

## 3. His own base commanders surrendered at once

Guan Yu's relations with his rear commanders were already bad:

「又南郡太守麋芳在江陵，將軍士仁屯公安，素皆嫌羽輕己」[2]; 「羽之出軍，芳、仁供給軍資，不悉相救」[2]; Guan Yu said he would deal with them on his return (「還當治之」[2]), and 「芳、仁咸懷懼不安。於是權陰誘芳、仁，芳、仁使人迎權」[2].

The result is recorded plainly: 「蒙至南郡，士仁、麋芳皆降」[17]; 「蒙到南郡，南郡太守糜芳以城降」[38]; and in the Shu appraisal, 「與羽有隙，叛迎孫權」[11]. The Wu record also has 「權征羽，先遣呂蒙襲公安，獲將軍士仁」[38]. A further rear official went over too: 「潘濬字承明，武陵人也……亦與關羽不穆。孫權襲羽，遂入吳」[11].

So Jiangling and Gong'an — his base, his stores and his families — changed hands without a siege. In the same campaign Wu also took the neighbouring commandery: 「陸遜別取宜都，獲秭歸、枝江、夷道，還屯夷陵，守峽口以備蜀」[38].

## 4. The loss of the families broke the army

This is the recorded mechanism. Lü Meng took the city and treated the families well: 「蒙入據城，盡得羽及將士家屬，皆撫慰，約令軍中不得乾歷人家，有所求取」[17]; 「羽府藏財寶，皆封閉以待權至」[17]. He then used Guan Yu's own messengers: 「羽還，在道路，數使人與蒙相聞，蒙輒厚遇其使，周遊城中，家家致問，或手書示信。羽人還，私相參訊，咸知家門無恙，見待過於平時，故羽吏士無鬬心」[18]. The Shu record puts it as 「權已據江陵，盡虜羽士眾妻子，羽軍遂散」[2]. The retreat and end: 「關羽還當陽，西保麥城」[38]; 「羽偽降，立幡旗爲像人於城上，因遁走，兵皆解散，尚十餘騎」[38]; and the capture 「十二月，璋司馬馬忠獲羽及其子平、都督趙累等於章鄉」[38]. The Shu record places the killing differently: 「權遣將逆擊羽，斬羽及子平於臨沮」[2].

The Wu attack and the capture fall inside the same year and are dated in the Wu record: 「閏月，權征羽」[38], 「十二月，璋司馬馬忠獲羽及其子平、都督趙累等於章鄉」[38].

## Inferences (marked as such)

- **Judging from [17] and [2], the two defeats are not independent.** Lü Meng's plan explicitly required Guan Yu to move his reserves north ([17]), and the northern advance was what created the undefended rear. So the northern success and the collapse are linked — but the link is Guan Yu's redistribution of troops, not the victory as such. The sources do not say the victory caused the collapse.
- **Judging from [1], [22] and [38], the northern front was already turning against him before the rear fell.** Fan城 still held ([1]), Xu Huang's relief force had engaged and driven him back ([22]), and Cao kept him hesitating with Sun Quan's letter ([38]). At the moment the rear fell, he was withdrawing from an unfinished siege, not sitting on a consolidated conquest.
- **Judging from [18] and [2], the speed of the collapse is best explained by the loss of the families rather than by battlefield casualties.** The records say his officers and men 「無鬬心」 and that the army 「遂散」 once they learned their families were safe in Lü Meng's hands. This points to a collapse of morale and cohesion; [38]'s "only a dozen or so riders left" is consistent with that.
- **Judging from [2], [11] and [17], the defection of Mi Fang and Shi Ren removed any chance of holding out.** Their fear of Guan Yu's promised punishment and their grievances gave Sun Quan collaborators inside the base, so the rear did not have to be taken by force.
- **On the attempted help:** Liu Feng and Meng Da were called on and refused — 「自關羽圍樊城、襄陽，連呼封、達，令發兵自助。封、達辭以山郡初附，未可動搖，不承羽命」[28] — and Liu Feng was later blamed 「不救羽」[27]. That they refused is recorded. Whether timely help from them would actually have saved Guan Yu is not settled by the sources, so I do not conclude that it would have.

Two further recorded points belonging to the background of the Wu decision rather than to the collapse itself: Guan Yu had earlier insulted Sun Quan's marriage envoy — 「權遣使為子索羽女，羽罵辱其使，不許婚，權大怒」[2] — and he had taken Wu's grain — 「託以糧乏，擅取湘關米。權聞之，遂行」[17]; the Wu record says Sun Quan 「內憚羽，外欲以為己功，箋與曹公，乞以討羽自效」[38].

q: The Oath of the Peach Garden: after Liu Pei, Kuan Yü and Chang Fei swore brotherhood, what was the order of seniority among the three?
reply:
## Conclusion

The "Oath of the Peach Garden" itself is **not in the *Sanguozhi*** — it comes from the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*. The histories record two relevant things: Liu Bei was the lord whom Guan Yu and Zhang Fei served and attended, and Guan Yu was older than Zhang Fei, who served Guan Yu as an elder brother. So the order of seniority as the record supports it runs Liu Bei (lord) → Guan Yu (the elder of the two followers) → Zhang Fei (the younger). The *Sanguozhi* gives no statement of Liu Bei's age relative to the other two, and no sworn ranking.

## Evidence

**1. Liu Bei treated Guan Yu and Zhang Fei with the affection of brothers, but the relationship described is lord-and-followers:**

> 「先主與二人寢則同床，恩若兄弟。而稠人廣坐，侍立終日，隨先主周旋，不避艱險。」[1]

("The Former Lord slept in the same bed with the two men, their affection like that of brothers. Yet in crowds and in public they stood in attendance all day, following the Former Lord about, not shrinking from hardship or danger.")

**2. Guan Yu was the elder, Zhang Fei the younger:**

> 「張飛字益德，涿郡人也，少與關羽俱事先主。羽年長數歲，飛兄事之。」[2]

("Zhang Fei, styled Yide, a man of Zhuo commandery, in his youth served the Former Lord together with Guan Yu. Guan Yu was several years older; Zhang Fei served him as an elder brother.")

This is the only age/seniority statement the *Sanguozhi* gives among the three, and it covers only Guan Yu vs. Zhang Fei.

**3. Elsewhere the three are simply listed together, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei as Liu Bei's military retainers:**

> 「關羽、張飛、馬超為爪牙」[11]

**4. In the appraisal they are jointly praised, with no mention of an oath:**

> 「關羽、張飛皆稱萬人之敵，為世虎臣。」[5]

## Inference

- Fact A: Liu Bei was the master whom Guan Yu and Zhang Fei "served" and at whose side they stood in attendance [1][2].
- Fact B: Guan Yu was "several years older" than Zhang Fei, and Zhang Fei "served him as an elder brother" [2].
- 据此推断 (On this basis): the order of seniority the record supports is Liu Bei first (the lord they served), Guan Yu second (the elder of the two followers), Zhang Fei third (the younger, who deferred to Guan Yu). This is inferred from status and age; the *Sanguozhi* does not state that the three became sworn brothers or in what order.

## Background

以下不是《三国志》的记载:

The Peach Garden Oath — Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei swearing brotherhood in a peach garden and ranking themselves as elder brother, second brother and third brother — is not recorded in the *Sanguozhi*; it comes from the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* or other non-official traditions.

> 「先主與二人寢則同床，恩若兄弟。而稠人廣坐，侍立終日，隨先主周旋，不避艱險。」[1]

("The Former Lord slept in the same bed with the two men, their affection like that of brothers. Yet in crowds and in public they stood in attendance all day, following the Former Lord about, not shrinking from hardship or danger.")

Note the structure: they *attended* him ("侍立終日"), i.e., he was the lord and they the subordinates.

**2. Guan Yu was the elder, Zhang Fei the younger:**

> 「張飛字益德，涿郡人也，少與關羽俱事先主。羽年長數歲，飛兄事之。」[2]

("Zhang Fei, styled Yide, a man of Zhuo commandery, in his youth served the Former Lord together with Guan Yu. Guan Yu was several years older; Zhang Fei served him as an elder brother.")

q: A Cao-Wei emperor left Luoyang to pay respects at the imperial tombs, and a senior minister who had long pleaded illness seized the chance to take control of the capital and force the other regent to surrender his power. What event was this, and who set it in motion?
reply:
## The event: the imperial visit to Gaoping Tomb (高平陵) and Sima Yi's seizure of Luoyang, 嘉平元年 (= 249 CE)

**Who set it in motion:** Sima Yi (司馬懿, styled Zhongda — in the sources 司馬宣王, by then 太傅), who had pleaded illness to keep out of the way of the regent Cao Shuang (曹爽), the Grand General (大將軍). The emperor who left the capital for the tomb was the Qi Wang (齊王), i.e. Cao Fang (曹芳).

### The two regents

Emperor Ming, dying, entrusted his successor to Sima Yi together with Cao Shuang:

> 「吾疾甚，以後事屬君，君其與爽輔少子。」[13]

Cao Shuang's own biography records the same arrangement:

> 「與太尉司馬宣王並受遺詔輔少主」[1]

and that after Emperor Ming's death the Qi Wang took the throne: 「明帝崩，齊王即位」[1].

### The feigned illness

> 「爽以宣王年德並高，恒父事之，不敢專行」[3]

Then Cao Shuang's party moved to sideline him — by having him promoted to a purely honorific post:

> 「丁謐畫策，使爽白天子，發詔轉宣王爲太傅，外以名號尊之，內欲令尚書奏事，先來由己，得制其輕重也。」[1]

> 「諸事希復由宣王」[3]

> 「宣王遂稱疾避爽」[3]

The illness was deliberately staged as cover, as his biography shows in the winter before the coup:

> 「九年冬，李勝出爲荊州刺史，往詣宣王。宣王稱疾困篤，示以羸形。勝不能覺，謂之信然。」[8]

### The emperor's visit to the tomb

The Qi Wang's annals date the affair:

> 「嘉平元年春正月甲午，車駕謁高平陵。」[2]

(The era tool gives 嘉平元年 = 249 CE.) The tomb was Emperor Ming's: the *Mingdi ji* records of him 「即日，帝崩于嘉福殿，時年三十六。癸丑，葬高平陵。」[13]

### The seizure of the capital

> 「十年正月，車駕朝高平陵，爽兄弟皆從。宣王部勒兵馬，先據武庫，遂出屯洛水浮橋。」[8]

He then memorialized against Cao Shuang (「奏爽曰」[8]), and in that memorial wrote:

> 「臣輙力疾，將兵屯洛水浮橋，伺察非常。」[16]

He reported the Empress Dowager's authorization:

> 「皇太後令勑臣如奏施行。」[8]

and the annals record the resulting act:

> 「太傅司馬宣王奏免大將軍曹爽、爽弟中領軍羲、武衞將軍訓、散騎常侍彥官，以侯就第。」[2]

### Cao Shuang surrenders his power

The emperor was with Cao Shuang, as Huan Fan's words to Cao Xi show: 「今卿與天子相隨」[9]. Huan Fan urged him to use that:

> 「範說爽使車駕幸許昌，招外兵。」[9]

Cao Shuang refused, and surrendered:

> 「侍中許允、尚書陳泰說爽，使早自歸罪。爽於是遣允、泰詣宣王，歸罪請死，乃通宣王奏事。遂免爽兄弟，以侯還第。」[9]

### Aftermath

On the Yellow Gate Zhang Dang's testimony (「有司奏収黃門張當付廷尉，考實其辭，爽與謀不軌」[2]), Cao Shuang and his associates were executed:

> 「於是收爽、羲、訓、晏、颺、謐、軌、勝、範、當等，皆伏誅，夷三族。」[17]

### By way of inference

Setting out the facts already cited: (1) Emperor Ming named Cao Shuang and Sima Yi jointly to assist the young ruler [1][13]; (2) Cao Shuang's party then pushed Sima Yi into the honorific post of Grand Tutor so that memorials would first pass through Cao Shuang [1], and "various affairs rarely passed through Sima Xuan-wang any more" [3]; (3) Sima Yi responded by pleading illness [3], and staged a convincing display of it for Li Sheng [8]; (4) he struck in the one month when Cao Shuang and his brothers had all accompanied the emperor out to Gaoping Tomb, occupying the arsenal and the Luo River bridge [8]; (5) Cao Shuang, with the emperor beside him [9], nonetheless gave up his offices [9]. From these it follows, by inference, that the two were co-regents in name but rivals in fact, and that the illness functioned as concealment for a strike timed to the imperial absence. The sources do not say the illness *caused* the surrender, nor that the surrender was the only possible outcome; Huan Fan's rejected plan [9] shows another course was argued for. Also by inference, the 「十年正月」of the biography [8] and the 「嘉平元年春正月甲午」of the annals [2] refer to the same affair, since the actors and acts recorded are the same.

## The event: the Gaoping Tombs incident (高平陵之變), 249 CE

**Who set it in motion:** Sima Yi (司馬懿, styled Zhongda, referred to in the sources as 司馬宣王 / 太傅), who had for years feigned illness to lull the regent Cao Shuang (曹爽). The emperor who left the capital to worship at the tomb was Cao Fang (曹芳), the "Qi Wang" / Prince of Qi (齊王).

### The emperor's visit to the tomb

The *Wei Annals* record it under 嘉平元年 (the first year of Jiaping, = 249 CE by the era tool):

> 「嘉平元年春正月甲午，車駕謁高平陵。」[04-0016]

"The first year of Jiaping, spring, first month, day jiawu: the imperial carriage went to worship at Gaoping Tomb." This tomb was that of Emperor Ming (明帝), who had died in 景初三年 and been buried at 高平陵 [03-0042].

### Sima Yi's feigned illness

> 「初，爽以宣王年德並高，恒父事之，不敢專行……宣王遂稱疾避爽。」[09-0025.0]

"Formerly Cao Shuang, because Sima Xuan-wang was advanced in years and prestige, always served him as a father and did not dare act arbitrarily…… Sima Xuan-wang then pleaded illness to keep out of Cao Shuang's way."

The sources show the feigned illness was deliberate and used as cover:

> 「九年冬，李勝出爲荊州刺史，往詣宣王。宣王稱疾困篤，示以羸形。勝不能覺，謂之信然。」[09-0025.1]

"In the winter of the ninth year, Li Sheng was appointed Inspector of Jing Province and went to visit Sima Xuan-wang. Sima Xuan-wang claimed to be gravely ill and showed him a wasted appearance. Li Sheng could not detect it and believed it genuine."

### The seizure of the capital

> 「十年正月，車駕朝高平陵，爽兄弟皆從。宣王部勒兵馬，先據武庫，遂出屯洛水浮橋。」[09-0025.1]

"In the first month of the tenth year, the imperial carriage went to worship at Gaoping Tomb, and Cao Shuang and his brothers all accompanied it. Sima Xuan-wang marshalled his troops and horses, first occupied the arsenal, and then marched out to camp at the floating bridge on the Luo River."

He then memorialized the throne accusing Cao Shuang, and (per the memorial) reported that the Empress Dowager had authorized him:

> 「臣輙力疾，將兵屯洛水浮橋，伺察非常。」[09-0026.1] — "I therefore, forcing myself despite illness, lead troops to camp at the floating bridge on the Luo River and watch for any untoward development."

> 「皇太後令勑臣如奏施行。」[09-0025.1] — "The Empress Dowager ordered me to carry out the memorial as submitted."

### Cao Shuang surrenders his power

Cao Shuang, cut off from the capital and holding the emperor with him, hesitated. Huan Fan (桓範) urged him to take the emperor to Xu Chang and summon outside troops, but Cao Shuang would not:

> 「侍中許允、尚書陳泰說爽，使早自歸罪。爽於是遣允、泰詣宣王，歸罪請死，乃通宣王奏事。遂免爽兄弟，以侯還第。」[09-0027]

"Shizhong Xu Yun and Shangshu Chen Tai persuaded Cao Shuang to go early and confess his guilt. Cao Shuang therefore sent Xu Yun and Chen Tai to Sima Xuan-wang to confess and beg to die, and then forwarded Sima Xuan-wang's memorial. Thereupon Cao Shuang and his brothers were stripped of office and returned to their residences as marquises."

That was the surrender of the other regent's power. (He was not merely dismissed: later, on the testimony of the eunuch Zhang Dang, Cao Shuang and his associates were tried and executed with the extermination of their three clans — 「於是收爽、羲、訓、晏、颺、謐、軌、勝、範、當等，皆伏誅，夷三族。」[09-0028].)

### By way of inference

Putting these facts together (they are all from the sources above, not new claims): Cao Shuang had earlier been named by Emperor Ming, together with Sima Yi, to receive the testamentary edict and assist the young ruler (「與太尉司馬宣王並受遺詔輔少主」[09-0023]), and had then moved to monopolize power and sideline Sima Yi, so that "various affairs rarely passed through Sima Xuan-wang any more" (「諸事希復由宣王」[09-0025.0]). It follows that the two were co-regents in name but rivals in practice, and that Sima Yi's "long illness" served as the concealment for a strike timed precisely for the one moment when Cao Shuang, escorting the emperor away from the capital, could not control Luoyang. The sources do not state that Cao Shuang's surrender was the *result* of the illness alone; they show the illness as the cover and the imperial absence as the occasion.

### Summary

- **Event:** the Gaoping Tombs incident, 嘉平元年 / 正始十年 = 249 CE.
- **Emperor away from Luoyang:** Cao Fang (齊王曹芳), worshiping at Emperor Ming's tomb, 高平陵.
- **Prime mover:** Sima Yi (司馬懿 / 司馬宣王), then Grand Tutor (太傅), who had pleaded illness and now occupied the arsenal and the Luo River bridge.
- **Regent stripped of power:** Cao Shuang (曹爽), the Grand General (大將軍).

The name "高平陵之變" (Gaoping Tombs incident) is the conventional later label; the *Sanguozhi* text simply records the events under the date, without giving the affair a name.

宣王遂稱疾避爽

嘉平元年春正月甲午，車駕謁高平陵。
即日，帝崩于嘉福殿，時年三十六。癸丑，葬高平陵。
十年正月，車駕朝高平陵，爽兄弟皆從。宣王部勒兵馬，先據武庫，遂出屯洛水浮橋。
奏爽曰
臣輙力疾，將兵屯洛水浮橋，伺察非常。
皇太後令勑臣如奏施行。
太傅司馬宣王奏免大將軍曹爽、爽弟中領軍羲、武衞將軍訓、散騎常侍彥官，以侯就第。

範說爽使車駕幸許昌，招外兵。

有司奏収黃門張當付廷尉，考實其辭，爽與謀不軌

q: Identify the stratagem: Wang Yun used Diaochan to sow suspicion between Dong Zhuo and Lü Bu, and in the end had Dong Zhuo killed by Lü Bu's hand. What is this stratagem usually called?
reply:
## 结论

按《三国演义》的叙述, 这个情节通常称为 **连环计** (也常与 **美人计** 并提)。但《三国志》里没有貂蝉这个人, 也没有王允用貂蝉离间董卓、吕布的记载; 正史里能查到的是另一回事(见下)。这个名称和这一情节都不出自《三国志》。

## 《三国志》里的相关记载

- 吕布确实与董卓的一名侍婢私通, 原文没写她的名字, 也没有王允指使的成分: 「卓常使布守中閤，布與卓侍婢私通，恐事發覺，心不自安」[8]。
- 王允是利用吕布对董卓的私怨, 拉吕布做内应, 不是靠貂蝉: 「先是，司徒王允以布州里壯健，厚接納之。後布詣允，陳卓幾見殺狀。時允與僕射士孫瑞密謀誅卓，是以告布使為內應」[1]。吕布起初以父子名分犹豫, 王允说「君自姓呂，本非骨肉。今憂死不暇，何謂父子？」，吕布「遂許之，手刃刺卓」[1]。
- 参与密谋的是王允、士孙瑞、吕布三人, 不只是王允一人: 「三年四月，司徒王允、尚書僕射士孫瑞、卓將呂布共謀誅卓」[3]。原文把这件事的时间记作「三年四月」[3]。

q: Identify the person: when Cao Cao was routed at Wancheng, who held the camp gate and fought to the death to cover Cao Cao's retreat?
reply:
**Answer: Dian Wei (典韋), a man of Jiwu in Chenliu** — 「典韋，陳留己吾人也」[5]. His biography records exactly this scene.

**Facts (from the sources):**

- On the campaign: 「太祖征荊州，至宛，張繡迎降」[2] — Cao Cao campaigned against Jing province, reached Wan, and Zhang Xiu came to surrender.
- The revolt and the fight at the gate: 「後十餘日，繡反，襲太祖營，太祖出戰不利，輕騎引去。韋戰於門中，賊不得入。」[2] — some ten-odd days later Zhang Xiu revolted and raided Cao Cao's camp; Cao Cao came out to fight and was worsted, and withdrew with light cavalry; Dian Wei fought in the gateway, and the rebels could not get in.
- His men fought to the death: 「時韋校尚有十餘人，皆殊死戰，無不一當十。」[2]
- His death: 「韋被數十創，短兵接戰，賊前搏之」[2], and 「創重發，瞋目大罵而死。賊乃敢前，取其頭」[2] — he had taken several dozen wounds, fought hand to hand, and when his wounds burst open he glared, cursed loudly and died; only then did the rebels dare come forward and take his head.
- Cao Cao's reaction: 「太祖退住舞陰，聞韋死，為流涕，募間取其喪，親自臨哭之」[2] — Cao Cao withdrew to Wuyin; hearing Dian Wei was dead he wept, offered a reward to recover his body by a side road, and came in person to weep over it.

**Campaign context (from the Wudi ji):** 「二年春正月，公到宛。張繡降，旣而悔之，復反。公與戰，軍敗，爲流矢所中，長子昂、弟子安民遇害。公乃引兵還舞陰。」[3] — in the first month of spring of "the second year" Cao Cao reached Wan; Zhang Xiu surrendered, then regretted it and revolted; Cao Cao fought him, his army was defeated, he was struck by a stray arrow, and his eldest son Ang and his nephew Anmin were killed; he then led his troops back to Wuyin. The text gives only 「二年春正月」[3] without naming the era; if this "second year" is the second year of Jian'an, the era conversion gives AD 197 [era].

**Inference (my own, from the facts above):** The records place Dian Wei "fighting in the gateway" while Cao Cao "withdrew with light cavalry," and the rebels only dared advance after Dian Wei's death [2]. From this I infer that Dian Wei's stand at the gate coincided with and covered Cao Cao's withdrawal — but note that the sources state the two events side by side without saying his stand was undertaken "to cover" the retreat, and the Wudi ji's own account of the defeat does not name Dian Wei at all [3].

q: Changban: who rescued the infant A'dou at Changban Slope? And who stood on Changban Bridge and scared off Cao Cao's army with his shouts?
reply:
**Short answer:** At Changban (當陽長阪) the infant was rescued by **Zhao Yun (趙雲, courtesy name Zilong)**; the man who held the bridge and overawed Cao Cao's troops was **Zhang Fei (張飛, courtesy name Yide)**.

**Zhao Yun — the rescue of the child**

> 「及先主為曹公所追於當陽長阪，棄妻子南走，雲身抱弱子，即後主也，保護甘夫人，即後主母也，皆得免難。」[1]

Zhao Yun personally carried the young child — that is, the future Houzhu (後主), Liu Shan 劉禪, courtesy name Gongsi 公嗣 — and protected Lady Gan, the child's mother; both escaped harm. His posthumous commendation, in 裴注引《雲別傳》, refers to this same deed: 「當陽之役，義貫金石，忠以衛上」[3].

**Zhang Fei — the stand at the bridge**

> 「先主聞曹公卒至，棄妻子走，使飛將二十騎拒後。飛據水斷橋，瞋目橫矛曰：『身是張益德也，可來共決死！』敵皆無敢近者，故遂得免。」[12]

So Liu Bei, hearing Cao Cao had suddenly arrived, fled leaving his wife and children, and had Zhang Fei hold the rear with twenty riders. Zhang Fei took position by the water and broke down the bridge, glared, held his spear crosswise and shouted a challenge: "I am Zhang Yide — come and fight to the death with me!" None of the enemy dared approach, and Liu Bei thus got away. The record itself links the stand to the escape (「敵皆無敢近者，故遂得免」[12]).

**The setting (from Liu Bei's record)**

> 「曹公將精騎五千急追之，一日一夜行三百餘里，及於當陽之長坂。先主棄妻子，與諸葛亮、張飛、趙雲等數十騎走，曹公大獲其人眾輜重。」[9]

Cao Cao's 5,000 picked cavalry pursued at forced march and caught Liu Bei at Changban in Dangyang; Liu Bei abandoned his family and fled with only a few dozen riders including Zhuge Liang, Zhang Fei and Zhao Yun, while Cao Cao captured his people and baggage.

**Inference:** The record of Zhao Yun places his carrying of the child at the moment 「先主為曹公所追於當陽長阪」[1], and the records of Liu Bei [9] and Zhang Fei [12] describe the same pursuit at 當陽之長阪. 据此推断, Zhao Yun's rescue of the child and Lady Gan and Zhang Fei's rearguard stand at the bridge belong to the same rout, with Liu Bei and both men fleeing together. The text does not say the two acts were coordinated with each other.

q: Sequence of episodes: put the following in the order in which they occur in *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*: A. The Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage  B. The Battle of Guandu  C. The Oath of the Peach Garden  D. The Battle of Red Cliffs
reply:
## Conclusion

Ordering the four episodes as they occur: **C (Oath of the Peach Garden) → B (Battle of Guandu) → A (Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage) → D (Battle of Red Cliffs)**.

The *Sanguozhi* is not organized in "chapters" like the novel, but on the dates it records, this is the sequence (see the marked inference below).

## Evidence

**C. Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei at the start**

Liu Bei's earliest activity is placed at the end of Emperor Ling's reign:

「靈帝末，黃巾起，州郡各舉義兵，先主率其屬從校尉鄒靖討黃巾賊有功，除安喜尉。」[49] — "At the end of Emperor Ling's reign the Yellow Turbans rose; the provinces and commanderies each raised righteous troops, and the First Lord led his followers with the Colonel Zou Jing to attack the Yellow Turban rebels, and by his merit was appointed commandant of Anxi."

Guan Yu's biography describes the bond from those days:

「先主於鄉里合徒眾，而羽與張飛為之禦侮」[1] — "The First Lord gathered followers in his home district, and Yu and Zhang Fei fended off insults for him."

「先主與二人寢則同床，恩若兄弟。」[1] — "The First Lord slept in the same bed with the two men; their affection was like that of brothers."

**B. Guandu**

「建安五年，曹公與袁紹相拒於官渡，策陰欲襲許。」[24] — 建安五年 = AD 200. Cao Cao's own annals record the deployment: 「九月，公還許，分兵守官渡。」[22] and 「十二月，公軍官渡。」[22] The outcome: 「紹軍大潰，河北平。」[23]

**A. The Three Visits**

「由是先主遂詣亮，凡三往，乃見。」[12] — "Thereupon the First Lord went to Zhuge Liang; in all he went three times before he was received."

Zhuge Liang's own memorial says: 「先帝不以臣卑鄙，猥自枉屈，三顧臣於草廬之中，諮臣以當世之事」[44] — "The late Emperor did not disdain me as lowly, but humbled himself and thrice visited me in my thatched cottage, consulting me on the affairs of the day."

裴松之按: 「臣松之案：劉備以建安十三年敗，遣亮使吳」[14] and 「然則備始與亮相遇，在敗軍之前一年時也。」[14] — Liu Bei was defeated in 建安十三年 and sent Liang on a mission to Wu; Pei Songzhi concludes that their first meeting was in the year before that defeat. 建安十三年 = AD 208, and 建安十二年 = AD 207.

**D. Red Cliffs**

「曹公敗於赤壁，引軍歸鄴。」[33] and 「與曹公戰於赤壁，大破之，焚其舟船」[35]; the detailed account is in Zhou Yu's biography: 「權遂遣瑜及程普等與備並力逆曹公，遇於赤壁」[37] and 「頃之，煙炎張天，人馬燒溺死者甚眾，軍遂敗退」[37].

## Inference

Facts used: (i) the material places Liu Bei's gathering of followers with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei at the Yellow Turban rising at the end of Emperor Ling's reign [49][1], and in the *First Lord's* biography that passage precedes the 建安五年 passage [49][50]; (ii) Guandu is explicitly dated 建安五年 = AD 200 [24][22]; (iii) per Pei Songzhi, the meeting of Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang came in the year before Liu Bei's 建安十三年 defeat [14], i.e. 建安十二年 = AD 207; (iv) Red Cliffs is the battle that followed Zhuge Liang's mission to Sun Quan, which Pei Songzhi places in Liu Bei's defeat year [14][35][37].

据此推断: since the Yellow Turban episode stands at the beginning of Liu Bei's record, before the 建安五年 Guandu passage [49][50], Guandu falls in 建安五年 = AD 200 [24], the Three Visits fall in the year before the 建安十三年 defeat, that is 建安十二年 = AD 207 [14], and Red Cliffs follows the mission Pei Songzhi places in the 建安十三年 defeat year [14][35][37], the order is C → B → A → D.

## 以下不是《三国志》的记载:

The "Oath of the Peach Garden" (桃园结义) — the three men swearing brotherhood in a peach garden — is not recorded in the *Sanguozhi*; it may come from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* or other non-orthodox accounts.

Putting the dated facts together: Liu Bei gathered his followers and fought the Yellow Turbans at the end of Emperor Ling's reign [49], long before 建安五年 = AD 200, when Cao Cao and Yuan Shao faced each other at Guandu [24][22]; the Three Visits came in 建安十二年 = AD 207, the year before Liu Bei's defeat [14]; and Red Cliffs came in 建安十三年 = AD 208, when Cao Cao was beaten and burned out [35][37]. Hence, as *Sanguozhi* dates them, the sequence is C → B → A → D. (Note that in the *Romance*, the Three Visits are dramatized after Guandu and immediately before Red Cliffs, which matches the order above.)

The "Oath of the Peach Garden" (桃园结义) — the three men swearing brotherhood in a peach garden — is not recorded in the *Sanguozhi*; it may come from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* or other non-orthodox accounts. The *Sanguozhi* records only that Guan Yu and Zhang Fei served Liu Bei from his early days and that their affection was "like that of brothers" [1].

q: Borrowing Arrows with Straw Boats: what weather conditions did Zhuge Liang take advantage of when he borrowed the arrows, and why did those conditions help him carry out the plan?
reply:
## Conclusion

The story of "Borrowing Arrows with Straw Boats" does not appear in the *Sanguozhi* (Records of the Three Kingdoms) at all, so there is no record there of Zhuge Liang exploiting any weather conditions for such a plan. The *Sanguozhi* does contain a similar-sounding episode, but it belongs to **Sun Quan**, not Zhuge Liang, and the text mentions **no fog** — the only weather element in it is the "spring floodwaters." The fog and the whole arrow-borrowing scheme are a *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* invention.

## What the *Sanguozhi* actually records

**1. The arrow-receiving ship was Sun Quan's, and there was no fog.**

Pei Songzhi's note to the Sun Quan biography quotes the *Wei Lüe* (魏略):

> 「權乘大船來觀軍，公使弓弩亂發，箭著其船，船偏重將覆，權因回船，復以一面受箭，箭均船平，乃還。」[11]

*("Sun Quan came on a large ship to observe the army; the Duke [Cao Cao] had the crossbows shoot wildly, and the arrows struck his ship. The ship grew lopsided and was about to capsize, so Sun Quan turned the ship around and let the other side receive arrows; when the arrows were even and the ship level, he returned.")*

The same note, quoting the *Wu Li* (吳歷), records the surrounding context: Cao Cao's army coming out to Ruxu, Sun Quan's repeated challenges, Cao Cao's refusal to come out, and Sun Quan's letter to Cao Cao:

> 「春水方生，公宜速去」[11]

*("The spring floodwaters are just rising; you had better leave quickly.")*

The note itself gives **no year** for the arrow episode, and **no fog** is mentioned anywhere in the episode, nor any straw boats or bundles of straw. Separately, the main text of the Sun Quan biography records a Ruxu confrontation:

> 「十八年正月，曹公攻濡須，權與相拒月餘。」[64]

*("In the first month of the eighteenth year [of Jian'an], Cao Cao attacked Ruxu, and Sun Quan held him off for more than a month.")*

**2. Zhuge Liang's recorded role in the Red Cliffs campaign was diplomatic, not arrow-borrowing.**

The *Xianzhu Zhuan* states:

> 「先主遣諸葛亮自結於孫權，權遣周瑜、程普等水軍數萬，與先主并力，與曹公戰於赤壁，大破之，焚其舟船。」[21]

*("The Former Lord sent Zhuge Liang to make an alliance with Sun Quan on his own behalf; Sun Quan sent Zhou Yu, Cheng Pu and others with tens of thousands of marines, to join forces with the Former Lord and fight Cao Cao at Red Cliffs, greatly defeating him and burning his ships.")*

Zhuge Liang's own biography likewise records only that Sun Quan sent Zhou Yu, Cheng Pu, Lu Su and others with thirty thousand marines:

> 「權大悅，即遣周瑜、程普、魯肅等水軍三萬，隨亮詣先主，并力拒曹公。」[14]

**3. The weather condition the *Sanguozhi* does emphasize in this campaign is wind — for the fire attack, credited to Huang Gai and Zhou Yu, not to Zhuge Liang.**

> 「蓋放諸船，同時發火。時風盛猛，悉延燒岸上營落。」[34]

*("Huang Gai released the ships and set them alight all at once. At the time the wind was strong and fierce, and it spread the fire to all the camps on shore.")*

Huang Gai's own biography confirms he 「建策火攻」[32] — "proposed the fire attack."

## Inference

据此推断: the *Sanguozhi* contains (a) an episode in which Sun Quan deliberately let a ship take arrows on one side, then turned it so the other side took arrows until the ship was level [11]; and (b) an episode in which a strong wind made a fire attack devastating at Red Cliffs [34]. Neither episode is attached to Zhuge Liang, and neither mentions fog. Since these are the only passages in the searched material that supply either an arrow-receiving ship or notable weather in this campaign, the elements of the popular tale — fog, straw-covered boats, and Zhuge Liang as the planner — cannot be assembled from the *Sanguozhi*. If one asks where the "ship receiving arrows" motif comes from, the only passage in the material that matches it is the Sun Quan episode recorded in Pei's note [11].

## Background

q: Empty Fort Strategy: in the novel, where does Zhuge Liang use the Empty Fort Strategy, and which Wei commander leads the army that comes against him?
reply:
## Short answer

In Luo Guanzhong's novel the Empty Fort episode is set at **Xicheng** (西城), and the Wei army that advances on Zhuge Liang is commanded by **Sima Yi (司马懿)**. In the *Sanguozhi*, however, this story is **not** in Chen Shou's main text at all — it survives only in Pei Songzhi's commentary, quoted from Guo Chong's *San Shi* (郭冲《三事》), and there the place is **Yangping (阳平)**, not Xicheng. Pei Songzhi himself rejects the story as unreliable.

## What the sources actually say

The tale appears as a commentary block attached to Zhuge Liang's biography, Pei Songzhi's note quoting Guo Chong:

「亮屯于陽平，遣魏延諸軍並兵東下，亮惟留萬人守城。」[2]
(Zhuge Liang was encamped at Yangping; he sent Wei Yan and the other armies east in a combined force, leaving only ten thousand men to hold the city.)

「又令大開四城門，埽地卻洒。」[2]
(He also ordered the four city gates thrown wide open, and the ground swept and sprinkled.)

「宣帝常謂亮持重，而猥見勢弱，疑其有伏兵，於是引軍北趣山。」[2]
(Xuan-di — i.e. Sima Yi — had always considered Zhuge Liang cautious; now suddenly seeing this display of weakness, he suspected an ambush, and led his army north toward the mountains.)

Zhuge Liang's own remark the next day:

「司馬懿必謂吾怯，將有彊伏，循山走矣。」[2]
(Sima Yi must think I am afraid and that there is a strong ambush here, and has gone off along the mountains.)

The Wei commander is called **晉宣帝 / 宣帝** in this text — that is Sima Yi, posthumously Emperor Xuan of Jin; the passage itself uses the name 司馬懿 in Zhuge Liang's speech.

## Pei Songzhi's rebuttal

Pei Songzhi, who copied the anecdote in, then argues against it:

「案陽平在漢中。亮初屯陽平，宣帝尚為荊州都督，鎮宛城，至曹真死後，始與亮於關中相抗禦耳。」[2]
(Yangping is in Hanzhong. When Zhuge Liang first camped at Yangping, Xuan-di was still Inspector of Jingzhou, stationed at Wancheng; only after Cao Zhen's death did he begin confronting Zhuge Liang in Guanzhong.)

「此之前後，無復有於陽平交兵事。」[2]
(Before and after this, there was no further fighting at Yangping.)

And, citing the *Wei Yan zhuan*:

「亮尚不以延為萬人別統，豈得如沖言，頓使將重兵在前，而以輕弱自守乎？」[31]
(Zhuge Liang would not even let Wei Yan command ten thousand men separately — how could he, as Guo Chong says, suddenly put heavy forces under him in the front while holding the city with weak, light troops himself?)

## Conclusion (my inference, marked as such)

- The **only** version of the Empty Fort story in the *Sanguozhi* corpus is Pei Songzhi's quotation of Guo Chong's *San Shi*, and it is placed at **Yangping**, with **Sima Yi** leading the Wei force [2].
- Since Pei Songzhi records this as a quotation *in order to refute it*, and since he points out both a chronological impossibility and a contradiction with Wei Yan's biography [2][31], the episode is best described as a story that Chen Shou did not include and that Pei Songzhi judged false — not as established *Sanguozhi* fact.
- The novel's placement at Xicheng is therefore a difference from the commentary's Yangping; the commentary does mention Wei once sending Sima Yi from Wancheng by way of **Xicheng** to attack Shu, but that expedition was aborted by heavy rain [2].

以下不是《三国志》的记载: the Empty Fort scene as told in *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, with Zhuge Liang playing the qin on the city wall at Xicheng before Sima Yi's army, is not found in Chen Shou's main text; the closest recorded form of the tale, at Yangping, comes from Guo Chong's *San Shi* as quoted in Pei Songzhi's commentary and is disputed by Pei Songzhi.

- The novel's placement at Xicheng is therefore a difference from the commentary's Yangping; the commentary does mention Wei once sending Sima Yi from Wancheng by way of **Xicheng** to attack Shu, but that expedition was aborted by heavy rain [2].

以下不是《三国志》的记载: the Empty Fort scene as told in *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, with Zhuge Liang playing the qin on the city wall at Xicheng before Sima Yi's army, is not found in Chen Shou's main text; the closest recorded form of the tale, at Yangping, comes from Guo Chong's *San Shi* as quoted in Pei Songzhi's commentary and is disputed by Pei Songzhi.
review_raw:
## 结论

《三国志》正文里没有"空城计"这件事，也没有西城这个地点。资料里唯一一段类似记载，出自裴松之注所引郭冲《三事》，地点是**阳平**，率魏军前来的主帅是**司马懿**（这段文字里称他为"晋宣帝""宣帝"）。裴松之本人随即驳斥了这段记载。

## 依据

郭冲《三事》所述（裴注引）：

「亮屯于陽平，遣魏延諸軍並兵東下，亮惟留萬人守城。」[2]

「晉宣帝率二十萬眾拒亮，而與延軍錯道，徑至前，當亮六十里所」[2]

「又令大開四城門，埽地卻洒。」[2]

「宣帝常謂亮持重，而猥見勢弱，疑其有伏兵，於是引軍北趣山。」[2]

诸葛亮次日之言：

「司馬懿必謂吾怯，將有彊伏，循山走矣。」[2]

裴松之的反驳（就在同一段注里）：

「案陽平在漢中。亮初屯陽平，宣帝尚為荊州都督，鎮宛城，至曹真死後，始與亮於關中相抗禦耳。」[2]

「此之前後，無復有於陽平交兵事。」[2]

「就如沖言，宣帝既舉二十萬眾，已知亮兵少力弱，若疑其有伏兵，正可設防持重，何至便走乎？」[2]

裴松之又引《魏延传》并反问：

「延每隨亮出，輒欲請精兵萬人，與亮異道會于潼關，亮制而不許」[31]

「亮尚不以延為萬人別統，豈得如沖言，頓使將重兵在前，而以輕弱自守乎？」[31]

裴松之对郭冲五事的总评：

「臣松之以為亮之異美，誠所願聞，然沖之所說，實皆可疑」[23]

另，这段注里提到魏国曾派司马懿经西城伐蜀：

「魏嘗遣宣帝自宛由西城伐蜀，值霖雨，不果。」[2]

## 据此推断

把上面几条事实并起来看：一，这段空城式记载只出现在裴注所引郭冲《三事》里，正文没有；二，裴松之指出，诸葛亮初屯阳平时，司马懿还在荆州镇宛城，到曹真死后才与诸葛亮在关中相抗，此前后并无阳平交兵之事；三，裴松之还指出诸葛亮连让魏延单独统领万人都不同意，不会自己带弱兵守城、把重兵交给魏延。由此推断，这段记载是裴松之收进来又加以驳斥的异说，不能当作《三国志》正文的史实来用；至于西城，资料里只记魏国曾派司马懿从宛城经西城伐蜀、遇大雨未成[2]，并没有在那里发生空城对峙的事。

以下不是《三国志》的记载：问题里说的"西城"这一地点，以及把这件事说成"空城计"，《三国志》里没有记载，可能出自《三国演义》或其他非正史的说法；《三国志》注中保留的类似故事发生在阳平。

q: Huarong Trail: in the novel, why does Guan Yu let Cao Cao go at Huarong Trail? What conflict within his character does this episode bring out?
reply:
## Short answer

The episode as you describe it — Guan Yu intercepting Cao Cao at the Huarong Trail and deliberately letting him go — is not found in the *Sanguozhi* (I searched several ways: Cao Cao's flight, the Huarong Trail, Guan Yu blocking the retreat, Guan Yu repaying an old kindness, and found no such account). It is a famous scene from the novel (*Romance of the Three Kingdoms*). What the histories do record is (a) Cao Cao's actual retreat by the Huarong Trail, with only Liu Bei in pursuit, and (b) a real inner conflict in Guan Yu — repaying Cao Cao's kindness versus his oath of loyalty to Liu Bei — but that conflict is resolved at Baima in 200 AD, not at Huarong.

## What the histories actually say

**1. Cao Cao's retreat by the Huarong Trail — no Guan Yu.** Pei Songzhi's note to the *Wudi ji* quotes the *Shanyang Gong zaiji*:

> 「公船艦爲備所燒，引軍從華容道步歸，遇泥濘，道不通，天又大風，悉使羸兵負草填之，騎乃得過。羸兵爲人馬所蹈藉，陷泥中，死者甚衆。」[16]

(Cao Cao's ships were burned by Liu Bei; he led his army back on foot by the Huarong Trail, met mud so the road was impassable, and a great wind; he made the weak troops carry grass to fill the road so the cavalry could pass; the weak troops were trampled by men and horses and many died in the mud.) The only pursuer in this account is Liu Bei: 「劉備，吾儔也。但得計少晚；向使早放火，吾徒無類矣。」[16] and 「備尋亦放火而無所及。」[16] Guan Yu does not appear in this account.

**2. The "repayment" of Cao Cao's kindness was at Baima.** After Cao Cao captured Guan Yu (建安五年 = 200 AD [era]; 「五年，曹公東征先主，先主敗績。曹公盡收其眾，虜先主妻子，並禽關羽以歸」[41]), Guan Yu told Zhang Liao:

> 「吾極知曹公待我厚，然吾受劉將軍厚恩，誓以共死，不可背之。吾終不留，吾要當立效以報曹公乃去。」[2]

The service rendered was killing Yan Liang at Baima: 「羽望見良麾蓋，策馬刺良於萬眾之中，斬其首還」[2]. He then sealed up all the gifts, took leave by letter, and went to Liu Bei; Cao Cao forbade pursuit: 「彼各爲其主，勿追也。」[2] Pei Songzhi's comment: 「曹公知羽不留而心嘉其志，去不遣追以成其義」[42]. Chen Shou's appraisal pairs this with Zhang Fei's release of Yan Yan: 「羽報效曹公，飛義釋嚴顏，並有國士之風」[11].

**3. The other side of Guan Yu's feeling toward Cao Cao.** Pei Songzhi's note quotes the *Shu ji*: at the hunt at Xu, Guan Yu urged Liu Bei to kill Cao Cao and Liu Bei refused; later, at Jiangxia, Guan Yu said angrily, 「往日獵中，若從羽言，可無今日之困。」[7]

## Inference (marked as such)

据此推断: from [2] (Guan Yu declares he must render a service to repay Cao Cao and then leave) and [7] (Guan Yu once urged killing Cao Cao), the tension in Guan Yu's record is between personal gratitude to Cao Cao and total loyalty to Liu Bei, and in the *Sanguozhi* it is discharged by an act of war (killing Yan Liang at Baima [2]), not by a mercy scene. 据此推断, the novel's Huarong Trail scene dramatizes exactly this tension at the point where the two men's interests collide most sharply — the *Sanguozhi* records no such encounter, but the absence of a record does not by itself prove that no encounter occurred; it only means the histories do not attest it.

## Background

以下不是《三国志》的记载: the scene of Guan Yu letting Cao Cao go at the Huarong Trail is not recorded in the *Sanguozhi*; it comes from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* or other non-orthodox accounts. The Huarong Trail (華容道, the name used at the time) was in what is today the Hubei province area.

## Inference (marked as such)

From these facts: the *Sanguozhi* records a debt of gratitude (立效以報曹公) discharged by killing Yan Liang in 200 [2], and it records Guan Yu once urging Cao Cao's death [7]. So the *historical* tension in Guan Yu is between personal gratitude to Cao Cao and total loyalty to Liu Bei — and it was settled by action, not by a mercy scene. The Huarong Trail release is not attested; it is the novel's way of dramatizing exactly this tension (gratitude vs. duty) at the point where the two men's interests collide most sharply. Whether Guan Yu would actually have spared Cao Cao is not something the *Sanguozhi* lets us determine; the histories simply record no such encounter.

## Background (not from the *Sanguozhi*)

The scene of Guan Yu letting Cao Cao go at the Huarong Trail is not recorded in the *Sanguozhi*; it comes from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* and related popular tradition. The Huarong Trail (華容道) was a route in the Jianghan region of Jingzhou, in what is today Hubei province.

q: The chained ships: before the Battle of Red Cliffs, who advised Ts'ao Ts'ao to link his warships together with iron chains? Why did this arrangement magnify the damage done by the fire attack?
reply:
## Who advised chaining the ships?

**The *Sanguozhi* does not record anyone advising Cao Cao to link his warships.** I searched under several different phrasings (chained ships, iron chains, Pang Tong's stratagem, "who proposed it") and no advisor is named. What the text actually gives us is an observer of the arrangement, not its author — and the observer is on the *other* side:

> 「今寇眾我寡，難與持久。然觀操軍船艦，首尾相接，可燒而走也。」[1]

"Huang Gai, a subordinate commander of Zhou Yu, said: 'Now the enemy is many and we are few, so it is hard to hold out long. But I observe Cao's warships are joined bow-to-stern; they can be burned and driven off.'" (Zhou Yu's biography, *Wushu*)

The same biography records the result: 「蓋放諸船，同時發火。時風盛猛，悉延燒岸上營落。」[1] and 「人馬燒溺死者甚眾，軍遂敗退」[1] — "Huang Gai released the ships and set them alight all at once. The wind was strong and fierce, and the fire spread to burn all the camps on shore... many men and horses were burned or drowned, and the army retreated in defeat."

Pei Songzhi's note quoting the *Jiangbiao zhuan* adds the detail of the wind-driven spread: 「火烈風猛，往船如箭，飛埃絕爛，燒盡北船，延及岸邊營柴。」[14] — "The fire was fierce and the wind violent; the attacking ships went like arrows... they burned up all the northern ships and spread to the firewood of the camps along the bank."

## Why the arrangement magnified the fire's damage

**Inference (my reasoning, not a stated claim in the text):** The sources do not spell out a mechanism, but the facts they give support one. (1) Cao's ships were joined bow-to-stern [54]. (2) The attackers used fire ships, ignited simultaneously, driven by a strong wind [54][54]. (3) The fire consumed all the northern ships and spread to the shore camps [54]. q: Identify the posthumous ruse: in the saying 'a dead Zhuge frightens off a living Zhongda', who is 'Zhongda'? In the novel, how does the Shu army make him retreat?
reply:
## Conclusion

**"Zhongda" (仲达) is Sima Yi (司马懿), whose courtesy name was Zhongda.** In the *Sanguozhi* account, the "ruse" is **not a wooden statue**: after Zhuge Liang died, **Jiang Wei ordered Yang Yi to turn the banners around and beat the drums, as if about to charge at Sima Yi** — and Sima Yi then pulled back, not daring to press close. The Shu army only announced the death after withdrawing into the valley.

## The record

- The saying itself comes from Pei Songzhi's commentary quoting *Han Jin Chunqiu* (《漢晉春秋》), attached to Zhuge Liang's biography:

  「楊儀等整軍而出，百姓奔告宣王，宣王追焉。姜維令儀反旗鳴鼓，若將向宣王者，宣王乃退，不敢偪。於是儀結陳而去，入谷然後發喪。宣王之退也，百姓為之諺曰：『死諸葛走生仲達。』或以告宣王，宣王曰：『吾能料生，不便料死也。』」[2]

  (Yang Yi and the others formed up the army and marched out; the common people ran to tell Sima Xuanwang, and he pursued. Jiang Wei ordered Yang Yi to reverse the banners and beat the drums, as if about to advance on Sima Xuanwang, whereupon Sima Xuanwang withdrew, not daring to press in. Yang Yi then formed ranks and left, and only after entering the valley did they announce the death. When Sima Xuanwang withdrew, the people made a proverb of it: "A dead Zhuge frightens off a living Zhongda." Someone told Sima Xuanwang, and he said: "I can reckon with the living, but it is not easy to reckon with the dead.")

- The context in Chen Shou's main text: Zhuge Liang died in the army in the eighth month of the twelfth year of Jianxing [6], i.e. **234 CE** (Jianxing 12 = 234; converted with the era tool). After the army withdrew, Sima Yi inspected Zhuge Liang's camps and said, 「天下奇才也！」[6].

- "Zhongda" is confirmed as Sima Yi's courtesy name: he appears in the record as 司馬懿, 字仲達, and is also called 司馬宣王 / 晉宣帝 [who].

## What the ruse was — and what it was not

According to the *Sanguozhi* + Pei commentary, the trick was **a feigned counter-attack (turning the banners and sounding the drums) by Yang Yi, on Jiang Wei's order** — a bluff of a living army, made possible because the Shu troops kept their formation and concealed the death until they were safely in the valley [2]. Sima Yi is not said to have seen any image or likeness of Zhuge Liang; he simply withdrew when the Shu army appeared to be coming at him, and later admitted he could not calculate what a dead man would do [2].

## Background (not from the *Sanguozhi*)

以下不是《三国志》的记载： The version in which the Shu army wheels out a **wooden statue of Zhuge Liang** to frighten Sima Yi into retreat is not found in the *Sanguozhi* or its Pei commentary — the record gives only the banner-and-drum feint described above. That wooden-statue scene belongs to 《三国演义》 (and related popular tellings), not to the histories. (I searched for it specifically and found no such passage.)

review_raw:
## 结论

「仲達」是**司馬懿**的字。按《三国志》及裴注的记载，蜀军让司马懿退兵的办法**不是木像**，而是**姜维命杨仪反旗鸣鼓，做出要进攻司马懿的姿态**，司马懿于是退兵，不敢逼近；杨仪结阵离去，进谷之后才发丧。木像吓退魏军是《三国演义》一类非正史的说法。

## 依据（原文）

- 资料的人物表列：司马懿，字仲达；又称司马懿、司马仲达、司马宣王、晋宣王、晋宣帝。裴注引《漢晉春秋》里百姓的谚语正作「死諸葛走生仲達」，而谚语中被他追、被他退的正是「宣王」[2]。

- 裴注引《漢晉春秋》： 「楊儀等整軍而出，百姓奔告宣王，宣王追焉。姜維令儀反旗鳴鼓，若將向宣王者，宣王乃退，不敢偪。於是儀結陳而去，入谷然後發喪。宣王之退也，百姓為之諺曰：『死諸葛走生仲達。』或以告宣王，宣王曰：『吾能料生，不便料死也。』」[2]

- 《明帝紀》正文： 「司馬宣王與亮相持，連圍積日，亮數挑戰，宣王堅壘不應。會亮卒，其軍退還。」[4]

- 诸葛亮之死及蜀军退后的情形： 「十二年春，亮悉大眾由斜谷出，以流馬運，據武功五丈原，與司馬宣王對於渭南」，「其年八月，亮疾病，卒于軍，時年五十四」；「及軍退，宣王案行其營壘處所，曰：『天下奇才也！』」[6]（建兴十二年＝公元 234 年）

## 推断

据此推断：依 [2]，蜀军使司马懿退兵所用的手段，是杨仪反旗鸣鼓、摆出要向司马懿进攻的样子；[4] 也只说「會亮卒，其軍退還」。两份记载里都没有出现木像或任何诸葛亮形象的描写，所以从查到的原文看，这次退兵靠的是**装作要反击的姿态**，不是展示木像。这只是就现存记载而言——原文没有提到木像，不等于当时一定没有，只能说《三国志》及裴注的记载里没有这一节。

## 以下不是《三国志》的记载

问题里说的蜀军用木像（木雕诸葛亮）吓退魏军这一情节，《三国志》里没有记载，可能出自《三国演义》或其他非正史的说法。

q: Arrange 'county, province, commandery' from highest to lowest according to the usual local administrative hierarchy of the late Eastern Han.
reply:
**Conclusion (highest to lowest): 州 province → 郡 commandery → 縣 county.**

In the late Eastern Han local hierarchy, the province (州) sat above the commandery (郡), and the commandery sat above the county (縣).

**Evidence from the texts**

1. Province over commandery. The Wei history's appraisal says the Inspector (刺史) by late Han times commanded all commanderies of his province:
「自漢季以来，刺史總統諸郡，賦政于外」[1] — "Since the late Han, the Inspector has overseen all the commanderies and exercised government abroad."
And Jia Kui (賈逵), explaining the Inspector's function: 「州本以御史出監諸郡，以六条詔書察長吏二千石已下」[23] — "The province was originally an Imperial Clerk sent out to supervise the commanderies, examining the long officials of the 2000-bushel rank and below by the six-article edict."

2. Commandery over county. Xiahou Xuan (夏侯玄), describing the layers: 「今之長吏，皆君吏民，橫重以郡守，累以刺史」[11] — "Today's long officials already rule over the officials and people, yet on top of them are added the commandery Administrator (郡守), and piled on further the Inspector." He also notes the commandery's staff's job is to supervise the counties: 「幹郡之吏，職監諸縣」[3], and that the commandery takes in what the counties accomplish: 「郡受縣成」[3].

3. County = the bottom tier, headed by a Prefect (令) or Chief (長). Zhang Yi's (張翼) career runs up this ladder in order: 「為江陽長，徙涪陵令，遷梓潼太守」[14] — "He became Chief of Jiangyang, was transferred to be Prefect of Fuling, and was promoted to Administrator of Zitong." Likewise Pei Songzhi's note quoting the *Weilüe* (裴注引《魏略》) on Pei Mao (裴茂) lists his offices as 「歷縣令、郡守、尚書」[36] — "he successively served as county Prefect, commandery Administrator, and Master of Writing," going county → commandery → central court.

**Inference (drawn from the above)**

Taking these together — the Inspector oversees all commanderies [1][23], the Administrator sits above the county's 長/令 [11][3], and men were promoted from county 長/令 to commandery 太守 [14][36] — 据此推断, the ordering of the three tiers is **州 (province) > 郡 (commandery) > 縣 (county)**.

以下不是《三国志》的记载:
- The Inspector (刺史) was the office responsible for overseeing the commanderies of a province; the Administrator (太守) for governing a commandery; the Prefect (令) or Chief (長) for governing a county.

q: Chu-ko Liang was Chancellor of Shu-Han and also held the charge of 'Recorder of the Imperial Secretariat' (lu shangshu shi). Taking part in and overseeing what kind of business did that charge chiefly mean?
reply:
**Short answer:** The charge of *lu shangshu shi* (錄尚書事) meant overseeing the business of the Imperial Secretariat (尚書臺) — the handling of documents and state affairs: memorials, edicts, and the routine "myriad affairs" of government. In Zhuge Liang's case it was joined to his Chancellorship, and the records show that all civil government business came to be decided by him.

**What the sources say**

1. Zhuge Liang held the charge together with the Chancellorship. After Liu Bei took the imperial title: 「亮以丞相錄尚書事，假節」[2]. The biography states it again: 「備稱尊號，拜亮為丞相，錄尚書事」[40].

2. What it meant in practice was control of government business. In the accession year: 「政事無巨細，咸決於亮」[39]. After Liu Bei's death: 「事無巨細，亮皆專之」[40].

3. The charge was understood as being about documents. In an edict quoted in Pei's commentary from the *Weilue*, Sima Yi is assigned to 「督後諸軍，錄後臺文書事」 and Chen Qun to 「錄行尚書事」[29] (裴注引《魏略》). Here *lu* + *shangshu* is explicitly "overseeing the Secretariat's document affairs."

4. The Secretariat is the organ that handled the "myriad affairs" and relayed imperial orders. Cheng Xiao's memorial says: 「內有侍中尚書綜理萬機」[25]. In the passage of Wang Lang's son Wang Su it is said of the ancient office of Nayan that it is 「猶今尚書也，以出內帝命而已」[24].

**Inference (据此推断)**

The sources state that the Secretariat "comprehensively manages the myriad affairs" [25] and that it relays the emperor's commands in and out [24]; they also show *lu shangshu shi* described as overseeing the Secretariat's "document affairs" [29]. From these it follows that the charge chiefly meant superintending the flow of documents and the routine conduct of government — receiving and processing memorials and putting orders into effect — that is, everyday civil administration. This is consistent with the biography's statement that all government business "was decided by Liang" [39], though the sources do not state the one as the cause of the other.

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:** 录尚书事 (lu shangshu shi) was a charge by which a high minister supervised the Imperial Secretariat (尚書臺), the organ that handled memorials and edicts.

q: Both the 'Inspector' (cishi) and the 'Governor' (zhoumu) were offices tied to the province. What was the Inspector's original main function? And why can't every Inspector of the late Eastern Han simply be regarded as an official with supervisory powers only?
reply:
## Conclusion

According to the《三国志》and Pei Songzhi's annotations, the Inspector (刺史 cishi) was **originally a supervisory office, not a governing one**: it began as a censor (御史) sent out to supervise the commanderies, policing the commandery-level officials (those of "two thousand shi" and below) by means of the "six-article" edict (六條詔書). He had no fixed seat of administration, and his staff were "attendants" (從事 congshi) rather than his subjects.

But **not every late-Eastern-Han Inspector can be treated as merely a supervisor**, because the record states that from the late Han onward the cishi "commanded all the commanderies and exercised government abroad," and was no longer merely "inspecting." In this period the office of Governor (州牧 zhoumu) is recorded as being conferred on men of pure repute, and many cishi held troops and acted as real territorial power-holders.

## The Inspector's original function: supervision

- Jia Kui (賈逵), on becoming Inspector of Yuzhou, explains the office's origin:

  「州本以御史出監諸郡，以六条詔書察長吏二千石已下，故其狀皆言严能鹰扬有督察之才，不言安静寬仁有恺悌之德也。」[15]

  ("The province was originally a censor sent out to supervise the commanderies, examining by the six-article edict the long officials of two thousand shi and below; hence its evaluations all spoke of stern capability and a hawk-like talent for inspection, and did not speak of quiet generosity and kindly virtue.")

- Sima Yi (司馬宣王), replying to Xiahou Xuan, describes how the office worked in Han times:

  「秦時無刺史，但有郡守長吏。漢家雖有刺史，奉六條而已，故刺史稱傳車，其吏言從事，居無常治，吏不成臣，其後轉更爲官司耳。」[13]

  ("In Qin times there was no cishi, only commandery governors and long officials. Though the Han house had cishi, they merely enforced the six articles; hence the cishi was called 'relay-carriage,' his subordinates were called congshi, he had no fixed seat, his subordinates were not his subjects, and only later did it turn into a regular office.")

- Du Shu (杜恕) likewise says:

  「古之刺史，奉宣六条，以清静为名，威风著称，今可勿令领兵，以专民事。」[12]

- Xiahou Xuan's memorial traces the same logic: fear that the governing officials would not be well-run led to appointing overseers to manage them —

  「懼宰官之不脩，立監牧以董之」[6]

So the Inspector's **original main function was inspection/supervision (監察)**: to watch over the commandery governors and lower officials via the six-article edict, as a light circuit officer with no fixed administrative seat.

## Why a late-Han Inspector cannot be seen as supervisory-only

1. The assessment (評) for the officials in the 劉司馬梁張溫賈傳 states the change explicitly:

   「自漢季以来，刺史總統諸郡，賦政于外，非若曩時司察之而已。」[14]

   ("Since the late Han, the cishi commanded all the commanderies and exercised government abroad, and were not, as in former times, merely inspecting.")

2. In this period the Governor (州牧) post is recorded. Liu Yan (劉焉) proposed:

   「刺史、太守，貨賂為官，割剝百姓，以致離叛。可選清名重臣以為牧伯，鎮安方夏。」[20]

   ("Inspectors and governors bought their offices with bribes and fleeced the people, causing them to break away. One may select ministers of pure repute as pastors-and-elders [牧伯] to pacify the realm.")

   And Pei's note citing the《續漢書》records the appointments made on this basis:

   「虞等皆海內清名之士，或從列卿尚書以選為牧伯，各以本秩居任。」[1]

   Liu Yan himself was then appointed as an army-supervising envoy holding the office of Governor of Yizhou — 「出為監軍使者，領益州牧」[2] — so the post is recorded together with military and territorial duties, not mere oversight.

3. The cishi of the late Han appear as actual local power-holders who could be attacked, ousted, or killed by the governed: 「并州殺刺史張壹，涼州殺刺史耿鄙」[2]; and the Inspector of Jiaozhou, Zhang Jin, is described as 「兵弱敵強，歲歲興軍」 and 「津小檢攝，威武不足，為所陵侮，遂至殺沒」[8].

## Inference (from the evidence above)

Putting these facts together, **by inference (據此推斷)**: the record shows (a) the office began as a non-resident supervisory circuit officer enforcing the six articles [15][13][12]; (b) from the late Han it "commanded all the commanderies and exercised government abroad," no longer merely inspecting [14]; and (c) in this same period the Governor's post is recorded as conferred on "ministers of pure repute" and held together with military duty [20][1][2]. Therefore, although the Inspector's **original and formal function was supervisory**, by the late Eastern Han the same title had in practice become a territorial governorship combining civil administration and military power — which is why one cannot treat every late-Han cishi as an official with supervisory powers only.

Though the Han house had cishi, they merely enforced the six articles; hence the cishi was called 'relay-carriage,' his subordinates were called congshi, he had no fixed seat, his subordinates were not his subjects, and only later did it turn into a regular office.")

- Du Shu (杜恕) likewise says:

  「古之刺史，奉宣六条，以清静为名，威风著称，今可勿令领兵，以专民事。」[12]

- Xiahou Xuan's memorial traces the same logic: fear that the governing officials would not be well-run led to appointing overseers to manage them —

  「懼宰官之不脩，立監牧以董之」[6]

So the Inspector's **original main function was inspection/supervision (監察)**: to watch over the commandery governors and lower officials via the six-article edict, as a light circuit officer with no fixed administrative seat.

## Why a late-Han Inspector cannot be seen as supervisory-only

1. The assessment (評) for the officials in the 劉司馬梁張溫賈傳 states the change explicitly:

   「自漢季以来，刺史總統諸郡，賦政于外，非若曩時司察之而已。」[14]

   ("Since the late Han, the cishi commanded all the commanderies and exercised government abroad, and were not, as in former times, merely inspecting.")

2. In this period the Governor (州牧) post is recorded. Liu Yan (劉焉) proposed:

   「刺史、太守，貨賂為官，割剝百姓，以致離叛。可選清名重臣以為牧伯，鎮安方夏。」[20]

   ("Inspectors and governors bought their offices with bribes and fleeced the people, causing them to break away. One may select ministers of pure repute as pastors-and-elders [牧伯] to pacify the realm.")

   And Pei's note citing the《續漢書》records the appointments made on this basis:

   「虞等皆海內清名之士，或從列卿尚書以選為牧伯，各以本秩居任。」[1]

   Liu Yan himself was then appointed as an army-supervising envoy holding the office of Governor of Yizhou — 「出為監軍使者，領益州牧」[2] — so the post is recorded together with military and territorial duties, not mere oversight.

3. The cishi of the late Han appear as actual local power-holders who could be attacked, ousted, or killed by the governed: 「并州殺刺史張壹，涼州殺刺史耿鄙」[2]; and the Inspector of Jiaozhou, Zhang Jin, is described as 「兵弱敵強，歲歲興軍」 and 「津小檢攝，威武不足，為所陵侮，遂至殺沒」[8].

## Inference (from the evidence above)

Putting these facts together, **by inference (據此推斷)**: the record shows (a) the office began as a non-resident supervisory circuit officer enforcing the six articles [15][13][12]; (b) from the late Han it "commanded all the commanderies and exercised government abroad," no longer merely inspecting [14]; and (c) in this same period the Governor's post is recorded as conferred on "ministers of pure repute" and held together with military duty [20][1][2]. Therefore, although the Inspector's **original and formal function was supervisory**, by the late Eastern Han the same title had in practice become a territorial governorship combining civil administration and military power — which is why one cannot treat every late-Han cishi as an official with supervisory powers only.

q: In the late Eastern Han, was a 'Grand Administrator' (taishou) normally the chief official of a province, a commandery or a county?
reply:
## Conclusion

In the late Eastern Han, a **Grand Administrator (太守 tàishǒu) was the chief official of a commandery (郡 jùn)** — the middle tier of the 州 (province) → 郡 (commandery) → 县 (county) hierarchy. It was *not* the head of a province, and not the head of a county.

## Evidence

**1. A 太守 is always attached to a commandery (郡), never a province or a county.** The text consistently names them as "X commandery Grand Administrator":

- 「魏郡太守陳國吴瓘、清河太守樂安任燠、京兆太守济北顏斐、弘農太守太原令狐邵」[1] — Weijun, Qinghe, Jingzhao, Hongnong are all commanderies.
- 「策自領會稽太守，復以吴景爲丹楊太守，以孫賁爲豫章太守，分豫章爲廬陵郡，以賁弟輔爲廬陵太守，丹揚朱治爲吴郡太守」[2] — here Sun Ce even *splits* Yuzhang commandery to create Luling commandery, then appoints a Grand Administrator for it.

**2. The head of a province (州) is the 刺史 (Inspector) or 州牧 (Governor), a distinct office.** For example 「益州刺史郤儉」and 「領益州牧」[21]; the commentary on officials notes that 「自漢季以来，刺史總統諸郡」[20] — since late Han, the Inspector "oversaw all the commanderies" (諸郡), showing the commanderies sat under the province, not equal to it. Jia Kui likewise explains the province's role: 「州本以御史出監諸郡，以六条詔書察長吏二千石已下」[23] — the province was originally an imperial-clerk post sent out to supervise the commanderies and examine the 2000-shih officials and below.

**3. The head of a county (县) is the 令 or 长, not a 太守.** Examples: 「除盧令」[26]; Jiang Wan 「除廣都長」, and Zhuge Liang's praise that he was 「非百里之才」[35] (a "hundred-li" = a county); Lü Dai 「出補余姚長」[31].

**4. The text lays out the full ladder explicitly.** Xiahou Xuan's memorial criticizes the layered structure: 「今之長吏，皆君吏民，橫重以郡守，累以刺史」[29] — below are the 長吏 (county-level), then the 郡守 (Grand Administrator), then the 刺史 (Inspector). Bu Zhi similarly pairs them: 「若今郡守百里，皆各得其人」[27], where 「百里」 stands for the county magistrate. And the Grand Administrators are classed as 「良二千石」[1], the 2000-shih rank.

## Inference

Putting these together: since the province chief (刺史/州牧) supervised the commanderies [20][23], and the county chief (令/长) sat below the commandery [29][35], the 太守 — who is titled after a commandery and ranked 2000 shih [1] — must be the commandery's chief executive. **据此推断 (on this evidence), a Grand Administrator was the chief of a commandery, i.e. the middle tier between province and county.**

---

以下不是《三国志》的记载: In the late Eastern Han the local system was 州–郡–县 (province–commandery–county); the Grand Administrator was the chief of a commandery, the Inspector/Governor headed a province, and the Prefect (令) or Chief (长) headed a county.

q: Which cities normally served as the capitals of Ts'ao-Wei, Shu-Han and Sun-Wu respectively? For Wu, give the capital used over the long term after Sun Ch'üan moved the court.
reply:
**Short answer**

- **Wei (Ts'ao-Wei):** **Luoyang**. Cao Pi had the Luoyang palace built and entered Luoyang in the 12th month of Huangchu 1; a Pei Songzhi note quoting the *Weilüe* lists Chang'an, Qiao, Xuchang, Ye, and Luoyang as the "five capitals."
- **Shu-Han:** **Chengdu**. Liu Bei ascended the imperial throne at Chengdu, and Liu Shan succeeded him at Chengdu.
- **Wu (Sun-Wu):** the long-term capital after Sun Quan's move was **Jianye** (建業). Sun Quan moved the capital to Jianye in the 9th month of Huanglong 1 = **229 CE**. Earlier he had made his seat at E, renamed Wuchang, and after the move to Jianye Wuchang remained a base of importance, with the crown prince and Lu Xun left in charge of Wuchang affairs.

**Evidence**

Wei — Luoyang:
- 「十二月，初營洛陽宮，戊午幸洛陽。」[7] — In the 12th month he first had the Luoyang palace built, and on the *wuwu* day arrived at Luoyang.
- Pei note quoting the *Weilüe*: 「改長安、譙、許昌、鄴、洛陽爲五都」[5] — Chang'an, Qiao, Xuchang, Ye, and Luoyang were made the five capitals.

Shu-Han — Chengdu:
- 「即皇帝位於成都武擔之南。」[22] — He took the imperial throne south of Wudan in Chengdu.
- 「五月，後主襲位於成都，時年十七」[23] — In the 5th month the Later Ruler (Liu Shan) succeeded to the throne at Chengdu, aged seventeen.

Wu — Jianye:
- 「秋九月，權遷都建業，因固府不改館，徵上大將軍陸遜輔太子登，掌武昌留事。」[12] — In the 9th month of autumn, Sun Quan moved the capital to Jianye; he kept the existing offices and did not rebuild the palaces, and summoned Grand General Lu Xun to assist the crown prince Sun Deng in charge of Wuchang affairs. This entry is under Huanglong 1 = **229 CE** [era tool].
- Earlier, at Wuchang: 「權自公安都鄂，改名武昌」[16] — Sun Quan moved his seat from Gong'an to E, which he renamed Wuchang; this is recorded in the entry "二年四月" of the Wu text.
- A Pei note quoting the *Jiangbiao zhuan*: 「初，權移都建業，大會將相文武」[17] — At the time Sun Quan moved the capital to Jianye, he held a great assembly of civil and military officers.

**Inference (marked as such)**

From the facts above: Liu Bei took the throne at Chengdu and Liu Shan succeeded there, so Chengdu was the seat of Shu-Han's court; Cao Pi had Luoyang's palace built and entered Luoyang after ascending the throne, and a *Weilüe* note calls Luoyang one of the five capitals — so Luoyang was Wei's capital. For Wu, Sun Quan first seated himself at E/Wuchang and then moved the capital to Jianye; since he kept the crown prince and Lu Xun to oversee "Wuchang affairs" [12], it may be inferred that Wuchang continued to function as a base of importance after the move, while Jianye was the court's long-term seat.

- 「秋九月，權遷都建業，因固府不改館，徵上大將軍陸遜輔太子登，掌武昌留事。」[12] — In the 9th month of autumn, Sun Quan moved the capital to Jianye; he kept the existing offices and did not rebuild the palaces, and summoned Grand General Lu Xun to assist the crown prince Sun Deng in charge of Wuchang affairs. This entry is under Huanglong 1 = **229 CE** [era tool].
- Earlier, at Wuchang: 「權自公安都鄂，改名武昌」[16] — Sun Quan moved his seat from Gong'an to E, which he renamed Wuchang; this is recorded in the entry "二年四月" of the Wu text.
- A Pei note quoting the *Jiangbiao zhuan*: 「初，權移都建業，大會將相文武」[17] — At the time Sun Quan moved the capital to Jianye, he held a great assembly of civil and military officers.

q: Which present-day city roughly corresponds to Jianye of the Three Kingdoms period? What is the city that served as Shu-Han's capital called today?
reply:
## Short answer

**Jianye (建業)** corresponds roughly to present-day **Nanjing, Jiangsu province**. **Chengdu (成都)**, Shu-Han's capital, is still called **Chengdu** today — it is the modern city of Chengdu, Sichuan province.

## Jianye / Nanjing

The name Jianye was created by Sun Quan out of the older name Moling (秣陵):

- 「十六年，權徙治秣陵。明年，城石頭，改秣陵爲建業。」[5] — In the 16th year of Jian'an (211 CE, per the era converter), Sun Quan moved his seat of government to Moling; the next year he built the fortification at Shitou and renamed Moling "Jianye."
- Later he made it the Wu capital: 「黃龍元年，權遷都建業」[10] — In the first year of Huanglong, Sun Quan moved the capital to Jianye.
- Pei Songzhi's note quotes the *Jiangbiao zhuan* on the site's earlier history: 「秣陵，楚武王所置，名為金陵。」「昔秦始皇東巡會稽經此縣，望氣者云金陵地形有王者都邑之氣，故掘斷連岡，改名秣陵。」[21] — Moling was established by King Wu of Chu and was called Jinling; Qin Shihuang, on his eastern tour, was told by a qi-watcher that the terrain had the aura of a kingly capital, so he cut the connected ridges and renamed it Moling. The same note says Liu Bei also urged Sun Quan to make his capital there.

## Chengdu / Shu-Han's capital

- Liu Bei took the throne at Chengdu: 「即皇帝位於成都武擔之南」[12] — he assumed the imperial throne south of Wudan in Chengdu.
- His successor Liu Shan did the same: 「後主襲位於成都」[16] — the Later Ruler succeeded to the position in Chengdu.
- Zhuge Liang governed from there: 「先主外出，亮常鎮守成都，足食足兵」[30] — when Liu Bei was away, Zhuge Liang regularly guarded Chengdu, keeping it well supplied with food and troops.

**Inference (following the records above):** since Jianye is the place Sun Quan renamed from Moling and made his capital, and Moling/Jinling is the site on the lower Yangzi where the Wu capital stood, that site is what became the later city of Nanjing; Chengdu, named as the place where Liu Bei and Liu Shan took the throne, is the same city that bears the name today. That identification of the modern city is outside the *Sanguozhi* text itself (see below).

以下不是《三国志》的记载: 建業 (the Three Kingdoms-period name) is in present-day Nanjing, Jiangsu province. 成都 (Chengdu, the Shu-Han capital) is in present-day Chengdu, Sichuan province.

## 结论

- **建业**：孙权把秣陵改名为建业，并定都于此；其地在今江苏省南京市一带（今地对应见文末背景段）。
- **蜀汉都城成都**：刘备在成都即皇帝位，刘禅也在成都继位；成都这一名称沿用至今，即今四川省成都市一带（今地对应见文末背景段）。

## 依据

**建业**

- 建业是孙权由秣陵改名而来：「十六年，權徙治秣陵。明年，城石頭，改秣陵爲建業。」[5]。这里说的十六年即建安十六年，据年号换算为公元 211 年。
- 孙权后来把都城迁到建业：「黃龍元年，權遷都建業」[10]。

q: In the title 'Marquis of Hanshou Village' (Hanshou tinghou), is 'Marquis' an office or a rank of nobility? Did Guan Yu's receiving this title mean that he served as Prefect of Hanshou county?
reply:
## Short answer

「侯」here is a rank of nobility (爵), not an office (官): the sources class 亭侯 among the 爵, and record it as something *conferred* (封) on Guan Yu in the same passage where his *office* is separately conferred on him. Whether this meant he served as Prefect of Hanshou is not stated anywhere in the sources; the conclusion drawn below (that it did not) is marked as an inference.

## Facts from the sources

**1. His office and his title are recorded as two different acts, in one passage.**

「曹公禽羽以歸，拜為偏將軍，禮之甚厚」[1]
(Cao Cao captured Yu and brought him back; he was *appointed* Lieutenant-General [偏將軍] and treated with great courtesy.)
「曹公即表封羽為漢壽亭侯」[1]
(Cao Cao then memorialized to *enfeoff* Yu as Marquis of Hanshou Village.)

The passage opens with 「建安五年，曹公東征，先主奔袁紹」[1]; the enfeoffment is recorded inside this same passage, and the source gives it no separate date. 建安五年 = 200 CE (era conversion).

**2. 亭侯 stands inside a scale of 爵 in the sources.**

「自夫人以下爵凡十二等」[11]
(From 夫人 downward there are in all twelve grades of 爵.)
「昭儀比縣侯；昭華比鄉侯；脩容比亭侯；脩儀比關內侯」[11]
(Zhaoyi ranks with a county marquis; Zhaohua with a 鄉 marquis; Xiurong with a 亭 marquis; Xiuyi with a marquis within the passes.)

So 縣侯 / 鄉侯 / 亭侯 / 關內侯 appear in that descending order in the source.

**3. 侯 is expressly called 爵, and grades of 侯 are counted as 爵級.**

裴注引《魏書》:「置名號侯爵十八級，關中侯爵十七級，皆金印紫綬」[22]、「與舊列侯關內侯凡六等」[22]
(…set up "title marquis" as the eighteenth *noble grade*, "marquis within the passes" as the seventeenth, both with gold seals and purple cords… together with the old 列侯 and 關內侯, six grades in all.)
「三公封列侯，自林始也」[33]
(That the Three Excellencies were enfeoffed as 列侯 began with Cui Lin.)

**4. A 亭侯 has a fief of households (邑) and passes to an heir.**

「紹封攸孫彪爲陵樹亭侯，邑三百戸」[10]
(…enfeoffed Xun You's grandson Xun Biao as Marquis of Lingshu Village, with three hundred households.)
于禁: 「封益壽亭侯」[8]; 「子圭嗣，封益壽亭侯」[9]
(his son Yu Gui inherited and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yishou Village.)
Other place-named 亭侯: 全琮「於是封陽華亭侯」[2]; 滿寵「進封安昌亭侯」[4]; 是儀「後封都亭侯」[54]; 潘濬「封常遷亭侯」[6].

**5. 漢壽 is a place name.**

「潘濬字承明，武陵漢壽人也」[41]
「大將軍費禕為魏降人郭循所殺於漢壽」[39]

## Inference

From facts 1–5: the title 漢壽亭侯 is named after a place, exactly like 陽華、安昌、都、常遷、陵樹、益壽 in fact 4; it was conferred by 封 [1], it carries a fief of households [10], and it passes to an heir [9]. 据此推断: 漢壽亭侯 is a 爵 — a rank of nobility attached to the small fief (亭) of Hanshou — and not an appointment to a post; in the same passage his post is separately given as 偏將軍 [1].

Since the source never records Guan Yu holding 漢壽令 or 漢壽長, and since the fief named in the title is a 亭, which in the source's scale stands below 鄉侯 and 縣侯 [11], 据此推断: receiving 漢壽亭侯 did not mean that Guan Yu administered Hanshou county. (This is an inference: 资料里没有记载，不等于当时没有这种情况; but on the evidence the two things are distinct.)

The order 縣侯 → 鄉侯 → 亭侯 → 關內侯 in the 后妃傳序 [11] suggests the grades are distinguished by the size of the fief (縣 > 鄉 > 亭); 据此推断 a 亭侯's fief is smaller than a county. The source itself only says 比 ("ranks with"), so the fief-size explanation is inference, not quotation.

资料中未见某位亭侯同时任其封地县令、长的记载 (again: absence of record is not proof of absence).

## Background

以下不是《三国志》的记载: 问题里说的"受封汉寿亭侯即出任汉寿县令"，《三国志》里没有记载，可能出自后人对爵号与官职的混淆或其他非正史的说法。县令、长是一县的行政长官。

## The evidence

**1. The title is a fief-nobility rank, distinct from the office he held.**

In Guan Yu's biography the two things are recorded as two separate acts:

"拜為偏將軍" (an appointment to office) and "封……侯" (an enfeoffment) are different verbs applied to different things — the office was 偏將軍, the enfeoffment was 漢壽亭侯. This happened in Jian'an 5 = 200 CE [era].

**2. 亭侯 appears in the sources as a *grade of nobility*, in a hierarchy of fiefs.**

The "Empresses and Consorts" preface ranks palace titles against noble ones:

> 「昭儀比縣侯；昭華比鄉侯；脩容比亭侯；脩儀比關內侯」[11]

(Tr.: Zhaoyi ranks with a *county* marquis; Zhaohua with a *district* marquis; Xiurong with a *ting* marquis; Xiuyi with a marquis within the passes.)

So 縣侯 / 鄉侯 / 亭侯 / 關內侯 form a descending scale of noble rank, graded by the size of the fief (county → district → *ting*). A 亭侯 is therefore a marquis whose fief is a 亭 (a small local unit), not a county.

**3. 侯 is explicitly called 爵 (rank of nobility) in the sources.**

Pei Songzhi's note quoting the *Wei shu*: 「置名號侯爵十八級，關中侯爵十七級……與舊列侯關內侯凡六等」[22] (Tr.: [Cao Cao] established "title marquis" as the 18th *noble rank*, "marquis within the passes" as the 17th…, making six grades together with the old *liehou* and *guanneihou*.)

And when the office of one of the Three Excellencies was combined with a noble title: 「三公封列侯，自林始也」[33] (Tr.: that the Three Excellencies were enfeoffed as *liehou* began with Cui Lin.)

**4. 亭侯 carries a fief of revenue (食邑), and can be inherited — marks of a noble title, not an administrative post.**

> 「紹封攸孫彪爲陵樹亭侯，邑三百戸」[10]

(Tr.: [the court] enfeoffed Xun You's grandson Xun Biao as Marquis of Lingshu Village, with 300 households as his fief.)

Likewise 于禁 was 「封益壽亭侯」 and his son 「子圭嗣，封益壽亭侯」[8][9] — the title passes to the heir. Other examples are all place-named noble titles: 全琮 「封陽華亭侯」[2]; 滿寵 「進封安昌亭侯」[4]; 是儀 「封都亭侯」[54]; 潘濬 「封常遷亭侯」[6].

**5. 漢壽 was a place name (and there was a Hanshou county in Wuling commandery).**

Pan Jun is recorded as 「武陵漢壽人也」[41] (Tr.: a man of Hanshou, Wuling commandery), and Fei Yi is said to have died at Hanshou: 「大將軍費禕為魏降人郭循所殺於漢壽」[39]. So 漢壽 is a real place name — which is exactly why it appears in a fief-title.

## Inference

Putting these together: since 亭侯 titles (a) are placed in a graded scale of noble ranks by fief size [11], (b) are called 侯爵 / 爵 in the sources [22][33], (c) carry household revenue and pass to heirs [10][8], and (d) are named after places (陽華, 安昌, 都, 常遷, 陵樹, 益壽) — **we may conclude** that 漢壽亭侯 was a noble title whose fief was the 亭 of Hanshou, granting Guan Yu the revenue of that small fief and a rank in the noble hierarchy.

It was **not** an appointment as Prefect (令/長) of Hanshou county. A marquis's fief (侯國) was a source of income and rank, not a governorship; the sources show Guan Yu's actual office at that time as 偏將軍, and later inheritances of the same type of title by sons who did not thereby become county administrators. Note also that the fief is a 亭 ("village"), one step below a 鄉 and two below a 縣 in the scale [11], so the title does not even correspond to a whole county.

（不写公元年以外的东西；如需我可以再查关羽此后官职，如「先主為漢中王，拜羽為前將軍」之类。）

「三公封列侯，自林始也」[33]
(That the Three Excellencies were enfeoffed as 列侯 began with Cui Lin.)

**4. A 亭侯 has a fief of households (邑) and passes to an heir.**

「紹封攸孫彪爲陵樹亭侯，邑三百戸」[10]
(…enfeoffed Xun You's grandson Xun Biao as Marquis of Lingshu Village, with three hundred households.)
于禁: 「封益壽亭侯」[8]; 「子圭嗣，封益壽亭侯」[9]
(his son Yu Gui inherited and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yishou Village.)
Other place-named 亭侯: 全琮「於是封陽華亭侯」[2]; 滿寵「進封安昌亭侯」[4]; 是儀「後封都亭侯」[54]; 潘濬「封常遷亭侯」[6].

**5. 漢壽 is a place name.**

「潘濬字承明，武陵漢壽人也」[41]
「大將軍費禕為魏降人郭循所殺於漢壽」[39]

## Inference

From facts 1–5: the title 漢壽亭侯 is named after a place, exactly like 陽華、安昌、都、常遷、陵樹、益壽 in fact 4; it was conferred by 封 [1], it carries a fief of households [10], and it passes to an heir [9]. 据此推断: 漢壽亭侯 is a 爵 — a rank of nobility attached to the small fief (亭) of Hanshou — and not an appointment to a post; in the same passage his post is separately given as 偏將軍 [1].

Since the source never records Guan Yu holding 漢壽令 or 漢壽長, and since the fief named in the title is a 亭, which in the source's scale stands below 鄉侯 and 縣侯 [11], 据此推断: receiving 漢壽亭侯 did not mean that Guan Yu administered Hanshou county. (This is an inference: 资料里没有记载，不等于当时没有这种情况; but on the evidence the two things are distinct.)

The order 縣侯 → 鄉侯 → 亭侯 → 關內侯 in the 后妃傳序 [11] suggests the grades are distinguished by the size of the fief (縣 > 鄉 > 亭); 据此推断 a 亭侯's fief is smaller than a county. The source itself only says 比 ("ranks with"), so the fief-size explanation is inference, not quotation.

资料中未见某位亭侯同时任其封地县令、长的记载 (again: absence of record is not proof of absence).
