q: When Liu Shan surrendered to Teng Ai, how many households and how many people did the registers he sent over give for Shu-Han in total? How many soldiers and how many officials?
reply:
**Conclusion:** The registers Liu Shan sent to Deng Ai gave Shu-Han a total of **280,000 households** and **940,000 people (male and female)**, with **102,000 armored officers and men** and **40,000 officials**.

**Basis in the text:** The figure comes from Pei Songzhi's annotation to the 後主傳, quoting 王隱《蜀記》 (Wang Yin's *Shu Ji*). After Liu Shan sent envoys to surrender, the annotation records:

「禪又遣太常張峻、益州別駕汝超受節度，遣太僕蔣顯有命敕姜維。又遣尚書郎李虎送士民簿，領戶二十八萬，男女口九十四萬，帶甲將士十萬二千，吏四萬人，米四十餘萬斛，金銀各二千斤，錦綺採絹各二十萬匹，餘物稱此。」[7]

Translation: Liu Shan also sent Grand Master of Ceremonies Zhang Jun and Yi Province Attendant Officer Ru Chao to receive Deng Ai's orders, and sent Grand Coachman Jiang Xian with orders to Jiang Wei. He further sent Secretariat Gentleman Li Hu to deliver the registers of soldiers and people: **280,000 households; 940,000 male and female persons; 102,000 armored officers and men; 40,000 officials**; over 400,000 *hu* of grain; 2,000 *jin* each of gold and silver; 200,000 bolts each of brocade, fine silk, and colored silk; other goods in proportion. [7]

The main text of the 後主傳 records only the surrender ritual itself — that Liu Shan came to the camp gate with his coffin and bound hands, and that Deng Ai untied him, burned the coffin, and had him made General of Agile Cavalry: 「後主興櫬自縛，詣軍壘門。艾解縛焚櫬，延請相見。因承製拜後主為驃騎將軍。」[3] — and does not give the register figures.

**Note on the source:** The numbers are Pei Songzhi's annotation drawing on 王隱《蜀記》 (Wang Yin's *Shu Ji*), not Chen Shou's own text. If you are comparing with the Wu registers, those come from a different annotation, 《晉陽秋》 on Sun Hao's surrender: 「領州四，郡四十三，縣三百一十三，戶五十二萬三千，吏三萬二千，兵二十三萬，男女口二百三十萬，米穀二百八十萬斛，舟船五千餘艘，後宮五千餘人。」[15] — a separate record, not part of the Shu figure.

q: Is Hanzhong north or south of the Qinling mountains? Why was it such an important region for Shu-Han, both for defending against attack from the north and for sending armies northward?
reply:
# Hanzhong and the Qinling: Position and Strategic Value

## Conclusion

**Hanzhong lies south of the Qinling (秦嶺).** This is an inference from the routes recorded in the text (据此推断): Wei Yan's plan to strike Chang'an starts from Baozhong in Hanzhong, follows the Qinling eastward, then turns north by the Ziwu pass to reach Chang'an [34]; and every Wei attack on Hanzhong is described as entering from the north through those same passes, in one case explicitly as going south (「從子午道南入」) [70]. Since Chang'an is reached by going north over the Qinling from Hanzhong, and Hanzhong is reached by going south over it from Chang'an, the Qinling must separate the two, with Hanzhong on its southern side.

## The geography as the text shows it

Wei Yan's plan to strike Chang'an:

> 「今假延精兵五千，負糧五千，直從褒中出，循秦嶺而東，當子午而北，不過十日可到長安。」[34]

Wei attacks on Hanzhong entering by the passes:

- 「張郃由子午，曹真由斜谷」[33]
- 「分從斜谷、駱谷入」[49]
- 「從子午道南入」[70]

## Why it was vital for defending Shu

**It was called the throat of Yi province.** When Liu Bei was fighting for Hanzhong, Yang Hong told Zhuge Liang:

> 「漢中則益州咽喉，存亡之機會，若無漢中則無蜀矣，此家門之禍也。方今之事，男子當戰，女子當運，發兵何疑？」[3]

Pei Songzhi made the same point in his own comment: 「臣松之以為蜀與漢中，其由脣齒也。」[7]

**Whoever holds it can seal the passes.** Liu Ye warned Cao Cao that if he did not press on after taking Hanzhong, the Shu side would 「據險守要，則不可犯矣」[2]. Xu Huang likewise called the plank road 「漢中之險要咽喉也」[60].

**Losing it opens the road into Shu.** Liao Li recalled the earlier crisis: 「既亡漢中，使夏侯淵、張郃深入於巴，幾喪一州」[78]. And Wang Ping argued against letting an enemy in, because 「漢中去涪垂千里。賊若得關，便為禍也」[58].

**The defensive system worked.** Liu Bei left Wei Yan in charge, and the method was 「皆實兵諸圍以御外敵。敵若來攻，使不得入」[8]. It held repeatedly: Cao Shuang's thrust was stopped at Xingshi by Wang Ping [58]; Cao Zhen's multi-road attack was broken by rain and terrain, 「大雨道絕，真等皆還」[33], and 「會大霖雨三十餘日，或栈道斷絕，詔真還軍」[70]. Chen Qun had warned that 「斜谷阻险，難以进退，转运必见钞截」[67]. Even Cao Cao found it hard going: 「既至漢中，山峻難登，軍食頗乏」[10].

## Why it was the base for striking north

**It was the launch-pad for the northern campaigns.** Zhuge Liang 「率諸軍北駐漢中」[22], and from there 「六年春，亮出攻祁山，不克。冬，復出散關，圍陳倉，糧盡退。魏將王雙率軍追亮，亮與戰，破之，斬雙，還漢中。」[20]. Later Jiang Wei too was based there: 「隨大將軍蔣琬住漢中」[93].

**Fa Zheng spelled out the offensive value** of taking Hanzhong:

> 「廣農積谷，觀釁伺隙，上可以傾覆寇敵，尊獎王室，中可以蠶食雍、涼，廣拓境土，下可以固守要害，為持久之計。」[62]

**The mountains cut both ways.** The same Qinling passes that let Shu threaten Chang'an (Wei Yan's Ziwu scheme [34]) made a Shu offensive logistically brutal — every push north meant hauling grain through defiles where, as Chen Qun noted, supply lines are easily cut [67].

**It was also a political base.** After taking Hanzhong, Liu Bei was made King of Hanzhong (漢中王), the title taken from the region, with 「以漢中、巴、蜀、廣漢、犍為為國」[1].

## Inference

Pulling these facts together (据此推断): from the routes quoted above, the passes through the Qinling are the routes by which an army moves between Hanzhong and Chang'an — Wei Yan goes north over the Qinling to reach Chang'an [34], and Wei armies come south over the Qinling into Hanzhong [33][49][70]. Whoever holds Hanzhong therefore controls those routes in either direction. This is why the text calls it the throat of Yizhou and likens Shu and Hanzhong to lips and teeth [3][7], why losing it exposed Ba and Shu [78], and why it served as the assembly point for the northern expeditions [22][93]. This is an inference from the routes and the strategic statements quoted above, not a single explicit sentence in the record.

# Hanzhong and the Qinling: Position and Strategic Value

## Short answer

Hanzhong lies **south of the Qinling range**. The Qinling (秦嶺) runs east–west between the Hanzhong basin and the Guanzhong plain around Chang'an; the only routes north are the great plank-road passes cut through it — Ziwu (子午), Xiegu (斜谷), Luogu (駱谷) and the Baoxie road out of Baozhong (褒中). This is why the records always describe movement from Hanzhong to Chang'an as going **north through the Qinling**, and movement from Chang'an to Hanzhong as coming **south through the same passes**.

## The geography, as the text shows it

Wei Yan's plan to strike Chang'an starts at Baozhong (in Hanzhong) and heads north over the mountains:

> 「今假延精兵五千，負糧五千，直從褒中出，循秦嶺而東，當子午而北，不過十日可到長安。」[34]

(From Baozhong, follow the Qinling eastward, then go north by way of Ziwu — in ten days you reach Chang'an.)

Conversely, Wei invasions of Hanzhong are described as entering from the north through the same passes: 「張郃由子午，曹真由斜谷」[33]; 「分從斜谷、駱谷入」[49]; 「從子午道南入」[70]. So the Qinling is the wall between Hanzhong and Chang'an, and Hanzhong sits on its southern side.

## Why it was vital for defending Shu

**It was called the throat of Yi province.** When Liu Bei was fighting for Hanzhong, Yang Hong told Zhuge Liang:

> 「漢中則益州咽喉，存亡之機會，若無漢中則無蜀矣，此家門之禍也。方今之事，男子當戰，女子當運，發兵何疑？」[3]

(Hanzhong is the throat of Yizhou, the hinge of survival. Without Hanzhong there is no Shu. Men should fight, women should carry supplies — why hesitate to send troops?)

Pei Songzhi put it even more plainly: 「臣松之以為蜀與漢中，其由脣齒也。」[7] (Shu and Hanzhong are like lips and teeth.)

**Whoever holds it can seal the passes.** Liu Ye warned Cao Cao that if he did not press on after taking Hanzhong, the Shu side would 「據險守要，則不可犯矣」[2] (hold the defiles and key points, and become unassailable). Xu Huang likewise called the plank road 「漢中之險要咽喉也」[60].

**Losing it opens the road into Shu.** Liao Li recalled the earlier crisis: 「既亡漢中，使夏侯淵、張郃深入於巴，幾喪一州」[78] (having lost Hanzhong, Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He pushed deep into Ba and nearly cost us a province). And Wang Ping argued against letting an enemy in, because 「漢中去涪垂千里。賊若得關，便為禍也」[58] (Hanzhong is nearly a thousand li from Fu; if the enemy takes the pass it is disaster).

**The defensive system worked.** Liu Bei left Wei Yan in charge, and the method was 「皆實兵諸圍以御外敵。敵若來攻，使不得入」[8] (to fill every garrison with real troops so the enemy cannot get in). It held repeatedly: Cao Shuang's 100,000-man thrust was stopped at Xingshi by Wang Ping [58]; Cao Zhen's multi-road attack was broken by rain and terrain [33][70]; Chen Qun had warned that 「斜谷阻险，難以进退，转运必见钞截」[67] (the Xie valley is so confined that supply columns get cut off). Even Cao Cao found it hard going: 「既至漢中，山峻難登，軍食頗乏」[10].

## Why it was the base for striking north

**It was the launch-pad for every northern campaign.** Zhuge Liang 「率諸軍北駐漢中」[22] and from there attacked Qishan and Chencang and returned to Hanzhong [20][23]. Later Jiang Wei too was based there: 「隨大將軍蔣琬住漢中」[93], and from Hanzhong he repeatedly rode west into Wei territory.

**Fa Zheng spelled out the offensive value** of taking Hanzhong:

> 「廣農積谷，觀釁伺隙，上可以傾覆寇敵，尊獎王室，中可以蠶食雍、涼，廣拓境土，下可以固守要害，為持久之計。」[62]

(Open farmland and store grain, watch for openings: at best you can overthrow the enemy; in the middle case, nibble away at Yong and Liang and widen your territory; at worst you can hold the key points and plan for the long haul.)

**The mountains cut both ways.** The same Qinling passes that let Shu threaten Chang'an (Wei Yan's Ziwu scheme [34]) made a Shu offensive logistically brutal — every push north meant hauling grain through defiles where, as Chen Qun noted, supply lines are easily cut [67].

**It was also a political base.** After taking Hanzhong, Liu Bei was made King of Hanzhong (漢中王), with 「以漢中、巴、蜀、廣漢、犍為為國」[32-0018]; the title itself was taken from the region.

## Inference

Pulling these facts together: Hanzhong is the single corridor between the Guanzhong plain and the Sichuan basin. It sits south of the Qinling, so an army coming from the north (from Chang'an) must funnel through the Ziwu, Xiegu, or Luogu passes to reach it, and an army going north from Shu must funnel through those same passes to reach Chang'an. Whoever holds Hanzhong therefore controls the only door in either direction — which is why the text calls it the throat of Yizhou and likens Shu and Hanzhong to lips and teeth, why losing it exposed Ba and Shu, and why it served as the assembly point for the northern expeditions. # Hanzhong and the Qinling: Position and Strategic Value

## Conclusion

**Hanzhong lies south of the Qinling (秦嶺).** This is an inference from the routes recorded in the text (据此推断): Wei Yan's plan to strike Chang'an starts from Baozhong in Hanzhong, follows the Qinling eastward, then turns north by the Ziwu pass to reach Chang'an [34]; and every Wei attack on Hanzhong is described as entering from the north through those same passes, in one case explicitly as going south (「從子午道南入」) [70]. Since Chang'an is reached by going north over the Qinling from Hanzhong, and Hanzhong is reached by going south over it from Chang'an, the Qinling must separate the two, with Hanzhong on its southern side.

## The geography as the text shows it

Wei Yan's plan to strike Chang'an:

> 「今假延精兵五千，負糧五千，直從褒中出，循秦嶺而東，當子午而北，不過十日可到長安。」[34]

Wei attacks on Hanzhong entering by the passes:

- 「張郃由子午，曹真由斜谷」[33]
- 「分從斜谷、駱谷入」[49]
- 「從子午道南入」[70]

## Why it was vital for defending Shu

**It was called the throat of Yi province.** When Liu Bei was fighting for Hanzhong, Yang Hong told Zhuge Liang:

> 「漢中則益州咽喉，存亡之機會，若無漢中則無蜀矣，此家門之禍也。方今之事，男子當戰，女子當運，發兵何疑？」[3]

Pei Songzhi made the same point in his own comment: 「臣松之以為蜀與漢中，其由脣齒也。」[7]

**Whoever holds it can seal the passes.** Liu Ye warned Cao Cao that if he did not press on after taking Hanzhong, the Shu side would 「據險守要，則不可犯矣」[2]. Xu Huang likewise called the plank road 「漢中之險要咽喉也」[60].

**Losing it opens the road into Shu.** Liao Li recalled the earlier crisis: 「既亡漢中，使夏侯淵、張郃深入於巴，幾喪一州」[78]. And Wang Ping argued against letting an enemy in, because 「漢中去涪垂千里。賊若得關，便為禍也」[58].

**The defensive system worked.** Liu Bei left Wei Yan in charge, and the method was 「皆實兵諸圍以御外敵。敵若來攻，使不得入」[8]. It held repeatedly: Cao Shuang's thrust was stopped at Xingshi by Wang Ping [58]; Cao Zhen's multi-road attack was broken by rain and terrain, 「大雨道絕，真等皆還」[33], and 「會大霖雨三十餘日，或栈道斷絕，詔真還軍」[70]. Chen Qun had warned that 「斜谷阻险，難以进退，转运必见钞截」[67]. Even Cao Cao found it hard going: 「既至漢中，山峻難登，軍食頗乏」[10].

## Why it was the base for striking north

**It was the launch-pad for the northern campaigns.** Zhuge Liang 「率諸軍北駐漢中」[22], and from there 「亮出攻祁山，不克。冬，復出散關，圍陳倉，糧盡退……還漢中」[20]. Later Jiang Wei too was based there: 「隨大將軍蔣琬住漢中」[93].

**Fa Zheng spelled out the offensive value** of taking Hanzhong:

> 「廣農積谷，觀釁伺隙，上可以傾覆寇敵，尊獎王室，中可以蠶食雍、涼，廣拓境土，下可以固守要害，為持久之計。」[62]

**The mountains cut both ways.** The same Qinling passes that let Shu threaten Chang'an (Wei Yan's Ziwu scheme [34]) made a Shu offensive logistically brutal — every push north meant hauling grain through defiles where, as Chen Qun noted, supply lines are easily cut [67].

**It was also a political base.** After taking Hanzhong, Liu Bei was made King of Hanzhong (漢中王), the title taken from the region, with 「以漢中、巴、蜀、廣漢、犍為為國」[1].

## Inference

Pulling these facts together (据此推断): from the routes quoted above, the passes through the Qinling are the routes by which an army moves between Hanzhong and Chang'an — Wei Yan goes north over the Qinling to reach Chang'an [34], and Wei armies come south over the Qinling into Hanzhong [33][49][70]. Whoever holds Hanzhong therefore controls those routes in either direction. This is why the text calls it the throat of Yizhou and likens Shu and Hanzhong to lips and teeth [3][7], why losing it exposed Ba and Shu [78], and why it served as the assembly point for the northern expeditions [22][93]. This is an inference from the routes and the strategic statements quoted above, not a single explicit sentence in the record.

q: Can the 'Jing Province' of the late Eastern Han be equated directly with today's Jingzhou city in Hubei? Explain how the two differ as geographical concepts.
reply:
## Short answer

No. In the *Sanguozhi*, 荆州 (Jing Province) is a **province (州)** — a top-level administrative region governed by a 刺史/州牧 and subdivided into many **commanderies (郡)** spread over what is now several modern provinces. Today's Jingzhou City in Hubei corresponds at most to one small corner of that province (the old 南郡/江陵 area). The two are different in **administrative level** and in **territorial extent**, so they cannot be equated.

## Evidence from the sources

**1. Jing was a province with a provincial governor, not a city.**

Liu Biao took office as its governor: 「代王叡爲荊州刺史」[2], and later 「乃以表爲鎮南將軍、荊州牧」[1]. The office is a 刺史/州牧 — head of a 州.

**2. The province was divided into eight commanderies (八郡).**

Sima Biao's 《戰略》, quoted in Pei's commentary, has Kuai Yue tell Liu Biao: 「兵集衆附，南據江陵，北守襄陽，荊州八郡可傳檄而定」[6] — i.e., Jing comprised **eight commanderies**.

**3. Those commanderies are named, and they stretch across several modern provinces.**

- In the north: 南阳 and 襄阳 (the northern edge, around the Hubei–Henan border). Liu Biao's domain is described as 「南收零、桂，北據漢川，地方數千里，帶甲十餘萬」[1] — "several thousand li square."
- Named commanderies include 长沙 (长沙太守张羡叛 [1]), 江夏 (「以劉表大將文聘爲江夏太守」[4]), 长沙、零陵、桂阳 (「招納長沙、零陵、桂陽」[7]), and 南郡, 零陵, 武陵 (南郡太守糜芳、零陵太守郝普、荆州治中潘濬 [25]).

**4. The province was repeatedly partitioned, and the name was re-applied to different sets of commanderies.**

In 建安二十年 (215) the province was split between Sun Quan and Liu Bei: 「分荊州、江夏、長沙、桂陽東屬，南郡、零陵、武陵西屬」[18] (cf. [12]). Later, under Wei, 「以荊、揚、江表八郡爲荊州，孫權領牧故也；荊州江北諸郡爲郢州」[15] — the label "荆州" was shifted onto a *new* set of eight commanderies south of the Yangzi.

## Inference

Putting these together: a 州 (province) contained 郡 (commanderies), and each 郡 contained counties. Jing held eight commanderies at its height, spanning the region from 南阳/襄阳 in the north down through 江陵/南郡 to 长沙、零陵、桂阳、武陵 in the south — a span of "several thousand li." Therefore, a single modern city cannot represent it: today's Jingzhou City corresponds only to the old **南郡/江陵** core (one commandery, and only part of the province at that), while the province as a whole covered parts of present-day Hubei, Hunan, Henan and beyond.

---

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:**

Today's Jingzhou City (荆州市) is in Hubei Province; the ancient 南郡/江陵 — the provincial core and later a commandery seat under Zhou Yu, Mi Fang and Zhuge Jin [20][25] — lay in today's Hubei, in the Jingzhou area along the middle Yangzi.

**结论：不能等同。**《三国志》里的「荆州」是州一级的行政区，由刺史、州牧治理，下辖若干郡，横跨今天数省；今天的荆州市（湖北）至多只对应当时荆州的南郡、江陵一带。两者在行政层级和辖境范围上都不是一回事。

## 一、事实与依据

1. **荆州是州，长官为刺史、州牧。**刘表「代王叡爲荊州刺史」[2]，后来「乃以表爲鎮南將軍、荊州牧」[1]。

2. **荆州下分八郡。**裴注引司马彪《戰略》载蒯越之言：「兵集衆附，南據江陵，北守襄陽，荊州八郡可傳檄而定」[6]。

3. **这八郡在资料中可考见的有：**长沙（「長沙太守張羨叛表」[1]）、江夏（「以劉表大將文聘爲江夏太守」[4]）、长沙、零陵、桂阳（「使招納長沙、零陵、桂陽」[7]）、南郡、零陵、武陵（南郡太守糜芳、零陵太守郝普、荆州治中潘濬[25]）。

4. **辖境之大。**「南收零、桂，北據漢川，地方數千里，帶甲十餘萬」[1]。

5. **荆州屡被分割，名称还被移用到另一组郡上。**建安二十年（公元215年）「分荊州、江夏、長沙、桂陽東屬，南郡、零陵、武陵西屬」[18]；[12] 所记略同：「遂分荊州、長沙、江夏、桂陽以東屬權，南郡、零陵、武陵以西屬備」。此后魏文帝时又「以荊、揚、江表八郡爲荊州」[15]，而「荊州江北諸郡爲郢州」[15]。

## 二、推断（据此推断）

依据上文各条：州之下为郡，郡由县组成（[30] 记「分沛國蕭、相、竹邑、符離、蘄、銍、龍亢、山桑、洨、虹十縣爲汝陰郡」），而荆州一州含八郡[6]，其境「地方數千里」[1]，南收零陵、桂阳[1]，北据汉川、守襄阳[1][6]，核心为江陵、南郡[6][25]。据此推断：荆州是覆盖八郡、方圆数千里的省级区域，今天的荆州市只是其中南郡、江陵这一小块地方，二者在行政层级与辖境范围上都不能等同；而且「荆州」之名在不同时期被安到不同的郡组合上[15][18]，它本身也不是一个固定对应某座城市的地名。

南郡、江陵（当时的地名）在今天的湖北省荆州市一带；长沙、零陵、桂阳、武陵等郡大致在今天的湖南省一带。

q: When Sun Hao surrendered, how many households and how many people of Wu did Wang Jun take over? How many soldiers and how many officials?
reply:
## Answer

When Sun Hao (孫皓) surrendered, the registers taken over by Wang Jun (王濬) recorded:

- **Households (戶):** 523,000
- **Population, male and female (男女口):** 2,300,000
- **Soldiers (兵):** 230,000
- **Officials / clerks (吏):** 32,000

**Basis (Pei Songzhi's commentary quoting 《晉陽秋》):**

> 「濬收其圖籍，領州四，郡四十三，縣三百一十三，戶五十二萬三千，吏三萬二千，兵二十三萬，男女口二百三十萬，米穀二百八十萬斛，舟船五千餘艘，後宮五千餘人。」[14]

(Pei's note quoting *Jin Yang Qiu*: "Wang Jun collected its maps and registers: it governed 4 provinces, 43 commanderies, 313 counties; 523,000 households; 32,000 officials; 230,000 soldiers; 2,300,000 male and female population; 2,800,000 *hu* of grain; over 5,000 boats; and over 5,000 in the inner palace.")

The main text of the *Wu Shu* records only that Wang Jun was the first to arrive and received Sun Hao's surrender:

> 「壬申，王濬最先到，於是受皓之降，解縛焚櫬，延請相見。」[1]

("On the *renshen* day, Wang Jun arrived first, and thereupon accepted Hao's surrender, untied his bonds, burned the coffin, and invited him to an audience.")

So the totals of households, population, soldiers, and officials come from the *Jin Yang Qiu* passage cited in Pei Songzhi's commentary [14], not from Chen Shou's main text [1].

The same passage also gives, in addition to the four figures you asked about: 4 provinces, 43 commanderies, 313 counties, 2,800,000 *hu* of grain, over 5,000 boats, and over 5,000 inner-palace personnel [14].

q: Before the Battle of Red Cliffs, what did Chou Yü privately estimate to Sun Ch'üan as Ts'ao Ts'ao's actual troop strength? How many did Ts'ao Ts'ao claim in his letter? And how many picked troops did Chou Yü say would be enough to deal with them?
reply:
## Answer

**Cao Cao's claim in his letter:** In the letter Cao Cao sent to Sun Quan, he claimed to have **800,000 "naval troops"** (水軍八十萬).

**Zhou Yu's private estimate:** In a private night audience with Sun Quan after the council broke up, Zhou Yu said the letter's figure was inflated. His own reckoning was:
- the Central Plains troops Cao Cao actually led: **no more than 150,000–160,000** (十五六萬), and they were long exhausted;
- the troops he had taken over from Liu Biao: **at most 70,000–80,000** (七八萬), and still wavering.

**Troops Zhou Yu said would suffice:** He asked for **50,000 picked troops** (精兵五萬), saying that would be enough to master them.

## Sources

Cao Cao's letter (裴注引《江表傳》):

> 「近者奉辭伐罪，旄麾南指，劉琮束手。今治水軍八十萬眾，方與將軍會獵於吳。」[12]

Zhou Yu's private audience with Sun Quan (裴注引《江表傳》):

> 「諸人徒見操書，言水步八十萬，而各恐懾，不復料其虛實，便開此議，甚無謂也。今以實校之，彼所將中國人，不過十五六萬，且軍已久疲，所得表眾，亦極七八萬耳，尚懷狐疑。夫以疲病之卒，御狐疑之眾，眾數雖多，甚未足畏。得精兵五萬，自足制之，原將軍勿慮。」[1]

Sun Quan's reply is in the same passage: he said 50,000 could not be gathered quickly, but 30,000 had already been selected and would go ahead under Zhou Yu, with more to follow as reserves [1].

Note on the source: both the 800,000 claim and Zhou Yu's estimates come from the *Jiangbiao Zhuan*, quoted in Pei Songzhi's commentary (裴注引《江表傳》), not from Chen Shou's main text. Chen Shou's main biography of Zhou Yu states that Cao Cao obtained Liu Biao's navy, "船步兵數十萬" (ships and foot soldiers, several hundred thousand), at which Sun Quan's officers were all frightened:

> 「其年九月，曹公入荊州，劉琮舉眾降，曹公得其水軍，船步兵數十萬，將士聞之皆恐。」[3]

q: How old were the brothers Ma Liang and Ma Su, respectively, when they died?
reply:
**结论：**《三国志》明确记了两人的卒年岁数——马良死时三十六岁，马谡三十九岁。

**依据（原文）：**

- 「良死時年三十六，謖年三十九。」[1] 这是陈寿在《蜀书·马良传》末尾直接给出的岁数，两人卒时的年龄都写在同一句里。
- 两人是兄弟，马谡是弟弟：「良弟謖，字幼常」[1]。
- 马良其人：「馬良字季常，襄陽宜城人也。」[2]；兄弟五人都以才名见称，「兄弟五人，並有才名」，乡里的谚语说「馬氏五常，白眉最良」[2]。
- 马良死的事由：「及東征吳，遣良入武陵招納五溪蠻夷，蠻夷渠帥皆受印號，咸如意指。」[1]「會先主敗績於夷陵，良亦遇害。」[1]
- 马谡死的事由：「建興六年，亮出軍向祁山，時有宿將魏延、吳壹等，論者皆言以為宜令為先鋒，而亮違眾拔謖，統大眾在前，與魏將張郃戰於街亭，為郃所破，士卒離散。」[1]「謖下獄物故，亮為之流涕。」[1] 建兴六年即公元 228 年（据年号换算）。
- 资料里没有记马良、马谡其余几位兄弟的年龄，所以除这两人外无从回答。

**据此推断：** 依据上面两条事实——马谡是马良的弟弟（「良弟謖」），而马良卒年三十六、马谡卒年三十九——可知马谡虽为弟，卒时反比兄长多三岁，因此马谡去世必在马良去世三年以上之后；至于具体相差几年、各自生于哪一年，资料未载，不能推出。

**Evidence (Chen Shou's main text, "Book of Shu" 9, biography of Ma Liang):**

- 「良死時年三十六，謖年三十九。」[39-0007] — "When Liang died he was thirty-six years old; Su was thirty-nine."

- Ma Liang, styled Jichang, was a man of Yicheng in Xiangyang; he was one of the five Ma brothers known for their talent, and he died when he was sent to Wuling to win over the Five Streams barbarians and the First Sovereign (Liu Bei) was defeated at Yiling: 「會先主敗績於夷陵，良亦遇害。」[39-0007]

q: When Guan Yu flooded the seven armies, how many of Yu Jin's men did he capture? And how many men did Cao Ren have holding out in Fancheng at the time?
reply:
**Short answer**

- **Yu Jin's men captured:** According to Sun Quan's annals, Guan Yu took **30,000** of Yu Jin's infantry and cavalry alive and sent them to Jiangling [20].
- **Cao Ren's garrison at Fancheng:** Cao Ren held the city with **"several thousand"** men — the text says 「人馬數千人」, with no exact figure [2].

**Evidence**

On Yu Jin's force — Yu Jin's own biography says only that the seven armies were drowned and that Yu Jin surrendered:
「禁等七軍皆沒」[17], 「禁遂降」[1]

The number comes from Sun Quan's annals:
「會漢水暴起，羽以舟兵盡生虜禁等步騎三萬送江陵，惟城未拔」[20] — Guan Yu, with his naval force, took Yu Jin and the others, infantry and cavalry, 30,000 in all, alive, and sent them to Jiangling; only the city was not taken.

On Cao Ren's garrison:
「仁人馬數千人守城，城不沒者數板」[2] — Cao Ren, with several thousand men and horses, held the city; the part of the city wall not submerged was only a few planks' height.

**On the two figures**

据此推断: the 「三萬」 of [20] is stated as the troops of Yu Jin's relief force (the "seven armies") whom Guan Yu captured and sent to Jiangling, while the 「數千」 of [2] is stated as Cao Ren's own garrison holding Fancheng; since the two passages attach the numbers to different bodies of troops, the two figures cannot be added together or treated as one total. The text gives no exact number for Cao Ren's garrison, only the vague 「數千」.

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:** 樊城 (Fancheng) was in the area of present-day Xiangyang, Hubei.

q: What was Sima Yi's father's name? How old was he when he died, and in which year? How many sons did he have, and where did Sima Yi rank among them?
reply:
## Conclusion

**Father:** Sima Yi's father was **Sima Fang (司马防), courtesy name Jian'gong (建公)**. He was **71 years old** when he died, in the **24th year of Jian'an = 219 CE**. He had **eight sons**, and Sima Yi was the **second** (the eldest being Sima Lang).

## Evidence

The main source is a Pei Songzhi annotation to the biography of Sima Lang (Sima Yi's elder brother), quoting Sima Biao's *Xu Zhuan* (司马彪《序传》):

- On the father's identity: 「父防，字建公」 [1], and on his death: 「年七十一，建安二十四年終」 [1] — "His father Fang, courtesy name Jian'gong… at the age of seventy-one, he died in the 24th year of Jian'an."
- On the number of sons and Sima Yi's rank: 「有子八人，朗最長，次即晉宣皇帝也。」 [1] — "He had eight sons; Lang was the eldest, and the next was the Jin Emperor Xuan (i.e., Sima Yi)."

Sima Fang's identity as Sima Yi's father is confirmed elsewhere in the *Wei Shu*: in a note on the *Wudi ji*, discussing who recommended Cao Cao for office, the text says 「建公名防，司馬宣王之父」 [8] — "Jian'gong's name was Fang, the father of Sima Xuan-wang (Sima Yi)."

Sima Yi is listed in the name table with courtesy name 仲达 (Zhongda) [who]. The character 仲 in "Zhongda" conventionally marks the second-born, consistent with the record that he was the second son.

The year conversion is from the era tool: 建安二十四年 = 219 CE.

## Summary of the facts
| Item | Record |
|---|---|
| Father's name | Sima Fang (司马防), courtesy name Jian'gong (建公) [1] |
| Age at death | 71 (七十一) [1] |
| Year of death | 24th year of Jian'an = 219 CE [1] (era tool) |
| Number of sons | Eight (八人) [1] |
| Sima Yi's rank | Second son, after eldest Sima Lang [1] |

Note: This detail survives only in Pei Songzhi's annotation quoting Sima Biao's *Xu Zhuan*, not in Chen Shou's main text, since Sima Yi has no biography of his own in the *Sanguozhi*.

q: Jiange chiefly controls traffic between which two regions? Why is it so well suited to defense?
reply:
## Conclusion

Jiange (劍閣) controls the traffic between the **Hanzhong region to the north** (and, behind it, the Guanzhong direction from which Wei's armies came) and the **Fu county–Chengdu plain of Shu to the south**. It is well suited to defense because it sits on the mountain defile of this main road into Shu: a defender who "deploys camps and holds the defiles" can stop a far larger army, while the attacker, blocked outside the pass, has his supply line stretched and his men starving, and is reduced to discussing withdrawal.

## Evidence

**1. Jiange lay on the main invasion road, which Wei's main army had to pass.** Wei's army under Zhong Hui entered Hanzhong from the Xie and Luo valleys, then pushed on; Jiang Wei withdrew and finally fell back to hold Jiange:

> 「會統十餘萬眾，分從斜谷、駱谷入」[36]
> 「維遂東引，還守劍閣。鍾會攻維未能克」[2]
> 「適與翼、厥合，皆退保劍閣以拒會」[11]

**2. It did in fact hold against the main army:**

> 「進攻劍閣，不克，引退，蜀軍保險拒守」[1]
> 「維不答書，列營守險。會不能克，糧運縣遠，將議還歸」[16]
> 「維與諸將列營守險，會不得進，已議還計，全蜀之功，幾乎立矣」[14]

Pei's commentary quoting the *Yuanzi*:
> 「鍾會以二十萬眾留劍閣而不得進，三軍之士已飢」[21]

**3. To get around it, a side road had to be used.** Deng Ai's memorial:

> 「從陰平由邪徑經漢德陽亭趣涪，出劍閣西百里，去成都三百餘里，奇兵衝其腹心。劍閣之守必還赴涪，則會方軌而進；劍閣之軍不還，則應涪之兵寡矣」[2]

**4. The road it guards is long.** Wang Ping, on the defense of Hanzhong:

> 「漢中去涪垂千里」[28]

**5. The defending force.** In Zhong Hui's report: 「維等所統步騎四五萬人」[20].

## Inference

From fact 1 (Zhong Hui entered Hanzhong, pushed west, and after Jiange advanced to Fu) [36][1], together with fact 4 (Hanzhong to Fu is nearly a thousand li) [28] and fact 3 (the Yinping side road comes out 100 li *west* of Jiange and is 300-plus li from Chengdu) [2], I infer that Jiange sits on the corridor linking Hanzhong in the north with Fu and Chengdu in the south — that is, the two regions it controls traffic between.

From facts 2 and 5 — the pass blocked an army of 200,000 [21] whose men were starving [21] and whose commander had "already discussed withdrawing" [14][16], while the defenders numbered some 40,000–50,000 [20] — I infer that holding this defile let a smaller force stop a much larger one and strangle its supply line.

As for the Yinping route: Deng Ai's memorial [2] comes right after Zhong Hui's failure to take Jiange, and the plan itself states that by going through Yinping, "the Jiange garrison will surely turn back to relieve Fu, and then Hui can advance in parallel ranks" [2]. So I infer (this is an inference, not a stated cause) that the Yinping side road was adopted in order to break the Jiange stalemate, by swinging west of the pass into the defenders' rear.
draft:
## 结论

剑阁（劍閣）控制的是**北面的汉中（以及汉中背后的关中方向）与南面的涪县—成都蜀地平原**之间往来的通道。它易守难攻，是因为它扼守在这条入蜀主道的山口险要上：守方只需在山险处"列营守险"，就能以少拒多，而攻方大军一旦被堵在关外，粮运线拉长、士众饥饿，只能议退。

## 依据

**一、剑阁是魏军入蜀主道上必须通过的要口。** 魏伐蜀，钟会大军从斜谷、骆谷进入汉中后向西推进，姜维从沓中、阴平一路东退，最终"退保剑阁"来挡他：

> 「維遂東引，還守劍閣。鍾會攻維未能克」[2]
> 「適與翼、厥合，皆退保劍閣以拒會」[11]

**二、它确实挡住了大军。** 钟会主力"进攻剑阁，不克，引退，蜀军保险拒守"[1]；姜维"列营守险，会不能克，粮运县远，将议还归"[16]；裴松之也说：

> 「維與諸將列營守險，會不得進，已議還計，全蜀之功，幾乎立矣」[14]

裴注引《袁子》更点出攻方二十万众被卡住的窘境：

> 「鍾會以二十萬眾留劍閣而不得進，三軍之士已飢」[21]

**三、绕开剑阁只能走偏僻小道。** 邓艾的上言说明：走主道要"出剑阁"，绕行则须"从阴平由邪径经汉德阳亭趣涪，出剑阁西百里，去成都三百余里"，走一条奇兵小路：

> 「從陰平由邪徑經漢德陽亭趣涪，出劍閣西百里，去成都三百餘里，奇兵衝其腹心。劍閣之守必還赴涪，則會方軌而進；劍閣之軍不還，則應涪之兵寡矣」[2]

**四、这条通道南北距离很长。** 王平论汉中防守时说：

> 「漢中去涪垂千里」[28]

即汉中到涪县将近千里，说明从汉中南下的入蜀道路既长又险，剑阁正卡在这条路的要害处。

## 推断

据上引几条事实推断：剑阁既然是魏军主道必经之口，而姜维凭险"列营守险"便使二十万大军"不得进""已议还计"，且攻方"粮运县远""三军之士已饥"——由此可知，守住这个山口，就能用较少兵力把整支入侵大军堵在关外，并靠拖长其补给线使其陷入困境。反过来，正因为它封住了主道，魏军才不得不另寻邓艾所走的阴平邪径，从剑阁以西绕到守军后方。因此剑阁的作用，正是控制"汉中—涪县/成都"这条南北走廊。

以下不是《三国志》的记载：剑阁（当时即称剑阁）在今四川省广元市剑阁县一带，是大剑山、小剑山之间的山口。

From facts 2 and 5 — the pass blocked an army of 200,000 [21] whose men were starving [21] and whose commander had "already discussed withdrawing" [14][16], while the defenders numbered some 40,000–50,000 [20] — I infer that holding this defile let a smaller force stop a much larger one and strangle its supply line.

As for the Yinping route: Deng Ai's memorial [2] comes right after Zhong Hui's failure to take Jiange, and the plan itself states that by going through Yinping, "the Jiange garrison will surely turn back to relieve Fu, and then Hui can advance in parallel ranks" [2]. So I infer (this is an inference, not a stated cause) that the Yinping side road was adopted in order to break the Jiange stalemate, by swinging west of the pass into the defenders' rear.

q: In the year Zhuge Liang died at Wuzhang Plains, which year of which reign era was it in Shu-Han, and which in Wei? What year is that in the Western calendar?
reply:
## Conclusion

In the year Zhuge Liang died at Wuzhang Plains:

- **In Shu-Han:** it was the **12th year of Jianxing (建興十二年)**.
- **In Wei (Cao Wei):** it was the **2nd year of Qinglong (青龍二年)**.
- **In the Western calendar:** both convert to **234 CE**.

## Evidence

**Shu-Han reckoning — Jianxing 12.** Zhuge Liang's biography in the *Shu Shu*:

> 「十二年春，亮悉大眾由斜谷出，以流馬運，據武功五丈原，與司馬宣王對於渭南。」[1]

> 「其年八月，亮疾病，卒于軍，時年五十四。」[1]

The same year is given in the *Houzhu zhuan* (biography of Liu Shan), which carries the Shu-Han calendar:

> 「十二年春二月，亮由斜谷出，始以流馬運。秋八月，亮卒渭濱。」[6]

**Wei reckoning — Qinglong 2.** Xin Pi's biography in the *Wei Shu*:

> 「青龍二年，諸葛亮率衆出渭南。」[15]

> 「亮卒，復還爲衞尉。」[15]

The *Mingdi ji* (Wei annals) records the same standoff and death:

> 「司馬宣王與亮相持，連圍積日，亮數挑戰，宣王堅壘不應。會亮卒，其軍退還。」[16]

**Conversion to the Western calendar.** The era tool gives 建興 12 (Shu-Han) = 234 CE, and 青龍 2 (Cao Wei) = 234 CE. So Shu-Han Jianxing 12 and Wei Qinglong 2 are the same year, 234 CE.

**Month of death.** Both the Zhuge Liang biography and the *Houzhu zhuan* place the death in the 8th month (八月) [1][6].

## Note on the sources

The accounts differ on the manner and place of death. Pei Songzhi's commentary cites the *Wei Shu*:

> 「亮糧盡勢窮，憂恚歐血，一夕燒營遁走，入谷，道發病卒。」[2]

裴注引《魏書》. In the same note, 《漢晉春秋》 says:

> 「亮卒于郭氏塢。」[2]

Pei Songzhi himself rejects the *Wei Shu* account:

> 「臣松之以為亮在渭濱，魏人躡跡，勝負之形，未可測量，而云歐血，蓋因亮自亡而自誇大也」[2]

裴松之按. So the sources disagree on the manner and place of death, while agreeing on the year.

q: In the year Cao Pi usurped the Han throne and declared himself emperor, how many times did the reign era change, and what were the era names? What year was that in the Western calendar?
reply:
**Answer**

In the year Cao Pi took the throne, the reign era changed **twice**, producing three era names within that single year, in this order: **Jian'an (建安) → Yankang (延康) → Huangchu (黃初)**. That year was **220 CE**.

**Evidence**

1. Cao Pi succeeded his father and changed the era to Yankang:
「太祖崩，嗣位爲丞相、魏王」[7] (When Taizu [Cao Cao] died, he succeeded as Chancellor and King of Wei.)
「改建安二十五年爲延康元年」[7] (He changed Jian'an 25 to the first year of Yankang.)

2. Wu's record confirms both changes within the same year:
「二十五年春正月，曹公薨。太子丕代爲丞相魏王，改年爲延康。」[1] (In the first month of spring of the 25th year, Duke Cao died. Heir Cao Pi succeeded as Chancellor and King of Wei and changed the era to Yankang.)
「冬，魏嗣王稱尊號，改元爲黃初。」[1] (In winter, the Wei heir took the imperial title and changed the era to Huangchu.)

3. Cao Pi's own annals record the second change at his accession:
「乃爲壇於繁陽。庚午，王升壇即阼，百官陪位。事訖，降壇，視燎成禮而反。改延康爲黃初，大赦。」[6] (He built an altar at Fanyang. On the gengwu day the King ascended the altar and took the throne, with the hundred officials in attendance. When the ceremony was done, he descended the altar, watched the burnt offering, and returned after the rite was complete. He changed Yankang to Huangchu and proclaimed a general amnesty.)

4. The Shu record also notes the same change from the outside:
「二十五年，魏文帝稱尊號，改年曰黃初。」[5] (In the 25th year, Emperor Wen of Wei took the imperial title and changed the era to Huangchu.)

5. The event itself is recorded as a received abdication:
裴注引《魏書》: 「文帝受禪，歆登壇相儀，奉皇帝璽綬，以成受命之禮。」[3] (Pei's commentary quoting the *Weishu*: When Emperor Wen received the abdication, Hua Xin ascended the altar to supervise the ceremony and presented the emperor's seal and ribbons, thus completing the rite of receiving the mandate.)

6. The era tool places all three era names in the same year: Jian'an 25 = 220 CE, Yankang 1 = 220 CE, Huangchu 1 = 220 CE.

**Inference (据此推断)**

From facts 1–3: the era name changed once when Cao Pi inherited the position of King of Wei (Jian'an 25 → Yankang), and again when he ascended the imperial throne (Yankang → Huangchu). Since the era tool places Jian'an 25, Yankang 1, and Huangchu 1 all in 220 CE, it follows that two era changes fell within that one calendar year, 220 CE.

- 王平传：「建興六年，屬參軍馬謖先鋒。謖捨水上山，舉措煩擾，平連規諫謖，謖不能用，大敗於街亭。」[2]
- 诸葛亮传亦记此事：「亮使馬謖督諸軍在前，與郃戰于街亭。謖違亮節度，舉動失宜，大為張郃所破。」[4]；后文诏书又称「街亭之役，咎由馬謖」[1]。（该段原文只作「六年春」，白话译文作建兴六年春）

q: What year in the Western calendar is the 'first year of Ganlu' in the Records of the Three Kingdoms?
reply:
**In the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*, "the first year of Ganlu" (甘露元年) is 256 AD if you mean the Wei reign period.**

The reign title "Ganlu" was used by more than one state, so there are two relevant first years:

- **Wei (曹魏): Ganlu 1 = 256 AD.** The *Wei* record of the boy-emperor Gaoguixiang Gong (Cao Mao) opens its Ganlu section with the date 「甘露元年春正月辛丑，青龍見軹縣井中。」[10] (In the first month of the first year of Ganlu, on the xinchou day, a blue dragon appeared in a well in Zhi County.) The reign title itself had been adopted in the preceding year, where the record says 「夏六月丙午，改元為甘露。」[1] (In the sixth month, on the bingwu day, the reign title was changed to Ganlu.)
- **Wu (孙吴): Ganlu 1 = 265 AD.** The *Wu* record of Sun Hao begins its Ganlu section with the date 「甘露元年三月」[2] (the third month of the first year of Ganlu), and the same section ends that year with 「十二月，晉受禪。」[2] (In the twelfth month, Jin received the abdication.)

So the answer depends on which Ganlu you mean: **Wei's first year of Ganlu is 256 AD; Wu's first year of Ganlu is 265 AD.**

The *Records* also cross-dates these calendars, e.g. it says of Sun Xiu's accession, 「是歲，於魏甘露三年也」[3] (that year was the third year of Wei's Ganlu), giving the Wu year by its Wei equivalent.

Inference: since the text supplies Wei's Ganlu year as the equivalent of a Wu year [3], and since the era tool lists a separate Wu Ganlu first year, it follows — 据此推断 — that "Ganlu" in the text can belong to either state's calendar, and which one is meant has to be decided from context rather than from the words "Ganlu" alone.

q: In which year did Sun Quan formally take the imperial title? Which year of which reign era was in use before he did so, and what era name did he adopt afterward? What year is that in the Western calendar?
reply:
**Conclusion:** Sun Quan formally took the imperial title in the summer (4th month) of the first year of Huanglong 黃龍 [1] — the same year that is counted as the 8th year of Huangwu 黃武 [2]. The era in use before he took the throne was therefore **Huangwu 黃武**; the era name he adopted upon ascending the throne was **Huanglong 黃龍** [1][2]. That year is **229 CE** (Huanglong 1 = 229 CE; Huangwu 8 = 229 CE).

**Evidence:**

- The main text of the *Wu Zhu Zhuan* (Biography of Sun Quan) records: 「黃龍元年春，公卿百司皆勸權正尊號。夏四月，夏口、武昌並言黃龍、鳳凰見。丙申，南郊即皇帝位。是日大赦。改年」[1] — "In the spring of the first year of Huanglong, the ministers and all the offices urged Quan to assume the honored title. In the summer, 4th month, Xiakou and Wuchang both reported that a yellow dragon and a phoenix had appeared. On the *bing-shen* day he ascended the imperial throne at the southern suburb. On that day there was a general amnesty. The era was changed." In the same passage he posthumously honored his father, his mother, and his elder brother: 「追尊父破虜將軍堅爲武烈皇帝，母吳氏爲武烈皇后，兄討逆將軍策爲長沙桓王」[1].
- That the preceding era was **Huangwu**, and that the era was changed on account of the auspicious omen, is stated in the biography of Hu Zong: 「黃武八年夏，黃龍見舉口，於是權稱尊號，因瑞改元」[2] — "In the summer of the 8th year of Huangwu, a yellow dragon appeared at Xiakou; thereupon Quan assumed the honored title and, because of the omen, changed the era [name]."
- The accession proclamation, quoted in Pei Songzhi's annotation from the *Wu Lu* (*Wu Lu*), has Sun Quan declaring: 「謹擇元日，登壇燎祭，即皇帝位」[12] (Pei note citing *Wu Lu*).
- Calendar conversion (per the era-conversion tool): Huanglong 1 = 229 CE; Huangwu 8 = 229 CE.

**Inference:** 据此推断, Huangwu 8 and Huanglong 1 denote the same year, 229 CE. The reasoning: [1] dates the accession to the 4th month of Huanglong 1, and [2] dates the same accession (稱尊號, 因瑞改元) to the summer of Huangwu 8; the era tool converts both to 229 CE. Hence the change of era from Huangwu to Huanglong fell within that year, and "the year of Huangwu before the accession" and "the year Huanglong began" are one and the same year.

**On the sources:** The *Wei Lüe*, cited in Pei Songzhi's annotation, presents Sun Quan's ambition as predating the accession: 「權聞魏文帝受禪而劉備稱帝，乃呼問知星者，己分野中星氣何如，遂有僭意」[8] (Pei note citing *Wei Lüe*). The main text [1] and Hu Zong's biography [2], by contrast, date the accession to the urging of the officials and the appearance of the auspicious omen. On the Shu Han side, the *Han Jin Chunqiu* cited in Pei Songzhi's annotation to the *Zhuge Liang Zhuan* records: 「是歲，孫權稱尊號，其群臣以並尊二帝來告」, and that Zhuge Liang argued for keeping the alliance, whereupon 「乃遣衛尉陳震慶權正號」[10] (Pei note citing *Han Jin Chunqiu*) — Commandant of the Guards Chen Zhen was sent to congratulate Sun Quan on his formal title.

- That the preceding era was **Huangwu**, and that the era was changed on account of the auspicious omen, is stated in the biography of Hu Zong: 「黃武八年夏，黃龍見舉口，於是權稱尊號，因瑞改元」[2] — "In the summer of the 8th year of Huangwu, a yellow dragon appeared at Xiakou; thereupon Quan assumed the honored title and, because of the omen, changed the era [name]."
- The accession proclamation, quoted in Pei Songzhi's annotation from the *Wu Lu* (*Wu Lu*), has Sun Quan declaring: 「謹擇元日，登壇燎祭，即皇帝位」[12] (Pei note citing *Wu Lu*).
- Calendar conversion (per the era-conversion tool): Huanglong 1 = 229 CE; Huangwu 8 = 229 CE.

**Inference:** 据此推断, Huangwu 8 and Huanglong 1 denote the same year, 229 CE. The reasoning: [1] dates the accession to the 4th month of Huanglong 1, and [2] dates the same accession (稱尊號, 因瑞改元) to the summer of Huangwu 8; the era tool converts both to 229 CE. On the Shu Han side, the *Han Jin Chunqiu* cited in Pei Songzhi's annotation to the *Zhuge Liang Zhuan* records: 「是歲，孫權稱尊號，其群臣以並尊二帝來告」, and that Zhuge Liang argued for keeping the alliance, whereupon 「乃遣衛尉陳震慶權正號」[10] (Pei note citing *Han Jin Chunqiu*) — Commandant of the Guards Chen Zhen was sent to congratulate Sun Quan on his formal title.

q: In which year did Zhuge Ke build the great dam at Dongxing and crush the Wei army? Is that 'first year of Jianxing' the same thing as the first year of Jianxing in Shu-Han in Zhuge Liang's day?
reply:
## Answer

**Conclusion: Zhuge Ke rebuilt the dam and crushed the Wei army at Dongxing in the first year of Jianxing (建興) of Sun Wu = AD 252. No — this is not the same "first year of Jianxing" as in Zhuge Liang's day: Shu-Han's Jianxing 1 = AD 223.**

### 1. The Dongxing campaign (facts)

The main account is in the *Wu Shu* biography of Zhuge Ke (the who tool identifies 诸葛恪, style name 元遜, also called 陽都侯):

> 「恪以建興元年十月會眾於東興，更作大堤，左右結山俠築兩城，各留千人，使全端、留略守之，引軍而還。」 [1]
> ("In the tenth month of the first year of Jianxing, Zhuge Ke assembled his forces at Dongxing and rebuilt the great dam...")

The Wei reaction and the defeat:

> 「魏以吳軍入其疆土，恥於受侮，命大將胡遵、諸葛誕等率眾七萬，欲攻圍兩塢，圖壞堤遏。恪興軍四萬，晨夜赴救。」 [1]
> 「魏軍驚擾散走，爭渡浮橋，橋壞絕，自投於水，更相蹈藉。樂安太守桓嘉等同時並沒，死者數萬。」 [1]

The annals of Sun Liang give the same year, with the months and days:

> 「冬十月，太傅恪率軍遏巢湖，城東興，使將軍全端守西城，都尉留略守東城。」 [2]
> 「十二月朔丙申，大風雷電，魏使將軍諸葛誕、胡遵等步騎七萬圍東興，將軍王昶攻南郡，毌丘儉向武昌。甲寅，恪以大兵赴敵。戊午，兵及東興，交戰，大破魏軍，殺將軍韓綜、桓嘉等。」 [2]

The Wei annals (the annals of the Qi Wang, 齊王) record the same campaign on the Wei side, dated "四年" (which the translation renders as Jiaping 4) and in the twelfth month:

> 「四年春正月癸卯，以撫軍大將軍司馬景王為大將軍。」 [8]
> 「十二月，吳大將軍諸葛恪拒戰，大破衆軍於東關。不利而還。」 [8]

The era tool gives 嘉平4年 = AD 252, and 建興1年 = AD 252 for 孙吴. So the dam was rebuilt at Dongxing in the **tenth month** and the Wei army was crushed at Dongxing in the **twelfth month** of the first year of Jianxing (Sun Wu) = **AD 252**.

### 2. The two "first years of Jianxing" (facts + inference)

The era tool shows that 建興 is a year name used by several regimes, and its first year falls on different years: 蜀汉 223, 孙吴 252, 西晋 313.

- **Sun Wu's Jianxing 1 = AD 252**, which is the era of the Sun Liang annals in which the Dongxing campaign is recorded [2].
- **Shu-Han's Jianxing 1 = AD 223**, which is the era of Liu Shan (後主 劉禪), under whom Zhuge Liang served as Chancellor. The Later Ruler's annals record events dated "八年秋" with "丞相亮" in the field:

> 「八年秋，魏使司馬懿由西城，張郃由子午，曹真由斜谷，欲攻漢中。丞相亮待之於城固、赤坂，大雨道絕，真等皆還。」 [11]

**据此推断:** the era tool gives Shu-Han Jianxing 1 as 223 and Sun Wu Jianxing 1 as 252, i.e. different years, so the two "first years of Jianxing" cannot be the same year — they merely happen to share the same era name. Consequently Zhuge Ke's Dongxing campaign belongs to the Sun Wu Jianxing era, not to the Shu-Han Jianxing era in which Zhuge Liang was active.

q: How many different people named Li Feng appear in the Records of the Three Kingdoms, and who were they?
reply:
## Answer

**Two different men named Li Feng (李豐) appear in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*** — one a Wei (曹魏) official, one a Shu (蜀漢) man, the son of Li Yan. They are not the same person.

---

### 1. Li Feng of Wei — 字安國 (per 《魏略》), also given as 字宣國

He was the son of 李義 (courtesy name 孝懿), a man of 馮翊; he rose to be 中書令 (Director of the Palace Secretariat) under the Wei.

- 「豐字安國，故衞尉李義子也」[2] — 裴注引《魏略》: his courtesy name was Anguo, son of the former Commandant of the Guards Li Yi.
- 「中書令李豐雖宿爲大將軍司馬景王所親待，然私心在玄」[10] — as 中書令 he was long trusted by Sima Shi, yet privately favored 夏侯玄.
- He joined 夏侯玄 and 張緝 in a plot; 「嘉平六年二月，當拜貴人，豐等欲因御臨軒，諸門有陛兵，誅大將軍，以玄代之，以緝爲驃騎將軍」[10] and was killed: 「大將軍微聞其謀，請豐相見，豐不知而往，即殺之」[10]. (嘉平六年 = 254 CE.)
- Note on the courtesy name: a note to the 裴潛 chapter says 「義子豐，字宣國，見《夏侯玄傳》」[21] — i.e. 字宣國. So the sources disagree (安國 vs. 宣國).
- His father's name is also disputed: 《傅子》 calls him 太僕李恢, and Pei Songzhi notes 「《魏略》曰李丰父名义，与此不同，义盖恢之别名也」[8].

### 2. Li Feng of Shu — son of 李嚴 (Li Yan / Li Ping)

He was the son of 李嚴 (later renamed 李平) of the Shu-Han court.

- 「亮表嚴子豐為江州都督督軍，典嚴後事」[33] — Zhuge Liang memorialized to make Li Yan's son Feng 江州都督督軍, in charge of Li Yan's rear affairs.
- 「是以表平子豐督主江州，隆崇其遇」[12] — he was given command at Jiangzhou with heightened honors.
- 「豐官至硃提太守」[12] — Li Feng's office reached Administrator of Zhuti.
- Zhuge Liang even wrote him a letter: 「吾與君父子戮力以獎漢室」[15] (裴注引《諸葛亮又與平子豐教》).

---

### Inference

These are two distinct persons, not one: one is a Wei 中書令 of 馮翊, son of 李義, executed by Sima Shi in 254; the other is a Shu officer, son of 李嚴 (李平), made 江州都督督軍 and later 硃提太守. They appear in different books of the *Records* (魏書 vs. 蜀書), have different fathers, careers, and fates — so the name 李豐 covers at least these two men. (Note also that the courtesy name of the Wei Li Feng is reported inconsistently as 安國 and 宣國, but that is a discrepancy within the sources about the same man, not a third person.)

- 「中書令李豐雖宿爲大將軍司馬景王所親待，然私心在玄」[10] — as 中書令 he was long trusted by Sima Shi, yet privately favored 夏侯玄.
- He joined 夏侯玄 and 張緝 in a plot; 「嘉平六年二月，當拜貴人，豐等欲因御臨軒……誅大將軍」[10] and was killed: 「大將軍微聞其謀，請豐相見，豐不知而往，即殺之」[10]. (嘉平六年 = 254 CE.)
- Note on the courtesy name: a note to the 裴潛 chapter says 「義子豐，字宣國，見《夏侯玄傳》」[21] — i.e. 字宣國. So the sources disagree (安國 vs. 宣國).
- His father's name is also disputed: 《傅子》 calls him 太僕李恢, and Pei Songzhi notes 「《魏略》曰李丰父名义，与此不同，义盖恢之别名也」[8].

### 2. Li Feng of Shu — son of 李嚴 (Li Yan / Li Ping)

He was the son of 李嚴 (later renamed 李平) of the Shu-Han court.

- 「亮表嚴子豐為江州都督督軍，典嚴後事」[33] — Zhuge Liang memorialized to make Li Yan's son Feng 江州都督督軍, in charge of Li Yan's rear affairs.
- 「是以表平子豐督主江州，隆崇其遇」[12] — he was given command at Jiangzhou with heightened honors.
- 「豐官至硃提太守」[12] — Li Feng's office reached Administrator of Zhuti.
- Zhuge Liang even wrote him a letter: 「吾與君父子戮力以獎漢室」[15] (裴注引《諸葛亮又與平子豐教》).

---

### Inference

These are two distinct persons, not one: one is a Wei 中書令 of 馮翊, son of 李義, executed by Sima Shi in 254; the other is a Shu officer, son of 李嚴 (李平), made 江州都督督軍 and later 硃提太守. They appear in different books of the *Records* (魏書 vs. 蜀書), have different fathers, careers, and fates — so the name 李豐 covers at least these two men. (Note also that the courtesy name of the Wei Li Feng is reported inconsistently as 安國 and 宣國, but that is a discrepancy within the sources about the same man, not a third person.)

## Answer

**《三国志》里出现的「李豐」是两个不同的人**——一个是曹魏的中书令李丰，一个是蜀汉李严（李平）的儿子李丰。二人不是同一个人。

---

### 一、魏国的李丰（字安国／宣国）

他是冯翊人李义的儿子，官至中书令。

- 裴注引《魏略》：「豐字安國，故衞尉李義子也」[2]。
- 他是冯翊人：「又與緝俱馮翊人」[10]（指李丰与张缉同为冯翊人）；裴注亦作「冯翊李丰」[7]。
- 官职为「中書令李豐雖宿爲大將軍司馬景王所親待，然私心在玄」[10]。
- 他与夏侯玄、张缉同谋：「嘉平六年二月，當拜貴人，豐等欲因御臨軒，諸門有陛兵，誅大將軍」[10]。
- 被杀：「大將軍微聞其謀，請豐相見，豐不知而往，即殺之」[10]。原文把这件事记在嘉平六年二月谋诛大将军之后。
- 字的异说：裴注所引作「義子豐，字宣國，見《夏侯玄傳》」[21]；而《魏略》作「豐字安國」[2]。
- 父名的异说：《傅子》作「畿与太仆李恢、东安太守郭智有好。恢子丰交结英俊」[8]，裴松之按语称「《魏略》曰李丰父名义，与此不同，义盖恢之别名也」[8]。
- 李义的字：裴注引《魏略》「李義字孝懿，皆馮翊東縣人也」[22]。

### 二、蜀汉的李丰（李严之子）

他是李严（后改名李平）的儿子。

- 「亮表嚴子豐為江州都督督軍，典嚴後事」[33]。
- 「是以表平子豐督主江州，隆崇其遇」[12]。
- 官职：「豐官至硃提太守」[12]。
- 诸葛亮曾给他写信：裴注引《諸葛亮又與平子豐教》「吾與君父子戮力以獎漢室」[15]。

---

### 推断

据上引事实推断：这两个李丰是两个人，而不是一人。依据是——其一为冯翊人、李义之子，任魏中书令，与夏侯玄、张缉同谋而死于司马师之手[2][10][21]；其二为李严（李平）之子，被诸葛亮表为江州都督督军，官至朱提太守[33][12][15]。两人的父亲、所属国别、任职与结局都不同，且分别见于《魏书》与《蜀书》，因此「李豐」至少指这两个人。至于魏国李丰的字，《魏略》作安国[2]、另一处作宣国[21]，这是同一人记载的歧异，不是第三个人。

q: Is the Zhang Wen under whom Sun Jian served on the western campaign against Liang Province the same person as the Wu statesman Zhang Wen who went as envoy to Shu?
reply:
**No — they are two different men who happen to share the name Zhang Wen.**

**The Zhang Wen of the Liang campaign (a Han official)**

Sun Jian served as a military aide (參軍事) under him when the Han court sent him west:

「邊章、韓遂作亂涼州，中郎將董卓拒討無功。中平三年，遣司空張溫行車騎將軍，西討章等。溫表請堅與參軍事，屯長安。」[46-0003]
*("Bian Zhang and Han Sui rebelled in Liang Province; the General of the Household Gentlemen Dong Zhuo failed to suppress them. In the third year of Zhongping, the court sent the Minister of Works Zhang Wen, acting as General of Chariots and Cavalry, west to attack Bian Zhang and the rest. Zhang Wen memorialized to have Sun Jian join him as a military aide, and they camped at Chang'an.")*

This Zhang Wen was a Han grandee: he was 司空 (Minister of Works) at the time, and later 太尉 (Grand Commandant) and then 衛尉 (Palace Guard Commander). He was killed by Dong Zhuo:

「故太尉張溫時爲衞尉，素不善卓，卓心怨之，因天有變，欲以塞咎，使人言溫與袁術交關，遂笞殺之。」[06-0005]
*("The former Grand Commandant Zhang Wen was then Palace Guard Commander; he had long been on bad terms with Dong Zhuo, who bore him a grudge, and seizing on an astronomical anomaly to shift the blame, he had someone accuse Zhang Wen of colluding with Yuan Shu, and had him beaten to death.")*

Tao Qian also served under this same man in the same campaign: 「後邊章、韓遂爲亂，司空張溫銜命征討；又請謙爲參軍事」[23]. And Pei's note quotes the *Fu Zi* listing him among those who bought the Three Excellencies' posts under Emperor Ling: 「於是太尉段熲、司徒崔烈、太尉樊陵、司空張溫之徒，皆入錢上千萬下五百萬以買三公」[38].

**The Wu envoy Zhang Wen**

「張溫字惠恕，吳郡吳人也。父允，以輕財重士，名顯州郡，為孫權東曹掾。」[15]
*("Zhang Wen, courtesy name Huishu, was a man of Wu county in Wu commandery. His father Zhang Yun, for despising wealth and valuing scholars, was famous throughout the province and commandery, and served Sun Quan as Eastern Bureau Chief.")*

He was sent to Shu as envoy: 「時年三十二，以輔義中郎將使蜀」[13] *(then aged thirty-two, he went to Shu as Bearer of Righteousness General of the Household Gentlemen)*. He was a Wu man who rose under Sun Quan (as Gentleman Consultant, Selection Bureau Director, then Tutor to the Heir Apparent), went to Shu during Zhuge Liang's regency, and was later disgraced over the Ji Yan affair and died of illness six years after his dismissal [20][24].

**Conclusion (inference)**

These are two distinct persons. The Liang-campaign Zhang Wen was a Han-dynasty Three Excellencies official who was beaten to death by Dong Zhuo in the Chang'an period [06-0005], whereas the envoy Zhang Wen was a Wu man of Wu commandery who served Sun Quan, was aged thirty-two when he went to Shu [13], and lived on into the Wu state's middle years. Since the Han Zhang Wen was already dead by the time of Dong Zhuo's ascendancy, he cannot be the man who later served as Sun Quan's envoy to Shu. The *Sanguozhi* indeed contains three different men named Zhang Wen (the Wu envoy Zhang Huishu; the Han Minister of Works/Grand Commandant killed by Dong Zhuo; and a Han Grand Commandant who had been Commandant of the Guards). The Zhang Wen of the western campaign against Liang Province is therefore **not** the Wu statesman Zhang Wen who went to Shu.

q: Is the Liu Tai of the Records of the Three Kingdoms a single person? Is the Liu Tai who was Inspector of Yen Province during the campaign against Tung Cho the same man as the Liu Tai whom Ts'ao Ts'ao later sent to attack Liu Pei?
reply:
**Conclusion: No — they are not the same man.** The *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (including Pei Songzhi's notes) contains references to **two different men named Liu Tai (劉岱)**, and — confusingly — both are styled **Gongshan (公山)**. The Liu Tai who was Inspector of Yan Province (兗州刺史) in the coalition against Dong Zhuo is **not** the Liu Tai whom Cao Cao later sent against Liu Bei. Here is the evidence.

## 1. The Inspector of Yan Province (the coalition leader)

- In the *Book of Wu*, Liu Yao's biography: 「劉繇，字正禮，東萊牟平人也。」 and 「繇兄岱，字公山，歷位侍中，兗州刺史。」[3] — Liu Tai, styled Gongshan, was the elder brother of Liu Yao and came from **Mouping in Donglai**; he served as Palace Attendant and Inspector of Yan Province.
- Pei's note quoting the *Xu Han Shu* and *Yingxiong Ji*: 「繇父輿，一名方，山陽太守。岱、繇皆有隽才。」 and 「《英雄記》稱岱孝悌仁恕，以虛己受人。」[22]
- Pei Songzhi's own note at the coalition passage: 「岱，劉繇之兄，事見《吳志》。」[30]
- In the *Annals of Emperor Wu*, for Chuping 1 (190): 「初平元年春正月，後將軍袁術、冀州牧韓馥、豫州刺史孔伷、兗州刺史劉岱、河內太守王匡、勃海太守袁紹、陳留太守張邈、東郡太守橋瑁、山陽太守袁遺、濟北相鮑信同時俱起兵，衆各數萬，推紹爲盟主。」[6]
- 「劉岱與橋瑁相惡，岱殺瑁，以王肱領東郡太守。」[13]
- He was killed by the Qingzhou Yellow Turbans: 「青州黃巾衆百萬入兗州，殺任城相鄭遂，轉入東平。劉岱欲擊之」[7], and 「岱不從，遂與戰，果爲所殺。」[7]; Cheng Yu's biography states plainly 「劉岱為黃巾所殺。」[29]

## 2. The Liu Tai sent against Liu Bei

- In the *Annals of Emperor Wu*: 「備之未東也，陰與董承等謀反，至下邳，遂殺徐州刺史車冑，舉兵屯沛。遣劉岱、王忠擊之，不克。」[16]; the same in Liu Bei's biography: 「曹公遣劉岱、王忠擊之，不克。」[12]
- Pei's note quoting the *Wei Wu Gushi*: 「岱字公山，沛國人。以司空長史從征伐有功，封列侯。」[11] — this Liu Tai is from **Pei**, and served as **Director of the Minister of Works (司空長史)**, enfeoffed as a Marquis.
- Pei's note quoting the *Xiandi Chunqiu*: 「備謂岱等曰：『使汝百人來，其無如我何；曹公自來，未可知耳！』」[11]

## Inference (from the facts above)

- Fact 1: The Inspector of Yan Province Liu Tai was **killed by the Yellow Turbans in Chuping 3 (192)** [7][29].
- Fact 2: The Liu Tai sent against Liu Bei was **still active years later**, in the events the text places just before Jian'an 5 (200) [12][16].
- Fact 3: The sources give them **different native places** (Donglai Mouping [3] vs. Pei [11]) and **different offices** (Palace Attendant / Inspector of Yan Province [3] vs. Director of the Minister of Works / Marquis [11]).

A man killed in 192 cannot be campaigning in 199–200. **Therefore the two must be different individuals.** It is worth noting that Pei Songzhi recorded both origins side by side without reconciling them: at the coalition passage he identifies this Liu Tai as Liu Yao's brother [30], while at the campaign against Liu Bei he quotes a source making him a man of Pei [11]. So the *Records* preserves two Liu Tai, both styled Gongshan — apparently a genuine coincidence of name and style.

**Conclusion: No — they are not the same man.** The *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (including Pei Songzhi's notes) contains references to **two different men named Liu Tai (劉岱)**, and — confusingly — both are styled **Gongshan (公山)**. The Liu Tai who was Inspector of Yan Province (兗州刺史) in the coalition against Dong Zhuo is **not** the Liu Tai whom Cao Cao later sent against Liu Bei. Here is the evidence.

## 1. The Inspector of Yan Province (the coalition leader)

- In the *Book of Wu*, Liu Yao's biography opens: 「劉繇，字正禮，東萊牟平人也……繇兄岱，字公山，歷位侍中，兗州刺史。」[3] — Liu Tai, styled Gongshan, was the elder brother of Liu Yao and came from **Mouping in Donglai**; he served as Palace Attendant and Inspector of Yan Province.
- Pei's note quoting the *Xu Han Shu* and *Yingxiong Ji*: 「繇父輿，一名方，山陽太守。岱、繇皆有隽才。」 and 「《英雄記》稱岱孝悌仁恕，以虛己受人。」[22]
- Pei Songzhi's own note at the coalition passage: 「岱，劉繇之兄，事見《吳志》。」[30]
- In the *Annals of Emperor Wu*, for Chuping 1 (190): 「初平元年春正月……兗州刺史劉岱……同時俱起兵，衆各數萬，推紹爲盟主。」[6]
- 「劉岱與橋瑁相惡，岱殺瑁，以王肱領東郡太守。」[13]
- He was killed by the Qingzhou Yellow Turbans: 「青州黃巾衆百萬入兗州……劉岱欲擊之……岱不從，遂與戰，果爲所殺。」[7]; Cheng Yu's biography states plainly 「劉岱為黃巾所殺。」[29]

## 2. The Liu Tai sent against Liu Bei

- In the *Annals of Emperor Wu*: 「備之未東也，陰與董承等謀反，至下邳，遂殺徐州刺史車冑，舉兵屯沛。遣劉岱、王忠擊之，不克。」[16]; the same in Liu Bei's biography: 「曹公遣劉岱、王忠擊之，不克。」[12]
- Pei's note quoting the *Wei Wu Gushi*: 「岱字公山，沛國人。以司空長史從征伐有功，封列侯。」[11] — this Liu Tai is from **Pei**, and served as **Director of the Minister of Works (司空長史)**, enfeoffed as a Marquis.
- Pei's note quoting the *Xiandi Chunqiu*: 「備謂岱等曰：『使汝百人來，其無如我何；曹公自來，未可知耳！』」[11]

## Inference (from the facts above)

- Fact 1: The Inspector of Yan Province Liu Tai was **killed by the Yellow Turbans in Chuping 3 (192)** [7][29].
- Fact 2: The Liu Tai sent against Liu Bei was **still active years later**, in the events the text places just before Jian'an 5 (200) [12][16].
- Fact 3: The sources give them **different native places** (Donglai Mouping [3] vs. Pei [11]) and **different offices** (Palace Attendant / Inspector of Yan Province [3] vs. Director of the Minister of Works / Marquis [11]).

A man killed in 192 cannot be campaigning in 199–200. **Therefore the two must be different individuals.** It is worth noting that Pei Songzhi recorded both origins side by side without reconciling them: at the coalition passage he identifies this Liu Tai as Liu Yao's brother [30], while at the campaign against Liu Bei he quotes a source making him a man of Pei [11]. So the *Records* preserves two Liu Tai, both styled Gongshan — apparently a genuine coincidence of name and style.

q: Is the general Zhang Xiu whom Zhuge Liang dealt with together with Ma Su when he executed Ma Su the same person as the Zhang Xiu in the entourage of Wu's crown prince Sun Deng?
reply:
**结论：不是同一个人。**《三国志》里有两个名叫张休的人，是不同的人物，只是同名而已。

**依据：**

**一、被诸葛亮与马谡一同诛杀的张休——蜀汉的将军**

《蜀书·王平传》记街亭之败后：「丞相亮既誅馬謖及將軍張休、李盛，奪將軍黃襲等兵。」[2] 可见此人是蜀汉的一位将军，与李盛一同在马谡被诛时被杀。他只在《王平传》中出现，没有自己的传。

**二、孙登东宫僚友的张休——吴张昭之子，字叔嗣**

《吴书·张昭传》附有其子张休的传：「休字叔嗣，弱冠與諸葛恪、顧譚等俱爲太子登僚友，以《漢書》授登。」[13]

《吴书·孙登传》记孙登为太子时「選置師傅，銓簡秀士，以爲賔友，於是諸葛恪、張休、顧譚、陳表等以選入」[16]；黄龙元年孙权称尊号、孙登为皇太子，「以恪爲左輔，休右弼，譚爲輔正，表爲翼正都尉，是爲四友」[16]。裴注引《吴书》还说他「休为人解达，登甚爱之，常在左右」[14]。

此张休后来「爲魯王霸友黨所譖，與顧譚、承俱以芍陂論功事，休、承與典軍陳恂通情，詐增其伐，並徙交州」[13]；中书令孙弘「因是譖訴」，终于「下詔書賜休死，時年四十一」[13]。

**据此推断：** 一人是蜀汉的将军，在街亭战败之后被诸葛亮诛杀，隶属蜀汉；一人是吴张昭之子，字叔嗣，在东吴太子孙登身边任僚友，最后被下诏赐死。两人分属蜀、吴两国，出身、经历、结局都不同，因此不可能是同一个人。

q: How many versions do the historical sources give of Cao Cao's killing of Lü Boshe's family? Which book gives which version?
reply:
**Conclusion:** Pei Songzhi's commentary preserves **three** distinct versions of the killing of Lü Boshe's household, each from a different source. Chen Shou's main text of the *Sanguozhi* does not record the incident: it says only that Cao Cao 「乃變易姓名，間行東歸」[19], and that he 「過中牟，爲亭長所疑，執詣縣」[19].

The three versions are all quoted in a single Pei note under the *Wudi ji* [1]:

**1. 《魏書》 — the household attacked first (self-defense):**
「《魏書》曰：太祖以卓終必覆敗，遂不就拜，逃歸鄉里。從數騎過故人成臯呂伯奢；伯奢不在，其子與賔客共劫太祖，取馬及物，太祖手刃擊殺數人。」[1]
(Lü Boshe was away; his son and his guests robbed Cao Cao of his horse and goods, and Cao Cao cut down several of them with his own hand.)

**2. 《世語》 — Cao Cao killed eight out of suspicion:**
「《世語》曰：太祖過伯奢。伯奢出行，五子皆在，備賔主禮。太祖自以背卓命，疑其圖己，手劔夜殺八人而去。」[1]
(Lü Boshe had gone out; his five sons were at home and received Cao Cao with the rites of host and guest; Cao Cao, because he had disobeyed Dong Zhuo's order, suspected them of plotting against him and killed eight people by sword at night, then left.)
That 《世語》 is Guo Ban's work is stated by Pei Songzhi elsewhere: 「惟頒撰魏晉《世語》」[42].

**3. 孫盛《雜記》 — Cao Cao mistook the sound of food vessels for a plot:**
「孫盛雜記曰：太祖聞其食器聲，以爲圖己，遂夜殺之。」[1]
(Cao Cao heard the sound of their food vessels, took it as a plot against himself, and killed them at night.) This version also carries the words spoken afterward: 「寧我負人，毋人負我！」[1].

**Points of difference:**
- **Motive:** Only the 《魏書》 version has the household robbing Cao Cao, so that his killing answers an attack; the 《世語》 and 《雜記》 versions have Cao Cao killing out of suspicion of a plot.
- **Number killed:** the 《魏書》 says "several" (「太祖手刃擊殺數人」[1]); the 《世語》 specifies eight (「手劔夜殺八人而去」[1]); the 《雜記》 gives no number.
- **Lü Boshe himself:** in the 《魏書》 version he is absent (「伯奢不在」[1]); in the 《世語》 version he has gone out (「伯奢出行」[1]); the 《雜記》 version says nothing about where he was. In none of the three versions is Lü Boshe himself said to be killed.

Pei's note simply lists the three side by side without judging between them, so the *Sanguozhi* itself does not settle which account is correct.

The main text merely records that Cao Cao, having been offered office by Dong Zhuo, 「乃變易姓名，間行東歸」 and was seized at Zhongmu — no mention of Lü Boshe [19]. Pei Songzhi's note supplies all three versions without choosing among them, so the *Sanguozhi* itself does not settle which account is correct.

**Conclusion:** Pei Songzhi's commentary preserves **three** distinct versions of the killing of Lü Boshe's household, each from a different source. Chen Shou's main text of the *Sanguozhi* does not record the incident: it says only that Cao Cao 「乃變易姓名，間行東歸」[19], and that he 「過中牟，爲亭長所疑，執詣縣」[19].

The three versions are all quoted in a single Pei note under the *Wudi ji* [1]:

**1. 《魏書》 — the household attacked first (self-defense):**
「《魏書》曰：太祖以卓終必覆敗，遂不就拜，逃歸鄉里。從數騎過故人成臯呂伯奢；伯奢不在，其子與賔客共劫太祖，取馬及物，太祖手刃擊殺數人。」[1]
(Lü Boshe was away; his son and his guests robbed Cao Cao of his horse and goods, and Cao Cao cut down several of them with his own hand.)

**2. 《世語》 — Cao Cao killed eight out of suspicion:**
「《世語》曰：太祖過伯奢。伯奢出行，五子皆在，備賔主禮。太祖自以背卓命，疑其圖己，手劔夜殺八人而去。」[1]
(Lü Boshe had gone out; his five sons were at home and received Cao Cao with the rites of host and guest; Cao Cao, because he had disobeyed Dong Zhuo's order, suspected them of plotting against him and killed eight people by sword at night, then left.)
That 《世語》 is Guo Ban's work is stated by Pei Songzhi elsewhere: 「惟頒撰魏晉《世語》」[42].

**3. 孫盛《雜記》 — Cao Cao mistook the sound of food vessels for a plot:**
「孫盛雜記曰：太祖聞其食器聲，以爲圖己，遂夜殺之。」[1]
(Cao Cao heard the sound of their food vessels, took it as a plot against himself, and killed them at night.) This version also carries the words spoken afterward: 「寧我負人，毋人負我！」[1].

**Points of difference:**
- **Motive:** Only the 《魏書》 version has the household robbing Cao Cao, so that his killing answers an attack; the 《世語》 and 《雜記》 versions have Cao Cao killing out of suspicion of a plot.
- **Number killed:** the 《魏書》 says "several" (「太祖手刃擊殺數人」[1]); the 《世語》 specifies eight (「手劔夜殺八人而去」[1]); the 《雜記》 gives no number.
- **Lü Boshe himself:** in the 《魏書》 version he is absent (「伯奢不在」[1]); in the 《世語》 version he has gone out (「伯奢出行」[1]); the 《雜記》 version says nothing about where he was. In none of the three versions is Lü Boshe himself said to be killed.

Pei's note simply lists the three side by side without judging between them, so the *Sanguozhi* itself does not settle which account is correct.

q: Did Liu Bei make three visits to the thatched cottage to recruit Zhuge Liang, or did Zhuge Liang go to see Liu Bei first? Do the historical sources agree?
reply:
## Conclusion

The *Sanguozhi*'s main text (正文) says **Liu Bei went to Zhuge Liang three times**. Pei Songzhi, however, preserves a rival account — from the *Weilüe*, with which the *Jiuzhou Chunqiu* agrees — that **Zhuge Liang went north to see Liu Bei first**. So the sources do **not** fully agree; Pei Songzhi himself rejects the rival account and rules for the three visits.

## Evidence

**1. The main text: three visits.** After Xu Shu recommends Zhuge Liang to Liu Bei:

「此人可就見，不可屈致也。將軍宜枉駕顧之。」由是先主遂詣亮，凡三往，乃見。[1]

("This man can be visited, but cannot be summoned to come. You, General, should condescend to go to him." So the Former Lord went to Zhuge Liang; in all he went three times, and only then met him.)

And in the appraisal section: 「時左將軍劉備以亮有殊量，乃三顧亮於草廬之中」[3] ("At that time General of the Left Liu Bei, considering Zhuge Liang to have exceptional capacity, went three times to Zhuge Liang in the thatched cottage.")

**2. The rival account preserved by Pei.** Pei quotes the *Weilüe*: 「亮乃北行見備，備與亮非舊，又以其年少，以諸生意待之。」[5] ("Zhuge Liang then went north to see Liu Bei; Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang were not old acquaintances, and because he was young, Liu Bei treated him as an ordinary scholar.") Pei adds: 「九州春秋所言亦如之」[5] ("What the *Jiuzhou Chunqiu* says is also the same.")

**3. Pei Songzhi's verdict.** Pei cites Zhuge Liang's own memorial: 「先帝不以臣卑鄙，猥自枉屈，三顧臣於草廬之中，諮臣以當世之事」[2], and concludes 「則非亮先詣備，明矣」[2] ("then it was clearly not Zhuge Liang who went to Liu Bei first"). He then remarks: 「雖聞見異辭，各生彼此，然乖背至是，亦良為可怪。」[2]

**4. Dating.** Pei reckons: 「劉備以建安十三年敗，遣亮使吳」[4], and 「然則備始與亮相遇，在敗軍之前一年時也」[4]. Jian'an 13 = 208 CE (per the era tool), so Pei places their first meeting one year before that defeat.

## Note on the disagreement

据此推断: The two accounts cannot both be right about who sought out whom. The main text has Liu Bei going three times to Zhuge Liang [1][3]; the *Weilüe*/*Jiuzhou Chunqiu* account has Zhuge Liang going north to Liu Bei [5]; Pei Songzhi, citing Zhuge Liang's own memorial, argues the latter is wrong [2]. From these facts it follows that the sources are in direct conflict on this point, and that Pei came down on the side of the main text — but the rival version is still preserved, so the sources are not unanimous.

This is Pei's reckoning, given in the text.

## Note on the disagreement

The two versions are **not compatible** as to who sought out whom, and the sources themselves flag this: the *Weilüe*/*Jiuzhou Chunqiu* version has Zhuge Liang taking the initiative, while Chen Shou's text and Zhuge Liang's own memorial (quoted by Pei) have Liu Bei making the repeated visits. Pei Songzhi rules for the latter. Per the instructions, I set out both versions rather than deciding the matter.

q: Is the Zhang Nan who led Liu Bei's vanguard at the Battle of Yiling the same man as the Zhang Nan who surrendered to Cao Cao?
reply:
**Conclusion (inference):** No — on the evidence in the sources these are two different men. The Yiling Zhang Nan was a man from Jingzhou who followed Liu Bei into Shu and was killed at Xiaoting; the Zhang Nan who went over to Cao Cao was a senior general of Yuan Xi in the north who turned on the Yuan brothers and surrendered his county. The reasoning is set out in §3.

**1. Zhang Nan, Liu Bei's vanguard at Yiling**

Order of battle (Lu Xun's biography):
- 「使將軍馮習為大督，張南為前部，輔匡，趙融、廖淳、傅肜等各為別督」[2] ("he made the general Feng Xi Grand Commander, Zhang Nan commander of the vanguard, and Fu Kuang, Zhao Rong, Liao Chun, Fu Rong and the others each separate commanders.")

Origin (Yang Xi's "Ji Han Fuchen Zan," Shu Shu):
- 「文進名南，亦自荊州隨先主入蜀，領兵從先主徵吳，與習俱死。」[43] ("Wenjin, named Nan, likewise followed the First Lord from Jingzhou into Shu; he led troops with the First Lord in the campaign against Wu and died together with Feng Xi.")

Death:
- 「斬張南、馮習及胡王沙靡柯等首」[4] ("they cut off the heads of Zhang Nan, Feng Xi and the Hu king Shamike and others.")
- 「將軍馮習、張南等皆沒」[5] ("the generals Feng Xi, Zhang Nan and others all perished.")

**2. Zhang Nan, who went over to Cao Cao**

- Annals of Emperor Wu: 「是月，袁熙大將焦觸、張南等叛攻熙、尚，熙、尚奔三郡烏丸。觸等舉其縣降，封爲列侯。」[14] ("In that month Yuan Xi's senior general Jiao Chu, Zhang Nan and others revolted and attacked Xi and Shang; Xi and Shang fled to the Wuhuan of the three commanderies. Jiao Chu and the others surrendered their counties and were enfeoffed as marquises.")
- Biography of Yuan Shao's sons: 「熙、尚爲其將焦觸、張南所攻，奔遼西烏丸。」[18] ("Xi and Shang were attacked by their general Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan, and fled to the Wuhuan of Liaoxi.")

**Dates:** the defection is recorded under 「十年春正月」[14] — 建安十年 = 公元205年; the Yiling campaign under 「二年春正月」[5] — 章武二年 = 公元222年 (both years via the era conversion).

**3. 据此推断 (inference)**

The facts laid out above are: (a) the Yiling Zhang Nan came from Jingzhou and followed Liu Bei into Shu, dying with Feng Xi [43][4][5]; (b) the Zhang Nan who surrendered was a senior general of Yuan Xi who attacked Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang, then handed over his county and was enfeoffed as a marquis [14][18]. From (a) and (b) it follows that the two notices describe men in different camps — one a subordinate of the Yuan family in the north who went over to Cao Cao, the other a Jingzhou follower of Liu Bei — and the Yiling man is explicitly said to have died at Xiaoting [4][5]. Therefore, 据此推断, they are not the same man; the sources I searched contain no passage linking the two "Zhang Nan" notices or identifying them as one person.
draft:
**Conclusion: No — they are two different men.** The sources give no link between them; one was a general from Jingzhou who followed Liu Bei, the other a general under Yuan Xi in the north who defected to Cao Cao about seventeen years earlier.

**The Zhang Nan at Yiling (Liu Bei's vanguard)**

The *Wu Shu* biography of Lu Xun records the order of battle for Liu Bei's invasion:

- 「使將軍馮習為大督，張南為前部，輔匡、趙融、廖淳、傅肜等各為別督」[2] — Liu Bei made Feng Xi Grand Commander and Zhang Nan commander of the vanguard (前部).

His origin is given in the *Shu Shu* "Ji Han Fuchen Zan" of Yang Xi's biography:

- 「文進名南，亦自荊州隨先主入蜀，領兵從先主徵吳，與習俱死。」[43] — Zhang Nan, courtesy name Wenjin (文進), *also* followed the First Lord from Jingzhou into Shu, and led troops with him in the campaign against Wu, dying together with Feng Xi.

His death is recorded in the Lu Xun biography and the First Lord's biography:

- 「斬張南、馮習及胡王沙靡柯等首」[4]
- 「將軍馮習、張南等皆沒」[5]

**The Zhang Nan who surrendered to Cao Cao**

The *Wei Shu* annals of Emperor Wu record, under the first month of the tenth year of Jian'an:

- 「是月，袁熙大將焦觸、張南等叛攻熙、尚，熙、尚奔三郡烏丸。觸等舉其縣降，封爲列侯。」[14] — Yuan Xi's senior general Zhang Nan, with Jiao Chu and others, revolted and attacked Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang, who fled to the Wuhuan of the three commanderies; Jiao Chu and the rest surrendered their counties and were enfeoffed as marquises.

The same event is given in the biography of Yuan Shao's sons:

- 「熙、尚爲其將焦觸、張南所攻，奔遼西烏丸。觸自號幽州刺史……」[18]

This is the tenth year of Jian'an, i.e. **205 CE** [era: 建安10年 = 公元205年]. The Yiling campaign is the second year of Zhangwu, i.e. **222 CE** [era: 章武2年 = 公元222年].

**Why they are not the same man**

Drawing only on the passages above:

1. The defecting Zhang Nan was a subordinate of **Yuan Xi** in the north (Jian'an 10, 205), who turned against the Yuan brothers and handed his county over to Cao Cao; the Yiling Zhang Nan was a man who came **from Jingzhou** and followed Liu Bei into Shu ([43]).
2. The defecting Zhang Nan survived his defection and was enfeoffed as a marquis in 205 [14]; the Yiling Zhang Nan was killed at Xiaoting in 222 [4][5].
3. Accordingly, the two notices belong to different armies, different theaters and different decades.

So the *Sanguozhi* treats them as separate individuals; there is no passage identifying the Jingzhou follower of Liu Bei with Yuan Xi's general. (Note: the Yiling commander is given a courtesy name, 文進/Wenjin, in the *Shu Shu* [43], whereas the Wei-side notices give the northern Zhang Nan no courtesy name.)

**Background note (not from the *Sanguozhi*):** The *Sanguozhi* (with Pei Songzhi's commentary) contains no passage that connects the two men or calls them one person, so there is nothing to correct; the question's premise of a possible single "Zhang Nan" simply is not supported by the text.

- 「斬張南、馮習及胡王沙靡柯等首」[4] ("they cut off the heads of Zhang Nan, Feng Xi and the Hu king Shamike and others.")
- 「將軍馮習、張南等皆沒」[5] ("the generals Feng Xi, Zhang Nan and others all perished.")

**2. Zhang Nan, who went over to Cao Cao**

- Annals of Emperor Wu: 「是月，袁熙大將焦觸、張南等叛攻熙、尚，熙、尚奔三郡烏丸。觸等舉其縣降，封爲列侯。」[14] ("In that month Yuan Xi's senior general Jiao Chu, Zhang Nan and others revolted and attacked Xi and Shang; Xi and Shang fled to the Wuhuan of the three commanderies. Jiao Chu and the others surrendered their counties and were enfeoffed as marquises.")
- Biography of Yuan Shao's sons: 「熙、尚爲其將焦觸、張南所攻，奔遼西烏丸。」[18] ("Xi and Shang were attacked by their general Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan, and fled to the Wuhuan of Liaoxi.")

**Dates:** the defection is recorded under 「十年春正月」[14] — 建安十年 = 公元205年; the Yiling campaign under 「二年春正月」[5] — 章武二年 = 公元222年 (both years via the era conversion).

**3. 据此推断 (inference)**

The facts laid out above are: (a) the Yiling Zhang Nan came from Jingzhou and followed Liu Bei into Shu, dying with Feng Xi [43][4][5]; (b) the Zhang Nan who surrendered was a senior general of Yuan Xi who attacked Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang, then handed over his county and was enfeoffed as a marquis [14][18]. From (a) and (b) it follows that the two notices describe men in different camps — one a subordinate of the Yuan family in the north who went over to Cao Cao, the other a Jingzhou follower of Liu Bei — and the Yiling man is explicitly said to have died at Xiaoting [4][5]. Therefore, 据此推断, they are not the same man; the sources I searched contain no passage linking the two "Zhang Nan" notices or identifying them as one person.

reply:
## 结论

《三国志》正文 (陈寿) 记载孙坚死于 **初平三年 (公元 192 年)**，是在围攻襄阳时、单骑上岘山，被黄祖的军士射杀。但裴松之注中引的其他史书**并不一致**: 《英雄记》作 **初平四年 (公元 193 年) 正月七日**，而且死法也有不同说法 (被暗箭射死 / 被落石砸头而死)。所以各家说法在**年份和死亡方式上都有分歧**。

## 依据

**1. 陈寿正文 (《吴书·孙破虏讨逆传》): 初平三年，被黄祖军士射杀**

「初平三年，術使堅征荊州，擊劉表。表遣黃祖逆於樊鄧之間。堅擊破之，追渡漢水，遂圍襄陽，單馬行峴山，爲祖軍士所射殺。」[1]

即袁术派孙坚攻打刘表，刘表派黄祖迎击；孙坚击败黄祖，追过汉水，包围襄阳，单骑走到岘山，被黄祖的军士射杀。初平三年 = 公元 192 年。

**2. 《魏书》刘表一段只说 "中流矢死"**

「袁術之在南陽也，與孫堅合從，欲襲奪表州，使堅攻表。堅爲流矢所中死，軍敗，術遂不能勝表。」[15]

这里只说孙坚被流箭射中而死，未记具体年份和地点。

**3. 裴注并列的几种不同说法**

裴注在这一段正文后引了三部书，本身就不一致：

- 裴注引《典略》:「堅悉其衆攻表，表閉門，夜遣將黃祖潛出發兵。祖將兵欲還，堅逆與戰。祖敗走，竄峴山中。堅乘勝夜追祖，祖部兵從竹木間暗射堅，殺之。」[4] (黄祖部下从竹木间暗中射杀孙坚)
- 裴注引《吴录》:「堅時年三十七。」[4] (孙坚时年三十七岁)
- 裴注引《英雄记》:「堅以初平四年正月七日死。」[4] (死于初平四年正月七日) 又云：「劉表將呂公將兵緣山向堅，堅輕騎尋山討公。公兵下石。中堅頭，應時腦出物故。」[4] (刘表部将吕公的兵扔石头击中孙坚头部，当场脑浆迸出而死)

这一段裴注把这几说并列在一起，没有替读者裁定哪一说为定论。

## 分歧归纳 (据以上资料)

- **年份**: 陈寿正文作初平三年 (192)；《英雄记》作初平四年 (193)。两说不一致。
- **死亡方式**: 陈寿正文、《典略》都说是被黄祖部下射杀 (《典略》强调是夜间追击时从竹木间暗射)；《英雄记》另记一说，是被吕公部下扔石砸头而死。
- **年龄**: 仅《吴录》给出 "年三十七"。

q: What is the relationship between the silent hermit Sun Deng whom Ji Kang met in the mountains and Sun Deng, Sun Quan's crown prince?
reply:
**结论：这是两个同名而不同的人，一个是孙权的长子、皇太子孙登（字子高），另一个是嵇康在汲郡山中遇到的隐者孙登（字公和）。《三国志》及裴注里没有记载二人之间有任何亲缘、交往或关联。**

我按人物全名分别检索、并读了相关传记的上下文和裴注，依据如下。

**一、孙权之子、太子孙登（字子高）**

- 传首即标其身份：「孫登字子高，權長子也。」[4]
- 立太子、置师傅宾客，诸葛恪、张休、顾谭、陈表等为"四友"；黄龙元年孙权称帝号，登为皇太子 [4]。
- 徐夫人以母养之恩抚养他：「使母養子登」[16]。
- 卒年与谥号：「立凡二十一年，年三十三卒。」[11]「謚登曰宣太子。」[9]
- 子嗣：「子璠、希，皆早卒，次子英，封吳侯。」[9]

**二、隐者孙登（字公和）**

- 裴注引《嵇康集目錄》：「登字公和，不知何許人，無家屬，於汲縣北山土窟中得之。夏則編草爲裳，冬則被髮自覆。好讀易鼓琴，見者皆親樂之。」[21-0011n0]
- 嵇康与他相遇、他默然不应：「初，康採藥於汲郡共北山中，見隱者孫登。康欲與之言，登默然不對。踰時將去，康曰：『先生竟無言乎？』登乃曰：『子才多識寡，難乎免於今之世。』」[12]
- 裴注又引《晉陽秋》：「康見孫登，登對之長嘯，踰時不言。康辭還，曰：『先生竟無言乎？』登曰：『惜哉！』」[21-0011n0]（此即问题所说"沉默的隐士"）
- 嵇康后来作诗自责，有「昔慙柳下。今愧孫登」之句 [21-0011n0]。

**三、为什么可以断定是两个人（推断）**

依据以上事实：其一，两人的字不同——太子字子高 [4]，隐者字公和 [21-0011n0]；其二，身份来历不同——太子明记为"權長子" [4]，隐者则"不知何許人，無家屬" [21-0011n0]；其三，两人分属书中完全不相干的两处——太子在《吴书·吴主五子传》，隐者出现在《魏书·王卫二刘傅传》所附嵇康的裴注里，且隐者活动地（汲郡共县北山）与太子的活动地（武昌、建业一带）无交集。据此推断：二人只是同名，并非一人，也非亲族，书里没有任何把他们联系起来的记载。

另需说明，资料中"孙登"之名还出现过第三处，与上述两人都无关：裴注引《魏書》载公孙度对柳毅、阳仪说「讖書云孫登當為天子，太守姓公孫，字升濟，升即登也。」[6]——这是谶书里的一个名字，公孙度用来附会自己，并不是一个具体的人。

以下不是《三国志》的记载:

把这位隐者与孙权的太子当作一人或认为两者有关系的说法，《三国志》及裴注里没有这样的记载，可能出自后世杂传或《三国演义》一类的非正史说法；在陈寿与裴松之的记载里，二人只有同名这一点相同。

- 裴注引《嵇康集目錄》：「登字公和，不知何許人，無家屬，於汲縣北山土窟中得之。夏則編草爲裳，冬則被髮自覆。好讀易鼓琴，見者皆親樂之。」[21-0011n0]

- 嵇康后来作诗自责，有「昔慙柳下。今愧孫登」之句 [21-0011n0]。

**三、为什么可以断定是两个人（推断）**

依据以上事实：其一，两人的字不同——太子字子高 [59-0000]，隐者字公和 [21-0011n0]；其二，身份来历不同——太子明记为"權長子" [59-0000]，隐者则"不知何許人，無家屬" [21-0011n0]；其三，两人分属书中完全不相干的两处——太子在《吴书·吴主五子传》，隐者出现在《魏书·王卫二刘傅传》所附嵇康的裴注里，且隐者活动地（汲郡共县北山）与太子的活动地（武昌、建业一带）无交集。据此推断：二人只是同名，并非一人，也非亲族，书里没有任何把他们联系起来的记载。

q: Is the story of Liu Bei's horse Dilu leaping across Tan Creek to save his life recorded in the Records of the Three Kingdoms? Is it credible?
reply:
## Conclusion

The Dilu (的盧) leaping-across-Tan-Creek story is **not found in the 《三国志》 main text**. It appears in Pei Songzhi's annotation, quoting the 《世語》[1], and the very same annotation records the historian Sun Sheng's explicit rejection of it [1]. So within the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* the episode is present, but as a disputed report carried in the commentary, not as accepted history. On credibility: it should be treated as doubtful, because the source itself contains a reasoned rebuttal.

## What the sources actually say

The main text of the *Xianzhu Zhuan* (Biography of Liu Bei) says only that after Cao Cao defeated Yuan Shao and turned south, Liu Bei made contact with Liu Biao, who welcomed him, added to his troops, and stationed him at Xinye; and that as more Jingzhou strongmen attached themselves to him, Liu Biao grew suspicious and secretly guarded against him:

> 「曹公既破紹，自南擊先主。先主遣麋竺、孫乾與劉表相聞，表自郊迎，以上賓禮待之，益其兵，使屯新野。」[21]
> 「荊州豪傑歸先主者日益多，表疑其心，陰禦之。」[21]

The Tan Creek episode is found only in the annotation to this passage, in the 《世語》:

> 「備屯樊城，劉表禮焉，憚其為人，不甚信用。曾請備宴會，蒯越、蔡瑁欲因會取備，備覺之，偽如廁，潛遁出。所乘馬名的盧，騎的盧走，墮襄陽城西檀溪水中，溺不得出。備急曰：『的盧：今日厄矣，可努力！』的盧乃一踴三丈，遂得過，乘桴渡河，中流而追者至，以表意謝之，曰：『何去之速乎！』」[1]

So according to this account: Liu Bei was camped at Fancheng; at a banquet Liu Biao gave for him, Kuai Yue and Cai Mao plotted to seize him; he noticed, pretended to go to the privy, and slipped away on his horse Dilu; the horse fell into Tan Creek west of Xiangyang and could not get out; Liu Bei urged it on, and Dilu leaped three *zhang* and cleared the creek; pursuers caught up mid-river and apologized in Liu Biao's name.

## The credibility problem — stated in the annotation itself

Immediately after the 《世語》 passage, the same annotation records Sun Sheng's flat rejection:

> 「孫盛曰：此不然之言。備時羈旅，客主勢殊，若有此變，豈敢晏然終表之世而無釁故乎？此皆世俗妄說，非事實也。」[1]

Sun Sheng's argument: Liu Bei was then a guest sojourning in Jingzhou, with the host-guest power relationship heavily tilted against him; had such a change really occurred, how would he have dared to pass the rest of Liu Biao's lifetime calmly and without any rupture? Therefore, he says, this is vulgar hearsay, not fact.

**Inference (据此推断):** The basis is (i) the 《三国志》 main text records only that Liu Biao "secretly guarded against" Liu Bei and does not record any attempt on his life [21]; (ii) the leap story is preserved only in Pei's annotation, quoting the 《世語》[1]; (iii) the same annotation carries Sun Sheng's refutation [1]. From these, what can be concluded is: the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* transmits the story but does not endorse it, and a reader following the sources should treat the leap as unverified and doubted, not as established history. What cannot be concluded from these materials is that the event definitely did not happen — Sun Sheng's verdict is an argument about plausibility, not a rival factual account.
